items.content: ICML 2027 Call For Papers The 44th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2027) will be held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, July 31-August 6 , as an in-person event. In addition to the main conference sessions, the conference will include tutorials, workshops and an expo. We invite submissions of papers on original and rigorous research of significant interest to the machine learning community for the main conference proceedings. All papers will be reviewed in a double-blind process and accepted papers will be presented at the conference. Papers must be prepared and submitted as a single file: 8 pages for the main paper, with unlimited pages for references, the impact statement, and appendices. There will be no separate deadline for the submission of supplementary material. The final versions of accepted papers will be allowed one extra page for the main paper. Note: ICML is planning to make some updates to the submission process (but not the submission format). We will announce them by late November, please stay tuned. Change in policy: two-stage reviewing process: ICML 2027 will review submissions in two stages. In the first stage, the area chair assigned to each paper decides whether it should proceed to the second stage. Papers that would clearly not be accepted receive a first-stage rejection. Every proposed first-stage reject must be confirmed by a senior area chair, and when in doubt, papers go to full review. Authors of papers that receive a first-stage rejection will be notified by February 23, 2027 with a short justification. All other papers go through the usual review process, and final decisions will be announced on May 3, 2027. This process is similar to the expedited initial review used by many top journals, where an editor or senior reviewer assesses whether a submission is sufficiently competitive to warrant a full round of external review. We recognize that any early-stage review process carries some risk that a good paper could be rejected prematurely. The requirement that every first-stage rejection be reviewed by both an AC and an SAC, together with the principle that papers should proceed to full review whenever there is doubt, is intended to minimize this risk. The goal of this process is to reduce the number of low-quality papers that go through full review. Change in policy: contribution type in submission/reviewing: ICML 2027 asks all authors to select the Contribution Type that best reflects the primary scientific contribution of their submission. The available types are General (most papers) , Theory , Application-driven , Concept and Feasibility , Negative Results , Datasets, Evaluations and Benchmarks, and Position papers. Contribution types were introduced at NeurIPS 2026. They will be used to help guide reviewing and as one factor in reviewer and Area Chair matching. Authors should select the type that best represents the main contribution of the paper, recognizing that submissions may naturally contain elements of multiple types. Please see the full ICML 2027 Contribution Types Policy and Guidance for detailed descriptions and reviewing expectations. Change in policy: LLM use in Reviewing: ICML 2027 will use a single policy for LLM use in reviewing, corresponding to Policy B of ICML 2026. In short, reviewers may use privacy-compliant LLMs to help understand the paper and related works and to polish their reviews. Delegating judgement and critique of the paper to LLMs is not allowed, and reviewers remain fully responsible for the content of their reviews. A single policy simplifies reviewer assignment and activities permitted under policy B have broad support even among authors/reviewers that chose policy A at ICML 2026 (see the paper ). The findings from ICML 2026 also suggest that effect of policy B on paper outcomes is minimal. Details and precise guidance for the reviewers are given on the LLM policy page . Change in policy: Use of Generative AI by Authors & Disclosure Policy ICML 2027 requires authors to disclose substantive use of generative AI tools in conducting the research or preparing the submission. This includes uses such as research ideation, mathematical reasoning, experimental design, code generation, data analysis, literature synthesis, and substantial manuscript drafting. Routine editorial assistance, such as spelling, grammar, formatting, and minor clarity edits, does not require disclosure. All submissions must include an AI Disclosure Statement. The statement does not count toward the paper page limit. Authors remain fully responsible for the correctness, originality, and integrity of all submitted content, including any material produced with AI assistance. When generative AI is part of the research methodology itself, its use must also be described in the paper with sufficient detail to understand and reproduce the work. Please see the full ICML 2027 Policy on the Use of Generative AI by Authors for requirements, examples, and guidance. Change in policy: Submission caps and reciprocal reviewing policy. Similar to ICLR 2027, ICML 2027 introduces submission quotas and strengthens reciprocal reviewing to cope with the growth in submissions. No author may appear on more than 20 submissions. Each submission must designate one of its authors as reciprocal reviewer, and an author can be designated as the reciprocal reviewer for at most 6 submissions. Each author may appear on at most one submission in which no author is an eligible reciprocal reviewer. Authors with 3 or more submissions must also serve on the program committee, as a reviewer, area chair or senior area chair. This also means that since serving on the program committee in any role requires meeting the reciprocal reviewer eligibility criteria, an author who does not meet them may appear on at most 2 submissions. Submissions that do not meet these requirements will be desk rejected. Eligibility criteria and further details are given in the guide on Submission Quotas and Reciprocal Reviewing . Please review Author Instructions , an Example Paper , and use the correct Style Files . Submitted papers that do not conform to these policies will be rejected without review. Topics of interest include (but are not limited to): general machine learning (active learning, clustering, online learning, ranking, supervised, semi- and self-supervised learning, time series analysis, etc.) deep learning (architectures, generative models, theory, etc.) evaluation (methodology, meta studies, replicability and validity, human-in-the-loop, etc.) theory of machine learning (statistical learning theory, bandits, game theory, decision theory, etc.) machine learning systems (improved implementation and scalability, hardware, libraries, distributed methods, etc.) optimization (convex and non-convex optimization, matrix/tensor methods, stochastic, online, non-smooth, composite, etc.) probabilistic methods (Bayesian methods, graphical models, Monte Carlo methods, etc.) reinforcement learning (decision and control, planning, hierarchical RL, robotics, etc.) trustworthy machine learning (reliability, causality, fairness, interpretability, privacy, robustness, safety, etc.) application-driven machine learning (innovative techniques, problems, and datasets that are of interest to the machine learning community and driven by the needs of end-users in applications such as healthcare, physical sciences, biosciences, social sciences, sustainability, and climate etc.) Similar to last year, we also invite submissions of position papers (see the call for paper ). This year, we adopt a simplified procedure: Position papers are submitted through the main track by selecting “Position Paper” as the Contribution Type. Papers published at ICML are indexed in the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research through the Journal of Machine Learning Research. We are recruiting reviewers: if you would like to volonteer, please fill this form: Self-nomination form for reviewing Important Dates and Submission Site Submission site opens: January 8, 2027. Suggested OpenReview account creation deadline: December 31, 2026 AOE. (If you do not already have an OpenReview account, please register by this date, otherwise we cannot guarantee that your account will be activated in time.**) Abstract submission deadline: January 14, 2027 11:59 PM AOE or Full paper submission deadline: January 22, 2027 11:59 PM AOE or Abstracts and papers can be submitted through OpenReview: https://openreview.net/group?id=ICML.cc/2027/Conference ** OpenReview: All authors must have an OpenReview account. It is strongly recommended that you sign up for OpenReview (or associate your existing account) with an institutional email. If you sign up for OpenReview with an institutional email, your account will be activated immediately; otherwise it can take up to two weeks for your account to be activated. Policies Optional in-Person Attendance Attendance for authors of accepted papers is optional. After acceptance notifications, the authors will be able to decide by a specified date whether they wish to present their paper in person at the conference or they just wish to include their paper in the proceedings (without presentation at the conference). Regardless of this choice, all the accepted papers will receive equivalent treatment in the proceedings. They will all be eligible for ICML awards as well as for the designations of distinction corresponding to the past “oral presentations” and “spotlight posters.” For proceedings-only papers, at least one of the authors must obtain virtual registration. Deadlines Abstract and paper submission deadlines are strict. In no circumstances will extensions be given. Changes to Abstract/Title/Authorship Authors should include a full title for their paper, complete author list, and complete abstract in the submission form by the abstract submission deadline. While it is possible to edit the title and abstract until the full paper submission deadline, submissions with “placeholder” abstracts that are substantially rewritten for the full submission risk being removed without consideration. The author list cannot be changed after the abstract deadline. After the abstract deadline, authors may be reordered, but not added or removed. Double-Blind Review All submissions must be anonymized and may not contain any information with the intention or consequence of violating the double-blind reviewing policy. Authors are allowed to post versions of their work on preprint servers such as arXiv. They are also allowed to give talks on the work(s) submitted to ICML during the review. However, under no circumstances should the work be advertised as an ICML submission at any time during the review period, i.e., from the time the authors submit the paper to the communication of the accept/reject decisions. If the authors have posted or plan to post a non-anonymized version of the paper online before the ICML decisions are made, the submitted version must not refer to the non-anonymized version. Dual and Concurrent Submission Authors may not submit papers that are identical, or substantially similar, to versions that have been previously published, accepted for publication, or submitted in parallel to other conferences or journals. Such submissions violate our dual submission policy, and the organizers have the right to reject such submissions, or to remove them from the proceedings. Any concurrent ICML submissions with an overlapping set of authors will also be treated as prior work (so, for example, if publishing one would render the other too incremental, then this may be considered grounds for rejection). Note that submissions that have been or are being presented at workshops without published proceedings do not violate the dual-submission policy. Reviewing Criteria Submissions should report original and rigorous research of significant interest to the machine learning community. All claims must be clearly stated and supported by reproducible experiments and/or sound theoretical analysis. The contributions must be situated in the context of the broader scientific and machine learning research literature, acknowledging and differentiating from relevant prior works as appropriate. See Reviewer Instructions for more information. Ethical Conduct for Peer Review Authors are expected to follow standard ethical conduct for peer review. In particular: Plagiarism in any form is forbidden. Prompt injection is forbidden. Advertising work (e.g., in a talk, on social media) as being under submission to ICML during the review period is forbidden. Any form of collusion, whether explicit or tacit (e.g., where authors cooperate with reviewers, ACs, or SACs to obtain favorable or unfavorable reviews) is forbidden. If you believe someone may be engaging in unethical conduct, please notify ICML by filling out the Ethics Violation Reporting form . You can also report suspected violations to program-chairs@icml.cc . All suspected unethical behaviors will be investigated by program chairs, integrity chair, or the ICML Oversight Committee, and individuals found violating the rules may face sanctions and/or have their submissions rejected. We will also collect names of individuals who are found to have violated ethics standards; if individuals representing conferences, journals, or other organizations request this list for decision-making purposes, we may make this information available to them. See Peer-review Ethics for additional details. Impact Statements Authors are required to include a statement of the potential broader impact of their work, including its ethical aspects and future societal consequences. This statement should be in a separate section at the end of the paper (co-located with Acknowledgements, before References), and does not count toward the paper page limit. In many cases, where the ethical impacts and expected societal implications are those that are well established when advancing the field of machine learning, substantial discussion is not required, and a simple statement such as: “This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.” The above statement can be used verbatim in such cases, but we encourage authors to think about whether there is content that does warrant further discussion, as this statement will be apparent if the paper is later flagged for ethics review. In particular, Reviewers and ACs may flag submissions for ethics review. Flagged submissions will be sent to an ethics review committee for comments. Ethics reviewers do not have the authority to reject papers, but in extreme cases, papers may be rejected by the program chairs on ethical grounds, regardless of scientific quality or contribution. For tips on writing the impact statement, see this post written for NeurIPS 2020 . Lay Summaries Authors of accepted papers will be required to submit a short “lay summary” of their work (also called "plain language summary") in OpenReview when submitting their camera-ready paper. As machine learning is becoming a more prevalent topic of interest in society, it is important to participate in science communication with the public. See this paper for guidelines. Additional details and examples will be provided prior to the camera-ready deadline. Self-Rankings Continuing the practice introduced at ICML 2026, authors with multiple submissions will be required to provide a self-assessment of the quality of their own submissions through a ranking. Disagreements between author rankings and reviewer scores will be used to flag papers that may warrant additional attention from area chairs and to help guide the assignment of emergency reviewers. Submitted self-rankings will be accessible only to the program chairs, associate program chairs, and integrity chairs. Area chairs will have access only to a coarse measure of disagreement between author rankings and reviewer scores. # Nov. 13th: initial version # Nov. 17h: clarification added "Since serving on the program committee in any role requires meeting the reciprocal reviewer eligibility criteria, an author who does not meet them may appear on at most 2 submissions." # Nov. 20th: call for position papers is out. Added position paper as contribution type.

Each submission must designate one of its authors as reciprocal reviewer, and an author can be designated as the reciprocal reviewer for at most 6 submissions. Each author may appear on at most one submission in which no author is an eligible reciprocal reviewer. Authors with 3 or more submissions must also serve on the program committee, as a reviewer, area chair or senior area chair. This also means that since serving on the program committee in any role requires meeting the reciprocal reviewer eligibility criteria, an author who does not meet them may appear on at most 2 submissions. Submissions that do not meet these requirements will be desk rejected. Eligibility criteria and further details are given in the guide on Submission Quotas and Reciprocal Reviewing . Please review Author Instructions , an Example Paper , and use the correct Style Files . Submitted papers that do not conform to these policies will be rejected without review. Topics of interest include (but are not limited to): general machine learning (active learning, clustering, online learning, ranking, supervised, semi- and self-supervised learning, time series analysis, etc.) deep learning (architectures, generative models, theory, etc.) evaluation (methodology, meta studies, replicability and validity, human-in-the-loop, etc.) theory of machine learning (statistical learning theory, bandits, game theory, decision theory, etc.) machine learning systems (improved implementation and scalability, hardware, libraries, distributed methods, etc.) optimization (convex and non-convex optimization, matrix/tensor methods, stochastic, online, non-smooth, composite, etc.) probabilistic methods (Bayesian methods, graphical models, Monte Carlo methods, etc.) reinforcement learning (decision and control, planning, hierarchical RL, robotics, etc.) trustworthy machine learning (reliability, causality, fairness, interpretability, privacy, robustness, safety, etc.) application-driven machine learning (innovative techniques, problems, and datasets that are of interest to the machine learning community and driven by the needs of end-users in applications such as healthcare, physical sciences, biosciences, social sciences, sustainability, and climate etc.) Similar to last year, we also invite submissions of position papers (see the call for paper ). This year, we adopt a simplified procedure: Position papers are submitted through the main track by selecting “Position Paper” as the Contribution Type. Papers published at ICML are indexed in the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research through the Journal of Machine Learning Research. We are recruiting reviewers: if you would like to volonteer, please fill this form: Self-nomination form for reviewing Important Dates and Submission Site Submission site opens: January 8, 2027. Suggested OpenReview account creation deadline: December 31, 2026 AOE. (If you do not already have an OpenReview account, please register by this date, otherwise we cannot guarantee that your account will be activated in time.**) Abstract submission deadline: January 14, 2027 11:59 PM AOE or Full paper submission deadline: January 22, 2027 11:59 PM AOE or Abstracts and papers can be submitted through OpenReview: https://openreview.net/group?id=ICML.cc/2027/Conference ** OpenReview: All authors must have an OpenReview account. It is strongly recommended that you sign up for OpenReview (or associate your existing account) with an institutional email. If you sign up for OpenReview with an institutional email, your account will be activated immediately; otherwise it can take up to two weeks for your account to be activated. Policies Optional in-Person Attendance Attendance for authors of accepted papers is optional. After acceptance notifications, the authors will be able to decide by a specified date whether they wish to present their paper in person at the conference or they just wish to include their paper in the proceedings (without presentation at the conference). Regardless of this choice, all the accepted papers will receive equivalent treatment in the proceedings. They will all be eligible for ICML awards as well as for the designations of distinction corresponding to the past “oral presentations” and “spotlight posters.” For proceedings-only papers, at least one of the authors must obtain virtual registration. Deadlines Abstract and paper submission deadlines are strict. In no circumstances will extensions be given. Changes to Abstract/Title/Authorship Authors should include a full title for their paper, complete author list, and complete abstract in the submission form by the abstract submission deadline. While it is possible to edit the title and abstract until the full paper submission deadline, submissions with “placeholder” abstracts that are substantially rewritten for the full submission risk being removed without consideration. The author list cannot be changed after the abstract deadline. After the abstract deadline, authors may be reordered, but not added or removed. Double-Blind Review All submissions must be anonymized and may not contain any information with the intention or consequence of violating the double-blind reviewing policy. Authors are allowed to post versions of their work on preprint servers such as arXiv. They are also allowed to give talks on the work(s) submitted to ICML during the review. However, under no circumstances should the work be advertised as an ICML submission at any time during the review period, i.e., from the time the authors submit the paper to the communication of the accept/reject decisions. If the authors have posted or plan to post a non-anonymized version of the paper online before the ICML decisions are made, the submitted version must not refer to the non-anonymized version. Dual and Concurrent Submission Authors may not submit papers that are identical, or substantially similar, to versions that have been previously published, accepted for publication, or submitted in parallel to other conferences or journals. Such submissions violate our dual submission policy, and the organizers have the right to reject such submissions, or to remove them from the proceedings. Any concurrent ICML submissions with an overlapping set of authors will also be treated as prior work (so, for example, if publishing one would render the other too incremental, then this may be considered grounds for rejection). Note that submissions that have been or are being presented at workshops without published proceedings do not violate the dual-submission policy. Reviewing Criteria Submissions should report original and rigorous research of significant interest to the machine learning community. All claims must be clearly stated and supported by reproducible experiments and/or sound theoretical analysis. The contributions must be situated in the context of the broader scientific and machine learning research literature, acknowledging and differentiating from relevant prior works as appropriate. See Reviewer Instructions for more information. Ethical Conduct for Peer Review Authors are expected to follow standard ethical conduct for peer review. In particular: Plagiarism in any form is forbidden. Prompt injection is forbidden. Advertising work (e.g., in a talk, on social media) as being under submission to ICML during the review period is forbidden. Any form of collusion, whether explicit or tacit (e.g., where authors cooperate with reviewers, ACs, or SACs to obtain favorable or unfavorable reviews) is forbidden. If you believe someone may be engaging in unethical conduct, please notify ICML by filling out the Ethics Violation Reporting form . You can also report suspected violations to program-chairs@icml.cc . All suspected unethical behaviors will be investigated by program chairs, integrity chair, or the ICML Oversight Committee, and individuals found violating the rules may face sanctions and/or have their submissions rejected. We will also collect names of individuals who are found to have violated ethics standards; if individuals representing conferences, journals, or other organizations request this list for decision-making purposes, we may make this information available to them. See Peer-review Ethics for additional details. Impact Statements Authors are required to include a statement of the potential broader impact of their work, including its ethical aspects and future societal consequences. This statement should be in a separate section at the end of the paper (co-located with Acknowledgements, before References), and does not count toward the paper page limit. In many cases, where the ethical impacts and expected societal implications are those that are well established when advancing the field of machine learning, substantial discussion is not required, and a simple statement such as: “This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.” The above statement can be used verbatim in such cases, but we encourage authors to think about whether there is content that does warrant further discussion, as this statement will be apparent if the paper is later flagged for ethics review. In particular, Reviewers and ACs may flag submissions for ethics review. Flagged submissions will be sent to an ethics review committee for comments. Ethics reviewers do not have the authority to reject papers, but in extreme cases, papers may be rejected by the program chairs on ethical grounds, regardless of scientific quality or contribution. For tips on writing the impact statement, see this post written for NeurIPS 2020 . Lay Summaries Authors of accepted papers will be required to submit a short “lay summary” of their work (also called "plain language summary") in OpenReview when submitting their camera-ready paper. As machine learning is becoming a more prevalent topic of interest in society, it is important to participate in science communication with the public. See this paper for guidelines. Additional details and examples will be provided prior to the camera-ready deadline. Self-Rankings Continuing the practice introduced at ICML 2026, authors with multiple submissions will be required to provide a self-assessment of the quality of their own submissions through a ranking. Disagreements between author rankings and reviewer scores will be used to flag papers that may warrant additional attention from area chairs and to help guide the assignment of emergency reviewers. Submitted self-rankings will be accessible only to the program chairs, associate program chairs, and integrity chairs. Area chairs will have access only to a coarse measure of disagreement between author rankings and reviewer scores. # Nov. 13th: initial version # Nov. 17h: clarification added "Since serving on the program committee in any role requires meeting the reciprocal reviewer eligibility criteria, an author who does not meet them may appear on at most 2 submissions." # Nov. 20th: call for position papers is out. Added position paper as contribution type.

items.content: ICML 2027 Position Papers We invite the submission of position papers to be published at the ICML 2027 conference. Position papers make an argument for a viewpoint or perspective about what should be done, in contrast to main track papers, which report on advances that have already been accomplished. Position papers also generally adopt a meta-level perspective on the field of machine learning, with wider scope than any individual area. The review criteria for position papers differs from those of the main track. Submissions to the main ICML conference track emphasize original research and novel results. In contrast, submissions to the position paper track will be judged primarily on whether they present a compelling position that warrants greater exposure within the machine learning community (regardless of whether a reviewer agrees with the position). The goal of this track is to highlight papers that stimulate constructive, civil discussion on timely topics that need our community’s attention. Controversial topics are welcome. Position papers should meet standard ICML expectations for scholarship, including the use of evidence and reasoning to support all claims, inclusion of relevant background and context, and the attribution of others’ work via appropriate citations. To constitute a proper scientific contribution, a position must be non-obvious, falsifiable and defendable against credible alternatives. We discourage technical papers that have a minor persuasive element, as well as nontechnical papers that promote unsupported opinion. Accepted position papers will be presented at the conference (as oral talks or posters) and included in the conference proceedings. We want to hear your positions. What is the field getting right? Getting wrong? Position papers may address any aspect relevant to machine learning (ML), including but not limited to: Concerns about data legality, copyright, and intellectual property in ML The role of privacy in ML training and deployment The role of open-source versus closed-source ML models for research Regulation of ML technology (licensing, evaluation, disclosures, post-deployment monitoring, etc.) Ethical considerations when conducting ML research and deploying ML systems User guidance for responsible use of ML tools, services, applications, etc. What the next generation of ML researchers needs to know How we can improve the beneficial impact of our community’s work We encourage you to browse the position papers that were published at ICML 2026 for examples (and ideas to build on, or from which to offer an alternative position). Policies and Requirements All requirements and policies are identical to those of the main conference (see the main track Call for Papers ), with the following exceptions: The Title should state the position and start with “Position:”. The paper must include an “Alternative Views” section in the main body of the paper (not an appendix) that describes and addresses one or more credible (not strawmen) positions that are opposed to the paper’s position. The following are not required for position papers: Impact Statements (the position paper itself should explain the impact) Lay Summaries (the position paper itself should be accessible to the public) The self-ranking requirement. Helpful tips on writing position papers: Make sure the Title states the position. These hypothetical paper titles do state a position: "Position: Quantum Atelic Learning Methods Should Employ Psychic Insights" "Position: Stop Research on Psychic Properties of Machine Learning" while these versions do not: "Position: Psychic Quantum Atelic Learning" "Position: A Perspective on Psychic Quantum Atelic Learning" The Abstract should identify the paper as a position paper and briefly state the position (e.g., “This position paper argues that <statement of the position>.”) The Introduction should state the position, using bold text. We encourage the inclusion of a "Call to Action" section that identifies plausible steps to realizing the aims of the stated position. By the end of the paper the reader should know what steps should be taken by whom to bring about these desired outcomes. Papers that describe technical research without advocating a real position (e.g. “everyone should use my new and better learning algorithm”) are not responsive to this call and should instead be submitted to the main paper track. Submission Procedure This year, ICML adopts a simplified procedure: Position papers are submitted through the main track by selecting “Position Paper” as the Contribution Type. They are subject to the same submission quotas and reciprocal reviewing requirements as all other submissions, but are evaluated according to dedicated reviewing guidelines. Reviewing Criteria Position papers will be reviewed according to the following criteria, which differ from those employed by the main track. Position: The paper clearly states a position on machine learning, see example aspects listed earlier in this CFP. Papers that describe technical research without advocating a position are not responsive to this call and should instead be submitted to the main paper track. Support: The paper supports its position with clear reasoning and evidence where appropriate. Significance: The paper demonstrates that the position is important, in terms of scope, impact, timeliness, risks, benefits, etc. Discussion potential: The position is likely to inspire constructive, civil discussion within the ICML community. The reviewer need not agree with the stated position. Alternative views: The paper describes and addresses one or more credible (not strawmen) positions that are opposed to the paper’s position. Call to Action: The paper identifies plausible steps to realizing the aims of the stated position. By the end of the paper the reader should know what steps should be taken by whom to bring about these desired outcomes. Communication quality: The paper is well organized and clearly written. Context: The paper includes a discussion of (and citations to) literature and events relevant to the stated position. Questions? Please select "Position Paper Chairs" on the help form and submit your questions here: https://icml.cc/Help/Contact

items.content: Submission quotas and reciprocal reviewing The number of submissions to ICML keeps growing faster than the number of qualified reviewers. To keep the review process fair and informative for all authors, ICML 2027 introduces submission quotas and strengthens its reciprocal reviewing requirement. These rules are similar to those adopted by ICLR 2027. Submission quotas No author may appear as a co-author on more than 20 submissions. Each author may appear as a co-author on at most one submission in which no author is an eligible reciprocal reviewer (see below). In plain terms: if neither you nor any of your co-authors has published at one of the venues listed below, you may submit at most one paper to ICML 2027. We welcome submissions from researchers who are new to the field, and these submissions are reviewed like all others. Quotas are checked when abstracts are registered. Authors who exceed a quota will be notified after the abstract deadline and can fix the problem by withdrawing submissions before the full paper deadline (January 22, 2027). Author lists cannot be changed after the abstract deadline. If a quota is still exceeded at the full paper deadline, the program chairs will desk reject excess submissions at random until every author is within the quotas. Who is an eligible reciprocal reviewer An author is an eligible reciprocal reviewer if they have at least one paper accepted at one of the following venues by the abstract registration deadline (January 14, 2027): ICML, NeurIPS, ICLR, UAI, AISTATS, JMLR, TMLR (including Datasets and Benchmarks tracks), ACL, EMNLP, EACL, NAACL, IJCNLP-AACL (including Findings), Computational Linguistics, TACL COLM CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, TPAMI, AAAI, IJCAI, JAIR, 3DV ICRA, IROS, RSS, CoRL KDD COLT Other publications associated with these venues do not count. This includes workshop papers, position papers, short papers, system demonstrations, industry papers and blog posts. Eligibility is determined from OpenReview profiles, so all authors must keep their profiles complete and up to date, including their publications or DBLP link. Incorrect profile information may lead to desk rejection. Reciprocal reviewing requirement Per-submission requirement: each submission must designate one of its authors as its reciprocal reviewer when the abstract is registered. The designated author must: be an eligible reciprocal reviewer; register as a reviewer for ICML 2027; complete their assigned reviews during the reviewing period (February 24–March 16, 2027). An author can be designated as the reciprocal reviewer for at most 6 submissions. Submissions in which no author is eligible are exempt from this requirement, but they count toward the one-submission quota above. Per-author requirement: authors with 3 or more submissions must serve on the program committee of ICML 2027, as a reviewer, area chair or senior area chair. Authors who serve as area chairs, senior area chairs or members of the organizing committee meet this requirement through that role. This also means that since serving on the program committee in any role requires meeting the reciprocal reviewer eligibility criteria, an author who does not meet them may appear on at most 2 submissions. Responsibilities and enforcement Reciprocal reviewers have the same obligations as all other reviewers. They must follow the reviewing guidelines and the LLM policy, submit their reviews on time, and take part in the discussion with authors and area chairs. The program chairs may desk reject the submissions for which an author is the designated reciprocal reviewer if that author: does not submit their reviews; submits reviews of very low quality;. Submissions that do not designate an eligible reciprocal reviewer when one is available among their authors may also be desk rejected.

items.content: The European AI Office supports the development and adoption of trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (AI) solutions, while protecting people against risks. The European AI Office was established within the European Commission as the foundation for a single AI governance system. It supports the EU approach to AI , playing a key role in implementing the AI Act – especially for general-purpose AI (GPAI) – guaranteeing the health, safety and fundamental rights of people and providing legal certainty to businesses. It also enforces the rules for GPAI models and supports the governance bodies in Member States in their tasks. This is underpinned by the powers given to the Commission by the AI Act, including the ability to conduct evaluations of GPAI models, request information and measures from model providers, and apply sanctions. The AI Office also promotes an innovative ecosystem of trustworthy AI , to reap the societal and economic benefits. It ensures a strategic, coherent and effective European approach to AI at international level , becoming a global reference point. The Structure of the AI Office The AI Office employs more than 125 staff, including technology specialists, administrative assistants, lawyers, policy specialists, and economists. It has 6 units and 2 advisers, reflecting its mandate: “Excellence in AI and Robotics” - unit A1 “Regulation and Compliance” - unit A2 “AI Safety” - unit A3 “AI Innovation and Policy Coordination” - unit A4 “AI for Societal Good” - unit A5 "AI in Health and Life Science" - unit A6 Lead Scientific Adviser International Affairs Adviser Tasks of the AI Office Supporting the AI Act and enforcing general-purpose AI rules The AI Office makes use of its expertise to support the implementation and enforcement of the AI Act by: Contributing to the coherent application of the AI Act across the Member States, including the set-up of advisory bodies at EU level, facilitating support and information exchange Developing tools, methodologies and benchmarks for evaluating capabilities and reach of general-purpose AI models, and classifying models with systemic risks Drawing up state-of-the-art codes of practice to detail out rules, in cooperation with leading AI developers, the scientific community and other experts Preparing guidance and guidelines, implementing and delegated acts , and other tools to support effective implementation of the AI Act and monitor compliance with the regulation Investigating possible infringements of the rules, including inspections, requests for technical documentation and access to models in order to assess models' capabilities Requesting providers to take corrective action and, in case of infringement, restrict the public availability of a model and issue direct fines for non-compliance Strengthening the development and use of trustworthy AI The AI Office, in collaboration with relevant public and private actors and the startup community, contributes to fostering trustworthy AI across the EU by: Advancing actions and policies to reap the societal and economic benefits of AI across the EU Providing advice on best practices and enabling ready-access to AI sandboxes, real-world testing and other European support structures for AI uptake Encouraging innovative ecosystems of trustworthy AI to enhance the EU’s competitiveness and economic growth Aiding the Commission in leveraging the use of transformative AI The European AI Office was established within the European Commission as the foundation for a single AI governance system. It supports the EU approach to AI , playing a key role in implementing the AI Act – especially for general-purpose AI (GPAI) – guaranteeing the health, safety and fundamental rights of people and providing legal certainty to businesses. It also enforces the rules for GPAI models and supports the governance bodies in Member States in their tasks. This is underpinned by the powers given to the Commission by the AI Act, including the ability to conduct evaluations of GPAI models, request information and measures from model providers, and apply sanctions. The AI Office also promotes an innovative ecosystem of trustworthy AI , to reap the societal and economic benefits. It ensures a strategic, coherent and effective European approach to AI at international level , becoming a global reference point. The Structure of the AI Office The AI Office employs more than 125 staff, including technology specialists, administrative assistants, lawyers, policy specialists, and economists. It has 6 units and 2 advisers, reflecting its mandate: “Excellence in AI and Robotics” - unit A1 “Regulation and Compliance” - unit A2 “AI Safety” - unit A3 “AI Innovation and Policy Coordination” - items.content: Featured projects TL;DR At the Singapore vLLM meetup, engineers from Inferact, NVIDIA, and Alibaba Cloud showcased how the community is advancing open source AI inference through pipeline parallelism optimizations, agent-written kernels, real-time multimodal world models, and day-zero support for next-generation hardware like NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin platform. Introduction On November 13, 2026, the vLLM community gathered at SGInnovate in Singapore for a half-day technical meetup hosted by Inferact and NVIDIA. Engineers from Inferact, NVIDIA and Alibaba Cloud, together with vLLM-Omni contributors, shared what they are building right now, from high-throughput prefill and RL training to running vLLM on workstation-class Blackwell GPUs and NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin platform. vLLM, born at UC Berkeley and now hosted under the PyTorch Foundation, serves hundreds of model architectures across a wide range of accelerators. Two themes ran through the day: squeezing throughput out of communication-bound layouts, and using AI agents to write and tune kernels. Highlights from the Meetup 1. Optimizing Pipeline Parallelism for High-Throughput Prefill in vLLM Thien Tran, Member of Technical Staff from Inferact made the case for pipeline parallelism (PP) as a throughput layout for prefill. In agentic traffic, one turn carries roughly 100K input tokens (about 95% cached), so a 3 s time-to-first-token (TTFT) target for 5K new tokens leaves a per-token budget about 33× tighter than decode’s. On MiniMax-M3.1-Flash on 2× GB300, PP2 delivered up to 1.37× the max throughput of TEP2 + SP, because PP removes most of the collectives that compete with compute. Thien walked through the fixes that make PP work in practice: balancing stages by measured time rather than layer count, capping step size to shrink pipeline fill and drain, and moving activation transfers onto the copy engines, which cut p50 TTFT by 13–20% near saturation and is now on by default on NVLink. With fixed step sizes, TEP2 + SP still wins at tight TTFT targets (0.75 s) while PP2 wins at looser ones. A new PP-aware scheduler sizes each micro-batch from the queue, matches the best hand-tuned step size with no tuning, and puts PP2 ahead from about 0.5 s upward. 2. vLLM on SM12x: From Usable to Efficient Jie Fang, DevTech Compute Engineer from NVIDIA showed how SM12x cards (RTX PRO and DGX Spark) went in six months from having no DeepSeek-V4 path in vLLM to near-peak efficiency. FlashInfer feature categories with dedicated SM12x kernels grew from 0 of 17 in January to 14 in October, and monthly SM12x pull requests rose from 6 to 121, helped by AI coding agents. Kernels only help if the framework selects them: a one-line dispatch fix gave +17.7% throughput, and preferring W4A4 for NVFP4 linears gave +23.8%. These cards have PCIe Gen5 but no NVLink, so the choice of parallelism sets the communication cost. TP2 × PP2 instead of TP4 gave 1.37× prefill throughput, and communication-aware weight offloading let DeepSeek-V4-Pro start on 8× RTX PRO 6000. The headline results: a 32K-token prefill in 939 ms on 8× RTX PRO 5000, MoE decode reading weights at 98–99% of measured DRAM peak, and video generation cut from 213.4 s to 4.92 s for a 5.17 s clip, a real-time factor of 0.95. 3. Making World Models Interactive: Real-Time Inference with vLLM-Omni Taichang Zhou, a vLLM-Omni committer, showed how vLLM-Omni, which extends vLLM from text-only models to omni-modality models and supports 100+ architectures, now serves LingBot-World 2.0, an interactive video world model, in real time for one session on 4× H200. The key piece is a new AR-Diffusion engine that reuses vLLM’s paged KV cache manager to generate video chunk by chunk. The rule of thumb is KV lifetime: if K/V lives for one request, the model runs on the DiffusionEngine; if it lives for a whole interactive session, it runs on the new engine. Ulysses sequence parallelism cut one block on H200 from 2,397 ms to 725 ms. Per 12-frame chunk, the latest main is 1.9× faster than September with no quality loss, and 2.75× faster (22.5 fps) with every opt-in option, well above the 12 fps real-time bar. The team also previewed Noisy PP, which lets later chunks start on earlier chunks’ in-progress KV and lifted steady-state throughput 2.85× on CausVid-Wan 1.3B, and announced OpenDirector, an open-source video agent built on vLLM-Omni. 4. Finish RL Training Faster: Zero-Mismatch Kernels and Simple Async RL Ao Shen, Member of Technical Staff from Inferact, presenting joint work with NVIDIA DevTech and NVIDIA Research, argued that an RL trainer must learn from exactly what the rollout produced. Floating-point addition is not associative, so vLLM rollout kernels and trainer kernels split the same sum differently and drift apart. On DeepSeek V4, standard kernels showed rising KL mismatch and the run collapsed within about 100 RL steps, while exact kernels held KL at 0. The team brought the cost of exact kernels down to about 10% of rollout speed with an agent loop that first makes each layer match bit for bit, then swaps in faster kernels and re-checks that the diff stays zero. The skill is open source and worked on Nemotron, DeepSeek V4.1 and Kimi K3.1, where zero diff was ready on the day the model came out. With exact kernels, async RL no longer needs clipping, gates or dropped samples: REINFORCE Zero simply reweights every token, reaching 48.80% accuracy against 48.91% for sync RL while cutting time per update from 49.4 s to 20.6 s, a 2.40× speedup. 5. vLLM on NVIDIA Vera Rubin: Architecture, Locality Domains and Kernels Hao Lu, Software Engineer from NVIDIA, speaking for a joint effort of the vLLM team, Inferact, Red Hat and NVIDIA, explained that vLLM ran on Vera Rubin from day 0 because Blackwell kernels run unchanged, but peak performance needs Rubin-specific kernels such as double-K MMA. The central idea is that Rubin behaves like a NUMA GPU: each of its two dies is a locality domain with its own SMs, L2 and HBM4 stacks, and by default about half of a kernel’s memory traffic crosses the L2 fabric. The rule is to co-locate memory and compute, and to query the locality-domain count rather than assume it. In vLLM, localizing MoE experts in decode brings the most benefit, and memory-bound decode kernels gained 8–29%, with TMA load rising from 13.4 to 18.7 TB/s against a 19.2 TB/s HBM peak. On InferenceX, MiniMax M3.1-Flash on Vera Rubin NVL72 reached about 4.3~6.5× the tokens per dollar of GB300 at matched interactivity. 6. Enterprise Scale Agent Infra Sean Zhan, Senior Director from Alibaba Cloud International, shared the session Enterprise Scale Agent Infra. As enterprise software shifts from “humans calling tools” to “agents executing autonomously,” risk and cost are moving down from the model layer to the execution layer. Agents need to run concurrently, mutate system state, and hold real credentials — every execution is a security-boundary event. MicroVMs deliver hardware-grade isolation, least-privilege policies constrain network egress and credentials, full audit trails make every action replayable, and snapshotting and hibernation make million-scale concurrency economically viable. Sean shared many insightful ideas during this session. Closing Thoughts From faster prefill and efficient support for new hardware to AI agents that write and tune kernels, this meetup showed a vLLM community that keeps pushing the boundaries of inference, together with its partners across the ecosystem. Our thanks go to Inferact and NVIDIA for hosting, to all the speakers, and to everyone who joined us at SGInnovate. As the core engine grows stronger and the hardware ecosystem keeps expanding, vLLM is becoming a solid foundation for putting large models into real-world use. We look forward to our next gathering and to the continued growth of the vLLM community!

The team also previewed Noisy PP, which lets later chunks start on earlier chunks’ in-progress KV and lifted steady-state throughput 2.85× on CausVid-Wan 1.3B, and announced OpenDirector, an open-source video agent built on vLLM-Omni. 4. Finish RL Training Faster: Zero-Mismatch Kernels and Simple Async RL Ao Shen, Member of Technical Staff from Inferact, presenting joint work with NVIDIA DevTech and NVIDIA Research, argued that an RL trainer must learn from exactly what the rollout produced. Floating-point addition is not associative, so vLLM rollout kernels and trainer kernels split the same sum differently and drift apart. On DeepSeek V4, standard kernels showed rising KL mismatch and the run collapsed within about 100 RL steps, while exact kernels held KL at 0. The team brought the cost of exact kernels down to about 10% of rollout speed with an agent loop that first makes each layer match bit for bit, then swaps in faster kernels and re-checks that the diff stays zero. The skill is open source and worked on Nemotron, DeepSeek V4.1 and Kimi K3.1, where zero diff was ready on the day the model came out. With exact kernels, async RL no longer needs clipping, gates or dropped samples: REINFORCE Zero simply reweights every token, reaching 48.80% accuracy against 48.91% for sync RL while cutting time per update from 49.4 s to 20.6 s, a 2.40× speedup. 5. vLLM on NVIDIA Vera Rubin: Architecture, Locality Domains and Kernels Hao Lu, Software Engineer from NVIDIA, speaking for a joint effort of the vLLM team, Inferact, Red Hat and NVIDIA, explained that vLLM ran on Vera Rubin from day 0 because Blackwell kernels run unchanged, but peak performance needs Rubin-specific kernels such as double-K MMA. The central idea is that Rubin behaves like a NUMA GPU: each of its two dies is a locality domain with its own SMs, L2 and HBM4 stacks, and by default about half of a kernel’s memory traffic crosses the L2 fabric. The rule is to co-locate memory and compute, and to query the locality-domain count rather than assume it. In vLLM, localizing MoE experts in decode brings the most benefit, and memory-bound decode kernels gained 8–29%, with TMA load rising from 13.4 to 18.7 TB/s against a 19.2 TB/s HBM peak. On InferenceX, MiniMax M3.1-Flash on Vera Rubin NVL72 reached about 4.3~6.5× the tokens per dollar of GB300 at matched interactivity. 6. Enterprise Scale Agent Infra Sean Zhan, Senior Director from Alibaba Cloud International, shared the session Enterprise Scale Agent Infra. As enterprise software shifts from “humans calling tools” to “agents executing autonomously,” risk and cost are moving down from the model layer to the execution layer. Agents need to run concurrently, mutate system state, and hold real credentials — every execution is a security-boundary event. MicroVMs deliver hardware-grade isolation, least-privilege policies constrain network egress and credentials, full audit trails make every action replayable, and snapshotting and hibernation make million-scale concurrency economically viable. Sean shared many insightful ideas during this session. Closing Thoughts From faster prefill and efficient support for new hardware to AI agents that write and tune kernels, this meetup showed a vLLM community that keeps pushing the boundaries of inference, together with its partners across the ecosystem. Our thanks go to Inferact and NVIDIA for hosting, to all the speakers, and to everyone who joined us at SGInnovate. As the core engine grows stronger and the hardware ecosystem keeps expanding, vLLM is becoming a solid foundation for putting large models into real-world use. We look forward to our next gathering and to the continued growth of the vLLM community!

items.content: Back to Articles Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference Enterprise + Article Published November 26, 2026 Upvote 3 Ryan Chesler emelryan Follow nvidia Marek Wawrzos mwawrzos Follow nvidia Steve Han steve-nvidia Follow nvidia We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse , a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents. Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference . We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion. What Parse 3.5 produces Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications. Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation. This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process. We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training : Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples : rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values. Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples : rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships. OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples : synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading. Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language. Figure 2. Parse recovers 18, 27, 39, and 54 from the chart geometry SFT teaches the capability; RLVR improves consistency We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading a page and representing its contents. We then continued with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) , using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) . Rewards check the quality of sampled extractions. For example, a chart extraction can earn a better reward for recovering the correct series and values, producing a usable structure, and finishing without repeatedly generating the same content. A difficult page can have several valid representations. These checks give the model flexibility to find a correct answer without prescribing one exact token sequence, while discouraging looping and unfinished output. Figure 3. A controlled comparison of SFT and GRPO with matched evaluation settings. These are development checkpoints, separate from the final released model. Loop counts use a repetition check. Methods . The matched comparison shows the benefit: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages—about 77% fewer —and outputs reaching the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35 . Overall score improves from 66.24 to 71.38 , including +5.18 points in tables and +4.15 in charts . Faster inference through architecture and DFlash2 A parser must generate substantial text and structure for every page. Alongside the training work, we optimized how Parse 3.5 processes images and decodes those outputs. Component Parse 2.0 Parse 3.5 Page preprocessing Fixed 2048 × 1664 canvas NaViT dynamic rectangular inputs Image-to-text connection Encoder–decoder cross-attention Compressed visual tokens as a causal prefix Decoder self-attention Multi-head attention GQA-8: 16 query heads, 8 key/value heads Speculative decoding One-token lookahead (MTP); optional DFlash2 NaViT preprocessing adapts the input shape to the page. A visual adapter compresses the image sequence, and the text decoder consumes it as a prefix, replacing encoder–decoder cross-attention. Grouped-query attention with eight key/value heads (GQA-8) reduces the decoder’s attention-cache memory. The built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head supplies one-token lookahead. Our DFlash2 speculator goes further: a small draft model proposes up to 32 tokens ahead , and Parse verifies the proposals together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it averages about 14 accepted draft tokens , or roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step including the target token. Figure 4. Native single-pass throughput on one H200, BF16, using the same 2,078 pages. Parse 2.0 uses one trial per point; Parse 3.5 shows three-trial medians. Arrows show the gain from Parse 3.5 base to DFlash2. Measurement details . In the native single-pass benchmark on one H200 in BF16, DFlash2 increased throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512, compared with Parse 3.5 with speculative decoding disabled. At 512, Parse 3.5 reaches 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 20.44 pages/s with DFlash2, versus 2.98 for Parse 2.0. Those are 4.53× and 6.86× the Parse 2.0 throughput, respectively. Fast parsing gives us room to revisit difficult regions. Start with a full-page prediction, then add focused reprocessing where the document needs it: Single pass - Parse the full page once for text, layout, tables, and charts. Double pass - use for dense tables and small chart details. Crop the table and chart regions found by the parser, re-parse them at higher detail, and merge the refinements into the page output. Triple pass - Instead of only using the models full page parsing bounding boxes, use a second pass of the model in detection mode in order to get verification that all boxes have been accurately found and text has not been missed and re-extract any found charts or tables in a third pass Figure 5. Additional stages focus computation on difficult regions. Multiple crops can require multiple requests. In the published reference evaluation, double and triple pass add 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass. The additional work lets applications trade some throughput for better extraction in difficult regions. Reference results and serving measurements . Apply the same SFT/RLVR approach to your documents We are sharing a Parse fine-tuning recipe that takes developers through paired data generation, NeMo Automodel SFT , and NeMo RL GRPO , using vLLM to generate candidate answers. The worked example uses a synthetic dental form with an odontogram : a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces. Before adaptation, Parse reads the printed tooth numbers but misses the intended procedure table. SFT teaches it to associate each marked tooth with a procedure and its placement on the tooth. Figure 6. A recorded recipe example: after SFT, all six chart rows match the target. Full image and native training label . RLVR then reinforces accuracy and consistent completion. In the dental reference run, the estimated first-attempt success rate (sampled pass@1) rose from 0.00% for the base model to 95.85% after SFT and 96.58% after RLVR. Figure 7. Matched evaluation on 256 held-out forms from the same synthetic generator, with eight samples per page. Success requires natural completion, exact chart content, and error-free normalized page text. Evaluation protocol . To adapt the recipe, supply your own image/label pairs and a verifier: checks that determine whether an extraction is correct. The included document reward components cover text fidelity, bounding boxes, tables, chart facts, and completion. Combine the components relevant to your task, add schema checks, and use completion and repetition checks to discourage looping or unfinished output. We are excited that the community has extended and improved Parse for Thai , Persian/Farsi , and Arabic already and we hope that these additional datasets and fine-tuning recipes will help encourage these efforts and future models. We thank Denis Ovchinnikov for his work on vLLM integration and independent performance validation, Oliver Holworthy for improving the fine-tuning recipe's runtime setup and reproducibility, and Bo Liu for technical review. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.34841 (cs) [Submitted on 25 Nov 2026] Title: Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent: Self-Structuring Learning through Question Answering Authors: Masahiro Kato View a PDF of the paper titled Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent: Self-Structuring Learning through Question Answering, by Masahiro Kato View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: We consider the problem of constructing knowledge bases for applications based on large language models, in which the structure of a knowledge base determines how an application can retrieve and connect the information needed to answer a question. We study Self-Structuring Learning, a setting in which questions and expected answers guide the construction of a persistent knowledge base whose editable structure can be a graph schema or the organization of linked knowledge documents. We propose Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent, which diagnoses discrepancies between expected answers and responses obtained through the current knowledge base. At each round, the method proposes a structural edit, rebuilds the knowledge base, and adopts the edit when the learning loss decreases. The retained structure is evaluated on other questions about the same sources. By randomizing over candidate edits, we express the loss change of an edit as a derivative with respect to the probability of selecting it, and we evaluate joint edits as single candidates because their changes interact. Schema Descent instantiates the method for graph schemas. In experiments on large documents, each a bundle of research papers, the updated knowledge cards and graph schemas obtain higher mean Answer F1 on held-out generated questions than their initial structures, with schema gains in every document. On human questions, mean F1 rises for schemas and falls for cards: the updated structures serve the kind of question they were learned from. items.content: Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent: Self-Structuring Learning through Question Answering Masahiro Kato † † thanks: Email: mkato-csecon@g.ecc.u-tokyo.ac.jp Affiliation: The University of Tokyo November 25, 2026 Abstract We consider the problem of constructing knowledge bases for applications based on large language models, in which the structure of a knowledge base determines how an application can retrieve and connect the information needed to answer a question. We study Self-Structuring Learning, a setting in which questions and expected answers guide the construction of a persistent knowledge base whose editable structure can be a graph schema or the organization of linked knowledge documents. We propose Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent, which diagnoses discrepancies between expected answers and responses obtained through the current knowledge base. At each round, the method proposes a structural edit, rebuilds the knowledge base, and adopts the edit when the learning loss decreases. The retained structure is evaluated on other questions about the same sources. By randomizing over candidate edits, we express the loss change of an edit as a derivative with respect to the probability of selecting it, and we evaluate joint edits as single candidates because their changes interact. Schema Descent instantiates the method for graph schemas. In experiments on large documents, each a bundle of research papers, the updated knowledge cards and graph schemas obtain higher mean Answer F1 on held-out generated questions than their initial structures, with schema gains in every document. On human questions, mean F1 rises for schemas and falls for cards: the updated structures serve the kind of question they were learned from. Keywords: knowledge bases, retrieval-augmented generation, knowledge graphs, schema design, large language models 1 Introduction Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) connects a large language model (LLM) to external knowledge ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) , but the application can fail on a question even when its sources contain the answer. In our experiments, one question asks how much a proposed model improves on the strongest baseline. A knowledge graph built from the paper under an initial schema returns the model’s absolute scores and qualitative comparisons, and the application answers that the question is unanswerable. After the schema is changed so that one item keeps a comparison together with its reported improvement and conditions, the application answers with the gains stated in the paper. Whether a question can be answered thus depends on how the knowledge base divides and connects its content. Constructing a knowledge base requires decisions about the units of knowledge and their connections. A knowledge graph uses a schema to specify entity types and their relationships, and the Open Knowledge Format (OKF) packages knowledge as linked Markdown documents with typed metadata ( McVeety & Hormati, 2026 ) . Ontology engineering has long used application questions to guide these decisions ( Grüninger & Fox, 1995 ) . LLM-based systems now automate parts of construction: GraphRAG builds a graph and community summaries from text, while AutoSchemaKG induces schemas during extraction ( Edge et al., 2025 ; Bai et al., 2026 ) . A knowledge base built in either way still has to be judged by the answers it gives, so we take the questions that the application must answer as the objective of construction. These questions can be prepared before the application is deployed: its specification describes the expected behavior, and during development a model can read the source material directly and help prepare questions with supported answers. When the application answers the same questions through its knowledge base, the differences from the supported answers point to changes in the stored knowledge and its organization. Checking the sources this closely is affordable during development, since the resulting structure and content then serve every later request. We call this learning setting Self-Structuring Learning . Within it, we propose Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent , which uses answer discrepancies to propose an edit, measures its effect after reconstruction, and adopts it when the learning loss decreases. Repeating this cycle updates the structure used by the application, which can be a graph schema or the organization of linked documents. Figure 1 shows how the setting, the method, and its instances relate. 1.1 Contributions Our contribution is a method for learning knowledge base structure from questions and expected answers. Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent separates the diagnosis that proposes an edit from the loss comparison that evaluates it. Each candidate results from one complete structural edit followed by reconstruction, so the comparison measures both repaired answers and errors introduced elsewhere. We formalize the method through edit directions, which are loss differences between an edited structure and its parent, and relate them to derivatives of a local mixture of candidate losses. Schema Descent is the instance of the method for graph schemas, and its relational model allows structural edits and their interactions to be calculated exactly. Experiments on five large documents, each a bundle of ten research papers, update the structure of knowledge cards and of a graph schema from questions that the application did not answer as expected. We evaluate the updated structures on held-out generated questions and on human questions about the same papers, and compare them with a baseline that retrieves source passages. Figure 1: Self-Structuring Learning specifies the learning setting. Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent is the proposed update method. Schema Descent applies it to graph schemas, and knowledge cards and linked documents use the same loss comparison with their own structural edits. 1.2 Related Work GraphRAG and AutoSchemaKG construct a graph or induce its schema from text ( Edge et al., 2025 ; Bai et al., 2026 ) , DIAL-KG addresses incremental construction and schema evolution, and TRACE-KG preserves contextual qualifiers and source traceability ( Bao et al., 2026 ; Abolhasani et al., 2026 ) . These systems obtain the structure from the text and from the knowledge already extracted, whereas we revise it from the answers that an application gives. Ontology design derives structure from application requirements through competency questions ( Grüninger & Fox, 1995 ) . The work closest to ours is Lim & Mori (2026) , who treat the schema of generative knowledge graph construction as an optimization target: an evolutionary search varies schemas with textual and structural operators and accepts a candidate when the triples generated under it match reference triples better on validation data. We share their view that a schema can be judged only by what is built under it. Our loss is the answer that an application gives through retrieval, which requires questions and expected answers but no reference triples and applies equally to knowledge cards, and we propose each edit from a diagnosis of the answers that failed. Systems that keep such a structure in use include GBrain, whose schema packs govern extraction, querying, and expert routing, and OKF, which separates the producers of knowledge documents from their consumers ( Tan & contributors, 2026 ; McVeety & Hormati, 2026 ) . Our update rule is related to feedback-guided optimization of prompts and compound systems. ProTeGi generates critiques from a prompt’s errors and uses them to propose edits for beam search ( Pryzant et al., 2023 ) . TextGrad propagates language-model feedback through compound systems ( Yuksekgonul et al., 2025 ) . We share with these methods the use of a model’s diagnosis of errors as the source of edits, and we apply it to a different object. An edited prompt is used as it is, whereas an edited structure takes effect only after the knowledge base is rebuilt from its sources, so each of our proposals costs a reconstruction. We propose one edit per round and accept it on the whole set of learning questions, where ProTeGi keeps a beam of candidate prompts. ARES uses synthetic data and human annotations to evaluate RAG components ( Saad-Falcon et al., 2024 ) ; we use reference questions to guide construction as well as to evaluate it. The graph instance uses established relational representations. Joins describe information recoverable from projections, and view selection allocates resources to useful materialized views ( Aho et al., 1979 ; Harinarayan et al., 1996 ) . Relation-instance entities express n-ary associations through binary edges ( Noy & Rector, 2006 ) , while higher-arity knowledge models preserve richer fact structure ( Wen et al., 2016 ; Rosso et al., 2020 ; Galkin et al., 2020 ) . Cross-sentence extraction obtains these relations from text ( Peng et al., 2017 ; Akimoto et al., 2019 ) . Our relational model fixes the source records and edits the declarations that associate their arguments, allowing the effects of those edits to be evaluated directly. 2 Setup In Self-Structuring Learning, a persistent knowledge structure is learned from questions and expected answers about an application’s sources. 2.1 Application Requirements An application specification τ \tau describes the information needs that the application serves, the requirements for acceptable responses, and any operating constraints. An internal question-answering service, for example, may require answers supported by the organization’s documents. Let D D denote a collection of source material and let x x denote a question about it. A reference record is ( D , x , y , e ) (D,x,y,e) , where y y is an expected answer or a set of scoring requirements and e e records the supporting evidence. Evidence may be a passage in D D or an explicit behavioral requirement in τ \tau . We write P τ P_{\tau} for the intended distribution of these records. We prepare questions, expected answers, and supporting evidence according to the specification to approximate this distribution. For learning on one document, D D remains fixed while the questions vary. 2.2 Knowledge Base Structure A structure S S specifies how source information is organized for repeated question answering. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.34762 (cs) [Submitted on 25 Nov 2026] Title: TASK Memory: Beyond Text-Only Memory with Activation Steering and Knowledge Editing against Memory Hallucination Authors: Jinkun Zhao , Wenjun Wu View a PDF of the paper titled TASK Memory: Beyond Text-Only Memory with Activation Steering and Knowledge Editing against Memory Hallucination, by Jinkun Zhao and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on external memory, yet they still hallucinate about what they remember. Often the correct memory is retrieved and placed in the prompt, but the answer contradicts it or the memory is applied to the wrong question. We call these use-time memory hallucinations. Across five open models, we find that they arise from the conflict between parametric knowledge and external memory and take three forms: memory-ignoring, where the model returns to a stale fact in its weights (up to 46% of queries); memory-misapplying, where it attributes the memory to unrelated entities (up to 24%, and 49% when retrieval is combined with weight editing); and version confusion, where 53% of answers about revised facts assert the superseded value when both versions remain stored. We propose TASK memory, which goes beyond text-only memory by combining a Text note with Activation Steering and Knowledge editing that share one in-model address. The text holds the content. A removable knowledge edit supplies the address through its subject key and supports multi-hop composition. A pair of steering vectors decides, query by query, whether the model adopts the memory or keeps its own answer; the vectors store no content and control how the text memory is used. On frozen models under a pre-registered, test-once protocol, TASK reduces memory-ignoring hallucinations to at most 1.5% in all ten model-dataset cells and cuts neighbour misuse from 39.2% to 7.5% (+10.8 pp composite on CounterFact). It improves a 300-memory library over BM25 RAG by 16.4 pp, an advantage that holds at 3,000 memories, resolves fact revisions without fact IDs, and adds 7.5 pp of multi-hop accuracy on MQuAKE. 21 of 23 cross-model comparisons (8B-27B, four families) are significant, and TASK beats three recent context-steering methods in 9 of 10 model-dataset cells.
