items.content: TASK Memory: Beyond T ext-Only Memory with A ctivation S teering and K nowledge Editing against Memory Hallucination Affiliation: Jinkun Zhao Affiliation: Wenjun Wu Affiliation: SKLCCSE, Institute of Artificial Intelligence Beihang University, Beijing, China Affiliation: Beijing Advanced Innovation Center for Future Blockchain and Privacy Computing Beihang University, Beijing, China wwj09315@buaa.edu.cn Abstract LLM agents increasingly rely on external memory, yet they still hallucinate about what they remember. Much of this is not a storage error: the correct memory is retrieved and placed in the prompt, but the answer contradicts it, or the memory is applied to the wrong question. We call these use-time memory hallucinations . Across five open models, we find that they come from the conflict between the model’s parametric knowledge and its external memory, and that they take three forms. In memory-ignoring hallucination, the model returns to a stale fact stored in its weights despite the memory, in up to 46% of queries. In memory-misapplying hallucination, it attributes the memory to unrelated neighbour entities, in up to 24% of cases, and in up to 49% once retrieval is combined with weight editing. In version confusion , 53% of answers about revised facts assert the superseded value when both versions remain stored. We propose TASK memory, a memory that is not text alone: each memory combines a T ext note with A ctivation S teering and K nowledge editing, which act inside the model. The three carriers share one in-model address. The text T holds the content. A local, removable knowledge edit E supplies the address through its subject key and supports multi-hop composition through its weight change. A pair of activation-steering vectors S decides, query by query, whether the model should adopt the memory or keep its own answer. S stores no content; it controls how the model uses the text memory, rather than writing new memory into the parameters. On frozen off-the-shelf models, under a pre-registered, test-once protocol, TASK reduces memory-ignoring hallucinations to ≤ \leq 1.5% in all ten model–dataset cells, and cuts neighbour misuse from 39.2% to 7.5% (+10.8 pp composite on CounterFact). It also improves a 300-memory library over BM25 RAG by 16.4 pp, an advantage that holds at 3,000 memories, resolves fact revisions without fact IDs, and adds 7.5 pp of multi-hop accuracy on MQuAKE. 21 of 23 cross-model comparisons (8B–27B, four families) are significant, and TASK beats three recent context-steering methods in 9 of 10 model–dataset cells. 1 Introduction Figure 1 : Memory hallucination: the memory is correct, the answer is not. (a) Text-only memory or RAG puts the retrieved note into the prompt and leaves the rest to the frozen model, where the note in the context conflicts with the stale fact in the weights. On a question about the memory, the weights win and the model answers with the stale fact (Type I, memory-ignoring). On a question about another entity, the note wins and the model assigns the memory to the wrong entity (Type II, memory-misapplying). Across our five models these rates reach 46% and 24%, and Type II reaches 49% when retrieval is combined with weight editing. (b) TASK memory goes beyond text-only memory. Each memory object holds T ext content, a K nowledge edit Δ ​ W m \Delta W_{m} whose key u ^ m \hat{u}_{m} serves as the in-model address, and a pair of A ctivation- S teering vectors ( v + , v − ) (v^{+},v^{-}) that carry no content. For a query x x , the address response r m ​ ( x ) r_{m}(x) is compared with the threshold τ m \tau_{m} . A relevant query shows T , loads E and adds v + v^{+} , so the model adopts the memory; an unrelated query leaves T and E off and adds v − v^{-} , so the model keeps its own answer. Agents built on large language models (LLMs) keep meeting facts that their weights do not contain, or contain in an outdated form: a person changes jobs, a user replaces a device, an API is deprecated. The dominant way to remember such facts is text memory . The fact is written as a note, stored in a memory store, and retrieved into the prompt when a related question arrives [ 22 , 36 , 37 , 62 , 8 , 54 ] . Agents with memory still hallucinate. HaluMem [ 6 ] shows that memory systems introduce hallucinations when they extract and update memories, and that these errors carry into question answering. That diagnosis locates the error in what is stored . Here we study the complementary failure: the stored memory is correct and is even in the prompt, yet the answer contradicts it, or the memory is applied where it does not belong. We call these use-time memory hallucinations . They are a form of context-conflicting (unfaithful) hallucination [ 57 , 16 ] in which the conflicting context is the agent’s own memory. Use-time memory hallucinations arise because the memory is not read by a blank slate. The model already holds parametric knowledge about the same entities, and the note and the weights compete inside every forward pass. Long-conversation benchmarks such as LoCoMo [ 30 ] and LongMemEval [ 51 ] measure whether the right memory is retrieved and answered from. These systems optimise what reaches the context . TASK is complementary: it keeps a text store and controls how the model uses what reaches the context. On LoCoMo we compare against Mem0 and A-Mem with the same answering model. Parametric memory: editing, parametric RAG and memory-native models. Knowledge editing writes facts into weights. Locate-then-edit methods treat MLPs as key–value stores [ 13 ] and insert closed-form updates: ROME [ 32 ] , MEMIT [ 33 ] , and AlphaEdit [ 11 ] with null-space constraints. Memory-based editors keep side memories with scope classifiers or codebooks: SERAC [ 35 ] , GRACE [ 15 ] , WISE [ 47 ] , Larimar [ 9 ] . IKE [ 60 ] edits in context, and RECIPE [ 7 ] , DeCK [ 3 ] and LightEdit [ 19 ] combine retrieval with prompts or decoding that suppress the old fact. Sequential editing remains fragile [ 26 , 56 ] . Our E follows the ROME lineage; what differs is how TASK uses it. The edit’s subject key also serves as the address that gates text and steering. Each memory keeps its own patch, loaded only when its address fires, and a patch is retired when its memory is revised. Parametric RAG turns documents into LoRA weights generated by a hypernetwork and combines them with text RAG [ 43 , 44 ] . This resembles our T + E , but without per-query arbitration. Memory-native models make memory part of the architecture. MemoryLLM [ 50 ] keeps a self-updating memory pool inside the transformer, and Temp-LoRA [ 49 ] trains a temporary adapter on the history. MemT-1.0 [ 31 ] is the most recent and most scaled example. It adds native memory blocks to selected layers. A dynamic per-trajectory memory state is written token by token with a gated delta rule and read through a parallel memory attention, and Mixture-of-Storage scales its capacity. The memory modules are trained with the backbone frozen, on 34B tokens of continued pre-training and post-training, by distilling the backbone that sees the full textual history. After writing, the history text is no longer needed in context. MemT-1.0 and TASK both bring memory into the model’s computation, but they put different things there ( Table 1 ). MemT-1.0 internalises the content of the history in a trained, fixed-size state; it is evaluated on recall and use of that history, and its training target is the backbone’s own full-context behaviour. TASK leaves the content in an inspectable text store and writes into the model only a per-memory use policy , an address and an adopt/restrain steering pair, which act on a frozen, off-the-shelf model without any pre-training. The two are therefore orthogonal. TASK targets the arbitration failures of Figure 2 , which full-context imitation does not address by construction. A memory-native model could also expose its memory readout to the same kind of address-gated steering. Knowledge conflicts and context faithfulness. LLMs can over-rely on parametric knowledge and ignore context [ 28 ] . They can also be very receptive to coherent but wrong context [ 52 ] . Both behaviours are surveyed by Xu et al. [53] . Existing remedies push the model towards the context, through contrastive decoding (CAD) [ 42 ] , attention-head or SAE-feature interventions [ 23 , 59 ] , adaptive gating of parametric participation [ 25 ] , or global steering directions that favour the context, such as ContextFocus [ 2 ] and the knowledge-selection direction (KSD) of Lou et al. [29] , a signed diff-of-means direction that transfers across conflict types and models. These methods treat faithfulness as a global property of a prompt. In an agent memory the same note is relevant to some queries and irrelevant to others, so a global push turns parametric override into memory override. TASK makes the decision per memory and per query: the address selects between an adopt and a restrain vector. We compare directly against CAD, KSD, ContextFocus and CAST on five models. Activation steering, and steering as memory. Adding vectors to the residual stream steers behaviour: ActAdd [ 46 ] , CAA [ 39 ] , ITI [ 24 ] , representation engineering [ 64 ] . CAST [ 20 ] applies a behaviour vector only when the hidden state is similar to a condition vector. We share the idea of gating, but our gate is a per-memory address taken from the edit key. Our steered behaviour is evidence use, not refusal. Several works store knowledge as activations or representation edits: SAKE [ 41 ] , REACT [ 61 ] , MEGA [ 4 ] , RILKE [ 27 ] . Neural Procedural Memory [ 58 ] stores agent skills as retrieved steering vectors and finds them complementary to textual workflow memory. Jumle [18] show that facts barely survive when stored as steering alone (at most 15% clean use, against 96–98% in context). This negative result is consistent with our design choice: TASK never asks S to carry content ( S alone: 1.7%), only to control how text content is used. Chavira Juárez et al. [5] argue conceptually that memory agents should divide labour among retrieval, steering and weight editing. TASK gives one concrete instance of that division, with experiments. items.content: 01 Introduction Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here . Introduction Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space. One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality . The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail. The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer. The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle. In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question , but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory. The second problem concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists don’t know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called bootstrapping . Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldn’t prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested. Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesn’t identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction. Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them. A note about Claude’s methods In August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing Claude’s capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each other’s progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks. The agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that Hongbin’s agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other. The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another one—which was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional space—turned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result recently proved by an OpenAI model . Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling can’t be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result. The Hawking-Page transition To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through New York City. Two equally good routes from Penn Station (A) to the High Line entrance (B). In theory, a quantum particle can take both simultaneously. Imagine that you’re heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes. You could walk west along West 33rd Street and turn south, or head south first and then walk west along West 30th Street. Either way, you have to pick one. In the quantum world, though, that’s not true: a particle can take both routes simultaneously. This is most clearly demonstrated in the famous double-slit experiment. In this test, you fire particles, one at a time, at a barrier cut with two narrow slits, and record where, on a screen behind it, each one lands. Each particle lands at a particular point on the screen, as a particle should. But as you fire more of them, they build up a pattern of stripes that would only be possible if each one had passed through both slits, like a wave. The double-slit experiment. When electrons are fired one at a time from a source (A) toward a barrier with two slits, each lands at a single point on the screen. The hits build up a pattern of stripes that is only possible if each one passed through both slits. To predict what a quantum particle will do more generally, physicists have to add up every path it could possibly take, known as its possible histories . Not every history counts equally; some contribute far more to the sum than others. It’s an extravagant and mysterious way to describe how a single particle behaves, but it’s also one of the most successful ideas in physics. This approach, known as the “sum over histories,” is well established for particles and anything made of them. But what about gravity? Einstein showed that gravity is a consequence of curved spacetime: objects with mass bend space and time around them, and we feel that bending as gravity. In a quantum theory of gravity, therefore, what gets summed over is the shape of spacetime itself, rather than just the paths of particles moving through it. To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out. Hawking and Page found a case where this sum is simple enough to handle but still interesting. To explain Hawking and Page’s work, we need to imagine a different kind of universe, called anti-de Sitter spacetime. Imagine you’re standing in a giant bowl. No matter how hard you throw an object, it will always roll back to the place you threw it from. Our universe isn’t like that. The difference comes down to a quantity called the cosmological constant , which describes the energy of empty space. In our universe, this energy is positive, which makes space expand ever faster. In anti-de Sitter spacetime, the energy is negative, so everything is pulled back to where it started. Hawking and Page chose this universe for their calculation because of how it behaves when it heats up: the bowl keeps heat in so it can stay at a steady temperature. At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a “history” means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particles—including gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. Whichever contributes more to the sum is, in effect, what we would observe—it “wins.” At low temperatures, the gas history wins, and the universe is full of gas; at high temperatures, the black-hole history wins, and the universe contains a black hole. At one particular temperature—which physicists now call the Hawking-Page temperature—the universe switches abruptly from one to the other. This is the phase transition. Which history wins depends on temperature. Below the Hawking-Page temperature (black line), the universe is filled with a gas of particles, including gravitons; above it, the universe contains a black hole. It’s a rare case where we can see two very different shapes of spacetime competing in the sum over histories, and can say which one wins. This is where the holographic principle enters the story. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Hawking found that the amount of information a black hole can hold is proportional to its surface area, not to its volume. That’s very different from ordinary matter, where every bit of volume holds roughly the same amount of information. In the early 1990s, Gerard ’t Hooft and Leonard Susskind proposed that this idea applies to gravity in general—that everything inside a region of space can be fully described by the information on its boundary, just as a flat hologram can display a three-dimensional image. In 1997, Juan Maldacena formalized the idea further. Gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl, he argued, is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory of particles, with no gravity at all, existing on the rim of the bowl (the universe’s outer boundary). These are the gravity side and the quantum side of the duality we described in the introduction—they’re two languages for describing the same underlying reality. In the case Claude studied, the quantum theory on the rim is called N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. It’s related to the theories that describe how particles interact in the real universe, but it has extra symmetries that make it much easier for physicists to work with. (Claude has worked with this theory before, calculating how particles interact within it to a new level of precision .) Since the gravity side predicts two histories competing with each other, the obvious question is: does N=4 super Yang-Mills theory (the quantum side) show the same thing? For now, physicists can analyze this theory in detail only when its particles barely interact with each other, a condition known as weak coupling . This is the opposite end of the spectrum from where Hawking and Page’s gravitational calculation works. Weak coupling on the quantum side corresponds to the small, blurry universe on the gravity side. So there was no guarantee that any of Hawking and Page’s findings would hold there. Remarkably, they do. Bo Sundborg in 1999, and after him Ofer Aharony, Joseph Marsano, Shiraz Minwalla, Kyriakos Papadodimas, and Mark Van Raamsdonk, showed that even at weak coupling, the theory on the rim goes through a transition as it heats up. This is its counterpart of the switch from gas to black hole inside the bowl. But it was still unknown whether this transition is abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth and gradual. When particles barely interact, physicists have to calculate how they behave one step at a time. They start with a simplified version of the theory in which particles don’t interact at all. Then they add a series of corrections, each more precise and harder to compute than the last. Physicists call these steps loops . In 2003, Aharony and his colleagues realized that whether the phase transition was an abrupt jump, as Hawking and Page predicted, or gradual, hinged on a single number that appeared only three loops in. Computing that number involves many thousands of terms, known as diagrams—far too many to work through by hand. In 2005, the same group completed the calculation for a simpler cousin of the theory and found an abrupt transition. But the version for N=4 super Yang-Mills, more than 10 times larger, was never completed. The scale of the computational problem, while daunting, wasn’t the only obstacle to completing the calculation. There was a conceptual issue, as well: naively adding up all the parts of the calculation gives an infinite answer, and those infinities have to be tamed carefully to extract a meaningful result. To solve the problem, Claude ran a small research group of agents, all copies of itself. Almost every piece of the calculation was done twice, by agents acting independently. For extra consistency checks, parts of the calculation could also be compared to previous results in the literature. The result Claude found is an abrupt jump as the temperature rises, exactly analogous to what Hawking and Page had found using the sum over spacetime histories. The emerging picture is very simple: the transition is abrupt at both weak and strong coupling—the blurry and the smooth ends, in the gravity description. The most natural possibility is that it stays abrupt everywhere in between. This is a beautiful outcome. It shows that a calculation using the sum over histories in gravity qualitatively matches the behavior of an ordinary quantum theory with no gravity at all. Many open questions remain. The abrupt transition Claude found is very much like the one we see whenever we boil water. One interesting feature of abrupt transitions is that the losing side of the competition can survive for a while: for instance, water can be superheated above 100°C without boiling, as you could see for yourself if you were to put a cup of extremely pure water in the microwave. (But please don’t do this; it’s dangerous, and Anthropic would rather not be responsible for an epidemic of scalded readers.) Something similar happens here. Above the Hawking-Page temperature, the hot gas of gravitons and other particles can survive for a long time in a superheated state. But at a higher temperature it can no longer survive: this is another transition, the Hagedorn transition, which is a characteristic signature of string theory. On the gravity side, that transition has many interesting properties of its own, and it would be valuable to check in detail whether they also appear in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. Another open question concerns the other possible histories of spacetime. Hawking and Page considered three: one in which their model universe is filled with gas, one that contains a large black hole, and one containing a smaller black hole that never comes to dominate the sum over histories. In principle, there are many more possible histories. As far as anyone knows, none of them ever dominates. But given certain changes to the starting conditions—if the universe is set spinning, for instance, or given a fixed amount of energy or charge—then some of these histories do take over. Working out exactly which ones win, and when, is an interesting problem for the future. The modular bootstrap As we saw earlier, one useful model universe has just two dimensions of space and one of time: it’s called “3D gravity” because it describes gravity in three spacetime dimensions. According to the principle of holographic duality, 3D gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory living on the bowl’s rim. As a model, 3D gravity is much simpler than the real thing, but it still allows for black holes and many of the same mysteries. It provides a useful laboratory for studying the sum over spacetime histories. It’s also a good place to test the idea that spacetime isn’t a basic ingredient of the universe, but emerges from something deeper. In general relativity, black holes look smooth. But in quantum gravity, if you zoom in to the smallest scales—the Planck length, around 10 -35 meters, where quantum effects on gravity become impossible to ignore—black holes are made of an enormous number of tiny, individual building blocks. Physicists believe the same is true in our own, four-dimensional universe, but the 3D version is much easier to analyze with holographic duality. Claude’s results build on a method called the bootstrap, a general strategy for solving quantum theories. Counterintuitively, the strategy doesn’t try to solve a theory directly. For 3D gravity, that isn’t even possible, because nobody knows how to define the theory precisely. Instead, the bootstrap rules theories out by showing that they contradict themselves. Physicists scan over all possible quantum theories and try to eliminate them one by one. Remarkably, in many cases this method makes it possible to pinpoint a single quantum theory and calculate precisely how it behaves. The requirements of relativity and quantum mechanics are so demanding, and so delicately balanced, that together they rule out every alternative. In 2012, the bootstrap was used to solve a quantum field theory called the 3D critical Ising model , a simple model of magnetism that also describes water at the point where liquid and vapor become indistinguishable. Since then, it has been applied to many different quantum systems. In 2009, Simeon Hellerman introduced a technique called the modular bootstrap , which applies the bootstrap method to 3D gravity. Its goal is to rule out inconsistent theories of quantum gravity in three spacetime dimensions. By combining it with other bootstrap methods, physicists hope to eventually eliminate every inconsistent theory. Whatever is left must be consistent. There could be no consistent theories, or just one, or whole families of them. Any of these outcomes would be interesting, because it would help us understand what spacetime looks like at the Planck scale in this simplified universe, and give us hints about the Planck scale in our own. Here’s how the modular bootstrap works. 3D gravity in anti-de Sitter spacetime has a quantity called the central charge (c), which roughly counts how many microscopic building blocks the universe is made of. When general relativity holds, c is very large, because large black holes contain an enormous number of building blocks. A second quantity, M₁, is the mass of the lightest black hole. items.raw_text: 01 Introduction Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here . Introduction Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space. One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality . The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail. The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer. The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle. In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question , but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory. The second problem concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists don’t know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called bootstrapping . Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldn’t prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested. Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesn’t identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction. Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them. A note about Claude’s methods In August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing Claude’s capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each other’s progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks. The agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that Hongbin’s agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other. The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another one—which was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional space—turned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result recently proved by an OpenAI model . Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling can’t be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result. The Hawking-Page transition To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through New York City. Two equally good routes from Penn Station (A) to the High Line entrance (B). In theory, a quantum particle can take both simultaneously. Imagine that you’re heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes. You could walk west along West 33rd Street and turn south, or head south first and then walk west along West 30th Street. Either way, you have to pick one. In the quantum world, though, that’s not true: a particle can take both routes simultaneously. This is most clearly demonstrated in the famous double-slit experiment. In this test, you fire particles, one at a time, at a barrier cut with two narrow slits, and record where, on a screen behind it, each one lands. Each particle lands at a particular point on the screen, as a particle should. But as you fire more of them, they build up a pattern of stripes that would only be possible if each one had passed through both slits, like a wave. The double-slit experiment. When electrons are fired one at a time from a source (A) toward a barrier with two slits, each lands at a single point on the screen. The hits build up a pattern of stripes that is only possible if each one passed through both slits. To predict what a quantum particle will do more generally, physicists have to add up every path it could possibly take, known as its possible histories . Not every history counts equally; some contribute far more to the sum than others. It’s an extravagant and mysterious way to describe how a single particle behaves, but it’s also one of the most successful ideas in physics. This approach, known as the “sum over histories,” is well established for particles and anything made of them. But what about gravity? Einstein showed that gravity is a consequence of curved spacetime: objects with mass bend space and time around them, and we feel that bending as gravity. In a quantum theory of gravity, therefore, what gets summed over is the shape of spacetime itself, rather than just the paths of particles moving through it. To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out. Hawking and Page found a case where this sum is simple enough to handle but still interesting. To explain Hawking and Page’s work, we need to imagine a different kind of universe, called anti-de Sitter spacetime. Imagine you’re standing in a giant bowl. No matter how hard you throw an object, it will always roll back to the place you threw it from. Our universe isn’t like that. The difference comes down to a quantity called the cosmological constant , which describes the energy of empty space. In our universe, this energy is positive, which makes space expand ever faster. In anti-de Sitter spacetime, the energy is negative, so everything is pulled back to where it started. Hawking and Page chose this universe for their calculation because of how it behaves when it heats up: the bowl keeps heat in so it can stay at a steady temperature. At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a “history” means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particles—including gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. Whichever contributes more to the sum is, in effect, what we would observe—it “wins.” At low temperatures, the gas history wins, and the universe is full of gas; at high temperatures, the black-hole history wins, and the universe contains a black hole. At one particular temperature—which physicists now call the Hawking-Page temperature—the universe switches abruptly from one to the other. This is the phase transition. Which history wins depends on temperature. Below the Hawking-Page temperature (black line), the universe is filled with a gas of particles, including gravitons; above it, the universe contains a black hole. It’s a rare case where we can see two very different shapes of spacetime competing in the sum over histories, and can say which one wins. This is where the holographic principle enters the story. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Hawking found that the amount of information a black hole can hold is proportional to its surface area, not to its volume. That’s very different from ordinary matter, where every bit of volume holds roughly the same amount of information. In the early 1990s, Gerard ’t Hooft and Leonard Susskind proposed that this idea applies to gravity in general—that everything inside a region of space can be fully described by the information on its boundary, just as a flat hologram can display a three-dimensional image. In 1997, Juan Maldacena formalized the idea further. Gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl, he argued, is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory of particles, with no gravity at all, existing on the rim of the bowl (the universe’s outer boundary). These are the gravity side and the quantum side of the duality we described in the introduction—they’re two languages for describing the same underlying reality. In the case Claude studied, the quantum theory on the rim is called N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. It’s related to the theories that describe how particles interact in the real universe, but it has extra symmetries that make it much easier for physicists to work with. (Claude has worked with this theory before, calculating how particles interact within it to a new level of precision .) Since the gravity side predicts two histories competing with each other, the obvious question is: does N=4 super Yang-Mills theory (the quantum side) show the same thing? For now, physicists can analyze this theory in detail only when its particles barely interact with each other, a condition known as weak coupling . This is the opposite end of the spectrum from where Hawking and Page’s gravitational calculation works. Weak coupling on the quantum side corresponds to the small, blurry universe on the gravity side. So there was no guarantee that any of Hawking and Page’s findings would hold there. Remarkably, they do. Bo Sundborg in 1999, and after him Ofer Aharony, Joseph Marsano, Shiraz Minwalla, Kyriakos Papadodimas, and Mark Van Raamsdonk, showed that even at weak coupling, the theory on the rim goes through a transition as it heats up. This is its counterpart of the switch from gas to black hole inside the bowl. But it was still unknown whether this transition is abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth and gradual. When particles barely interact, physicists have to calculate how they behave one step at a time. They start with a simplified version of the theory in which particles don’t interact at all. Then they add a series of corrections, each more precise and harder to compute than the last. Physicists call these steps loops . In 2003, Aharony and his colleagues realized that whether the phase transition was an abrupt jump, as Hawking and Page predicted, or gradual, hinged on a single number that appeared only three loops in. Computing that number involves many thousands of terms, known as diagrams—far too many to work through by hand. In 2005, the same group completed the calculation for a simpler cousin of the theory and found an abrupt transition. But the version for N=4 super Yang-Mills, more than 10 times larger, was never completed. The scale of the computational problem, while daunting, wasn’t the only obstacle to completing the calculation. There was a conceptual issue, as well: naively adding up all the parts of the calculation gives an infinite answer, and those infinities have to be tamed carefully to extract a meaningful result. To solve the problem, Claude ran a small research group of agents, all copies of itself. Almost every piece of the calculation was done twice, by agents acting independently. For extra consistency checks, parts of the calculation could also be compared to previous results in the literature. The result Claude found is an abrupt jump as the temperature rises, exactly analogous to what Hawking and Page had found using the sum over spacetime histories. The emerging picture is very simple: the transition is abrupt at both weak and strong coupling—the blurry and the smooth ends, in the gravity description. The most natural possibility is that it stays abrupt everywhere in between. This is a beautiful outcome. It shows that a calculation using the sum over histories in gravity qualitatively matches the behavior of an ordinary quantum theory with no gravity at all. Many open questions remain. The abrupt transition Claude found is very much like the one we see whenever we boil water. One interesting feature of abrupt transitions is that the losing side of the competition can survive for a while: for instance, water can be superheated above 100°C without boiling, as you could see for yourself if you were to put a cup of extremely pure water in the microwave. (But please don’t do this; it’s dangerous, and Anthropic would rather not be responsible for an epidemic of scalded readers.) Something similar happens here. Above the Hawking-Page temperature, the hot gas of gravitons and other particles can survive for a long time in a superheated state. But at a higher temperature it can no longer survive: this is another transition, the Hagedorn transition, which is a characteristic signature of string theory. On the gravity side, that transition has many interesting properties of its own, and it would be valuable to check in detail whether they also appear in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. Another open question concerns the other possible histories of spacetime. Hawking and Page considered three: one in which their model universe is filled with gas, one that contains a large black hole, and one containing a smaller black hole that never comes to dominate the sum over histories. In principle, there are many more possible histories. As far as anyone knows, none of them ever dominates. items.summary: Algorithms and theory Google’s mission presents many exciting algorithmic and optimization challenges across different product areas including Search, Ads, Social, and Google Infrastructure. These include optimizing internal systems such as scheduling the machines that power the numerous computations done each day, as well as optimizations that affect core products and users, from online allocation of ads to page-views to automatic management of ad campaigns, and from clustering large-scale graphs to finding best paths in transportation networks. These include optimizing internal systems such as scheduling the machines that power the numerous computations done each day, as well as optimizations that affect core products and users, from online allocation of ads to page-views to automatic management of ad campaigns, and from clustering large-scale graphs to finding best paths in transportation networks. Other than employing new algorithmic ideas to impact millions of users, Google researchers contribute to the state-of-the-art research in these areas by publishing in top conferences and journals. Recent Publications See More The Visibility VC-Dimension of Simple Polygons is Six Dror Aiger Sariel Har-Peled 2027 Preview Preview abstract We prove that no simple polygon P ⊂ R 2 contains a visibility-shattered set of seven points, establishing that the maximum visibility VC-dimension over all simple polygons is six. Combined with Valtr’s lower bound [Val98], this resolves the visibility VC-dimension problem for simple polygons, improving the upper bound of 23 due to Valtr [Val98] and 14 due to Gilbers and Klein [GK14] to the exact value 6. We also exhibit an explicit 968-vertex simple polygon with rational vertex coordinates that shatters six points in strictly convex position, confirming maxP VC-dim(P) = maxP VC-dimconvex(P) = 6. Our proof combines a general-position perturbation, a structural decomposition of the convex hull of a shattered seven-point set into a contiguous block of certified front vertices and non-certified hull vertices, an extended polygonenclosure calculus, and a sound chirotope reduction whose geometric soundness implications are machine-checked in Lean 4 and independently verified via Z3 real-arithmetic proofs and dual CDCL SAT solvers. View details Hadwiger’s Covering Conjecture in Three Dimensions Dror Aiger Sariel Har-Peled Goran Žužić 2027 Preview Preview abstract Let K in R^3 be an arbitrary convex body, that is, a compact convex subset of R^3 with nonempty interior. We prove unconditionally that K can be covered by eight smaller positive homothetic copies of itself: there exist a scalar lambda in (0, 1) and translation vectors v_1, ..., v_8 in R^3 such that K is contained in the union of (lambda K + v_i) for i = 1, ..., 8. This resolves Hadwiger's covering conjecture in three dimensions. The proof works in Boltyanski's equivalent boundary illumination formulation and is completely self-contained. Parallelepipeds are covered directly by eight translates of (2/3)K. For any convex body K that is not a parallelepiped, we place its centrally symmetric halved difference body S = (1/2)(K - K) in John's position (B^3 subseteq S) and show that the spherical average of its support function satisfies 8 int_{S^2} h_S d sigma_tilde < 12, with equality only for orthogonal cubes. Using outer polyhedral approximations together with Cauchy's planar perimeter formula, the full spherical measure of directions not parallel to any boundary segment of K, and lower semicontinuity of curve variation, we find a unit vector w_* in S^2 whose shadow boundary Sigma(K, w_*) on K itself is a continuous closed curve of S-length strictly less than 12. Splitting Sigma(K, w_*) into six contiguous arcs of S-length strictly less than 2 and applying Helly's theorem in R^3 illuminates each arc with one direction, while +-w_* illuminate the remainder of partial K. The proof was discovered using an experimental harness on top of Gemini 4 Carbon and formally verified in Lean 4. View details Depth-CoT Tradeoffs in Transformers: A Look at Path Following Clayton Sanford Matus Telgarsky Justin D. Li 2027 Preview Preview abstract Modern transformers have been scaled up in size, data, training-time compute, and more recently test-time compute based on Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the consequences of trading off these parameters are unknown. We construct explicit tradeoffs between two of these aspects: the number of layers in a transformer and the number of CoT tokens. Our first result is general: with mild assumptions and a single-token prompt, for any integer k, a transformer using soft attention and SwiGLU MLP layers with L layers and n CoT tokens can be converted to a transformer with at most ckL layers and ⌈n/k⌉ CoT tokens, and vice versa, although with an increase to the size of other parameters. We then a multi-token prompt path following task, finding that additional preprocessing from the multi-token prompt changes the depth-CoT relationship in this case. We construct an attention-only network with L layers and 2^(L−2) heads that can traverse 2^(L−1) − 1 edges along a path with a single CoT token, demonstrating at least an exponential relationship between increases in depth and reductions in the number of CoT tokens needed to traverse the entire path. This relationship for the path following task holds empirically as well, as demonstrated by training networks with up to 5 layers, with the tradeoff between depth and the maximum number of edge traversals in a single CoT token exactly matching our theoretical constructions. View details Geo-Contextual AI Concierge: Minimizing Internal Support Friction Through Proactive Knowledge Synthesis Neeraj Choudhary Dónal Doyle Technical Report (2026) Preview Preview abstract In large-scale distributed enterprises, traditional Knowledge Management (KM) systems face a critical failure mode: static documentation cannot keep pace with evolving operational realities and regional nuances. This "knowledge latency" forces employees out of self-service workflows and into costly support ticketing queues. This paper introduces SENTINEL, a geo-contextual AI framework designed to shift enterprise support from reactive retrieval to proactive interception. The architecture employs a novel dual-engine system integrated into an omni-present interface. The first engine utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct pre-emptive, historical case-grounded audits of documentation, generating a "Contextual Density" score that identifies friction zones. The second engine is an autonomous Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) agent that surfaces in-situ via a location-intelligent assistant window, resolving queries in real-time. By functioning as a strategic "defensive barrier" at the point of origin, SENTINEL demonstrates how a proactive AI assistant can drive high-fidelity, in-situ case deflection. View details Rational Transductors Mehryar Mohri ICML 2026 Preview Preview abstract Standard Transformers excel at semantic modeling but struggle with rigid sequential logic and state tracking, fundamentally limited to AC0 complexity without intermediate chain-of- thought. In this work, we introduce Rational Transductors, a dual-stream architecture that augments the Transformer with a linear, matrix-valued recurrence derived from Weighted Finite Automata (WFA). By injecting rational state information into the attention mechanism via a Deep Rational Injection scheme, our framework strictly generalizes the expressive power of Transformers to capture all Regular Languages and NC1-complete problems (such as Parity and Modular Counting) while preserving O(log T) parallel training efficiency. View details Marginalized Bundle Adjustment: Multi-View Camera Pose from Monocular Depth Estimates Shengjie Zhu Ahmed Abdelkader Mark Matthews Xiaoming Liu Vincent Chu International Conference on 3D Vision (2026) Preview Preview abstract Structure-from-Motion (SfM) is a classical 3D vision task for recovering camera parameters and scene geometry from multi-view images. Recent advances in deep learning enable accurate monocular depth estimation (MDE) that infers structure from a single image without depending on camera motion. But integrating MDE into SfM remains challenging. Unlike classical triangulated sparse pointclouds, MDE produces dense depthmaps with significantly higher error variance. Inspired by modern RANSAC estimators, we propose a Marginalized Bundle Adjustment (MBA) to accommodate MDE error variance with its density. With MBA, we show that MDE depthmaps are sufficiently accurate to support SoTA or competitive results in Structure-from-Motion and camera relocalization. Our benchmark demonstrates consistent remarkable results from two-view, few-frames small multiview, to thousands-frames large multiview system. Our method highlights the significant potential of MDE on multi-view 3D vision tasks. items.title: AI Act scientific panel holds second regular meeting
items.summary: On 23 November, the AI Act Scientific Panel held its second regular meeting in Brussels and online, the first time the panel met in person. The experts of AI Act Scientific Panel – appointed in June 2026 in their personal capacity – contribute independent scientific expertise to the enforcement of the AI Act's rules for general-purpose AI, including by alerting to systemic risks. Since its special meeting on 9 October with Executive Vice-President Virkkunen, the panel has contributed questions to the AI Office's requests for information to OpenAI and Anthropic on recent loss-of-control incidents. The companies were asked about all instances in which models breached containment, whether the EU was affected and what they have changed in their risk assessment and their safety and security practices as a result. In the morning, the AI Office updated panel members on its first enforcement actions under the AI Act and on its priorities to date which require scientific inputs from the panel.

The experts of AI Act Scientific Panel – appointed in June 2026 in their personal capacity – contribute independent scientific expertise to the enforcement of the AI Act's rules for general-purpose AI, including by alerting to systemic risks. Since its special meeting on 9 October with Executive Vice-President Virkkunen, the panel has contributed questions to the AI Office's requests for information to OpenAI and Anthropic on recent loss-of-control incidents. The companies were asked about all instances in which models breached containment, whether the EU was affected and what they have changed in their risk assessment and their safety and security practices as a result. In the morning, the AI Office updated panel members on its first enforcement actions under the AI Act and on its priorities to date which require scientific inputs from the panel. Panel members were also invited to put forward topics for the panel's future work, for discussion with the AI Office. In the afternoon, in-depth discussions were held on scoping the panel's initial work in the areas of evaluations, cyber risk, harmful manipulation and socio-technical risks, chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear (CBRN) risks and loss of control. Building on these discussions, the panel will continue to develop its work in the coming months, in close cooperation with the AI Office. Last update 25 November 2026 Print as PDF

items.summary: Make america healthy again President Trump launched the Make America Healthy Again initiative to confront chronic disease, improve nutrition, and lower healthcare costs. This year, the administration advanced reforms targeting childhood health, food quality, and preventive care while increasing transparency and accountability in healthcare systems. These actions are laying the foundation for a healthier, stronger America. By prioritizing prevention over treatment and empowering families with better information and choices, the administration is addressing the root causes of poor health outcomes. These efforts are improving quality of life, strengthening communities, and ensuring a healthier future for the next generation of Americans. items.content: Simulation / Modeling / Design How to Optimize NVFP4 Attention on NVIDIA RTX Blackwell Through Register Recycling Nov 25, 2026 By Atharva Joshi Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVFP4 enables hardware-accelerated 4-bit matrix multiplication on NVIDIA RTX Blackwell GPUs, offering higher Tensor Core throughput than BF16 for attention workloads. An optimized SageAttention3 kernel splits each N128 score tile into two N64 register slots, reusing registers after softmax quantization to overlap the next tile's QK computation with the current tile's remaining operations. This register-recycling schedule reduces Tensor Core idle time without allocating a second full score buffer, improving NVFP4 attention kernel latency by up to 1.64x on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell. Reactor integrated the optimized kernel into its production serving stack for world models, achieving end-to-end inference latency reductions of up to 15.34% across LongLive, Helios, OmniDreams, and Cosmos 3 Nano workloads. The core optimization has been merged into the FlashInfer main branch for broader adoption. Next Steps Clone the FlashInfer main branch with its submodules and follow the source installation guide. Integrate the SM120 NVFP4 attention API into supported attention layers on NVIDIA RTX Blackwell and compare end-to-end latency and output quality against a BF16 baseline. Read Integrating NVF4 Attention into Real-Time Models on Reactor to learn how Reactor deployed this kernel for real customer traffic. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Attention can be a major bottleneck when serving world foundation models , where long sequences make inference computationally demanding. On NVIDIA Hopper and NVIDIA Blackwell data center GPUs, FlashAttention3 and FlashAttention4 improve attention performance by overlapping matrix multiply-accumulate (MMA) operations through softmax within a thread block. However, these hardware-specific pipelines cannot be applied directly to the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Series (SM120), which uses a different Tensor Core architecture. For video generation models using BF16 inference, attention remains primarily MMA-bound on NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPUs, while softmax is a major bottleneck in forward attention on Blackwell data center GPUs. Introduced with NVIDIA Blackwell architecture, NVFP4 offers hardware-accelerated 4-bit matrix multiplication, enabling higher Tensor Core throughput and creating an opportunity to accelerate attention beyond BF16. But sustaining high throughput requires careful coordination of softmax, data movement, and intermediate storage. Dependencies between these stages can leave Tensor Cores idle, limiting how effectively the kernel uses the available compute. This post explains how to accelerate NVFP4 attention on the SM120 architecture through register recycling and improved scheduling. By reclaiming score registers after the softmax outputs have been packed into NVFP4, the next tile’s matrix multiplication can overlap with remaining softmax work on the current tile. This creates a more efficient pipeline that reduces Tensor Core idle time and improves utilization without requiring a second full score buffer. Reactor , a developer platform that provides global low-latency infrastructure and APIs for deploying and scaling real-time video, robotics, and world models, integrated this kernel in their production serving stack to serve real customer traffic and saw tremendous speedups. Their benchmarks are shared in this post. Improving throughput with NVFP4 NVIDIA RTX Blackwell has lower BF16 matmul throughput compared to the data center variants. While data center workloads are bounded by softmax (FlashAttention4 tries to solve this through pipelining and exp2 emulation), the NVIDIA RTX Blackwell is bounded by MMA on BF16 Attention. Due to higher TFLOP/s for NVFP4, throughput can be improved to achieve better performance. Attention compute The general attention computation and the two core matrix multiplications it involves are: Query-Key matrix multiplication (\(QK\)) : The first matmul in attention, \(QKᵀ\), where \(Q\) contains query vectors and \(K\) contains key vectors. It computes the attention scores used by softmax. Attention-Weight Value matrix multiplication (\(PV\)) : The second matmul in attention, \(PV\), where \(P\) contains softmax-derived attention weights and \(V\) contains value vectors. It combines the value vectors according to their attention weights to produce the output. In the tiled attention kernel discussed here, \(P\) contains unnormalized softmax weights, and final normalization is applied after the output has been accumulated across tiles (similar to FlashAttention). How SageAttention3 accelerates attention using NVFP4 SageAttention3 is a native NVFP4 attention mechanism specifically designed for NVIDIA RTX Blackwell streaming multiprocessor (SM) 120. It performs both \(QK\) and \(PV\) using NVFP4​. Its primary innovation came from performing two-level scaling for \(P\).​ NVFP4 quantization generates two tensors: an NVFP4 data tensor and an FP8 scaling tensor. Because ​softmax outputs are bound to a narrow [0, 1] range, they can underutilize the NVFP4 dynamic range, resulting in accuracy degradation. Two-level scaling addresses this by first normalizing the values to fully utilize dynamic range before quantizing the result. SageAttention3 cooperative thread array stable state design The SageAttention3 cooperative thread array (CTA) design is as follows: The CTA uses four producer warps and eight consumer warps. For each N128 tile, consumers execute \(QK\), softmax and probability quantization, and \(PV\) in sequence. While consumers perform softmax, scaling, and quantization, tensor-core activity has gaps. Video 1 illustrates this sequential execution. # Current SageAttention 3 CTA Execution (per N tile) # CTA Structure: 12 warps total (4 Producer, 8 Consumer) For each N tile: # 1. Producer Role: Data Loading # Q is loaded once per M tile AsyncLoad(Q) # K, V, Scale Factors, and delta_s use 3-stage async TMA pipeline AsyncLoad(K, V, Scale_Factors, delta_s) # 2. Consumer Role: Dependency Chain (Serial Execution) # 8 Consumer warps (256-thread MMA collective) # A. QK Computation Execute_QK_OMMA() Apply_delta_s_correction() # B. Softmax & Quantization Apply_Masking() Execute_Online_Softmax() Execute_NVFP4_Probability_Quantization() # C. PV Computation Execute_PV_OMMA() # Note: Execution is strictly serial per N tile # No overlapping or independent fragments in flight The following observations can be drawn from this CTA design and the parallel thread execution (PTX) and instruction set architecture (ISA) for NVIDIA RTX Blackwell GPUs: First, TMA Loads are bound to Shapes of 128×128, not utilizing the entire shape would mean underutilizing our GPU bandwidth. Second, the NVIDIA Blackwell RTX OMMA operation remains constrained to m16, n8, k64 (where m and n represent LHS/RHS free dimensions, while k is the contraction axis), as specified by the PTX instruction mma.sync.aligned.kind::mxf4nvf4.block_scale.scale_vec::4X.m16n8k64 .​ To cover the full contraction dimension of k=128, two MMA instructions with k=64 must be issued. The current CTA design issues these instructions for \(QK\) in succession. Because MMA execution is synchronous, the issuing consumer warps wait for completion before proceeding to online softmax and intermediate quantization. This means that the operations within the stable loop are sequentially pipelined. There is a large gap in MMA activity, as there is no compute scheduled on the tensor cores. The warps are busy computing the softmax, scaling, and quantization operations. Video 1 shows the attention-kernel timeline, including sequential \(QK\) matrix multiplication, softmax, and \(PV\) matrix multiplication. Video 1. CTA timeline for original CTA design of SageAttention3 Register constraints Producer warps use 3,072 registers, and consumer warps use 59,392 registers. The total of 62,464 registers occupies approximately 95.3% of the SM’s register capacity. This leaves little room to hold an additional score tile while processing the current tile. Optimized CTA design The design retains four producer warps, eight consumer warps, and complete N128 K/V tile loads. The change is in how consumers compute and store attention scores. Each N128 score tile is split into two N64 halves, and each occupies a separate register slot. After one half has been exponentiated and quantized, its score registers are reused to compute the corresponding \(QK\) half of the next tile. This interleaves the next tile’s \(QK\) to work with the current tile’s remaining softmax, quantization, and \(PV\) operations. The online-softmax state is still updated across the complete N128 score tile before either half is consumed. Video 2 shows how this schedule fills gaps in tensor-core activity without allocating a second complete score tile. Video 2. CTA Timeline for optimized SageAttention3 The following pseudocode illustrates the optimized schedule, including the initial score computation, steady-state register reuse, and processing of the final tile. Unlike the original design, which completes \(QK\), softmax, quantization, and \(PV\) sequentially for each N128 tile, the optimized design splits the score tile into two N64 register slots. When half is quantized, its score registers are reused for the next tile’s \(QK\) computation. This allows work from adjacent tiles to be interleaved without allocating a second complete score tile, while retaining the same four producer warps and eight consumer warps. # Optimized CuTe DSL CTA Execution # N64/N64 Cross-Block Ping-Pong # CTA Structure: 12 warps total (4 Producer, 8 Consumer) # # All 8 consumer warps remain active. # Each N128 score tile is represented by two N64 register slots: # ScoreSlot0 = columns [0:64] # ScoreSlot1 = columns [64:128] # 1. Producer Role: Three-Stage Data Pipeline # Q and its scale factors are loaded once per M128 query tile. AsyncLoad(Q, Q_ScaleFactors) # Producer warps continuously prefetch complete N128 K/V tiles. # K and V retain separate three-stage pipelines. for N_tile in traversal_order: AsyncPrefetch( K[N_tile], V[N_tile], K_ScaleFactors[N_tile], V_ScaleFactors[N_tile], delta_s[N_tile], ) # 2. Consumer Prologue: Produce the First Score Tile CurrentTile = First_N_Tile() # Compute one complete QK score tile as two symmetric N64 halves. ScoreSlot0 = Execute_QK_OMMA_N64(Q, K[CurrentTile, 0:64], delta_s[CurrentTile, 0:64],) ScoreSlot1 = Execute_QK_OMMA_N64(Q, K[CurrentTile, 64:128], delta_s[CurrentTile, 64:128],) # 3. Consumer Steady State: Cross-Block Ping-Pong while HasNextTile(CurrentTile): NextTile = Next_N_Tile(CurrentTile) # Calculate the maximum, online-softmax update, and output rescaling # jointly across the complete current N128 score tile. Update_Online_Softmax_State(ScoreSlot0, ScoreSlot1, OnlineMax, OnlineSum,) Rescale_Output_Accumulator(Output, OnlineMax) # --------------------------------------------------------------- # Process current N64 half 0. # --------------------------------------------------------------- # Convert the current score half into packed NVFP4 probabilities. Probability0 = Exponentiate_And_NVFP4_Quantize(ScoreSlot0) # ScoreSlot0 is now dead. Reuse those same registers for QK belonging # to the next N tile-no second complete score allocation is needed. ScoreSlot0 = Execute_QK_OMMA_N64(Q, K[NextTile, 0:64], delta_s[NextTile, 0:64],) # Accumulate the current tile's first probability half into the output. Output += Execute_PV_OMMA_N64(Probability0, V[CurrentTile, 0:64],) # --------------------------------------------------------------- # Process current N64 half 1. # --------------------------------------------------------------- Probability1 = Exponentiate_And_NVFP4_Quantize(ScoreSlot1) # Reuse the second dead score slot for the next tile. ScoreSlot1 = Execute_QK_OMMA_N64(Q, K[NextTile, 64:128], delta_s[NextTile, 64:128],) Output += Execute_PV_OMMA_N64(Probability1, V[CurrentTile, 64:128],) # ScoreSlot0 and ScoreSlot1 now contain the complete score for NextTile, # while PV for CurrentTile has finished. CurrentTile = NextTile # 4. Pipeline Drain: Consume the Final Score Tile # There is no following tile, so the final score slots are not overwritten # with another QK operation. Update_Online_Softmax_State(ScoreSlot0, ScoreSlot1, OnlineMax, OnlineSum,) Rescale_Output_Accumulator(Output, OnlineMax) Probability0 = Exponentiate_And_NVFP4_Quantize(ScoreSlot0) Output += Execute_PV_OMMA_N64(Probability0, V[CurrentTile, 0:64],) Probability1 = Exponentiate_And_NVFP4_Quantize(ScoreSlot1) Output += Execute_PV_OMMA_N64(Probability1, V[CurrentTile, 64:128],) # 5. Epilogue Output = Output / OnlineSum AsyncStore_BF16(Output) NVFP4 attention kernel integration latency results Reactor evaluated the optimized kernel on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU with 96 GB of memory (SM120), measuring its impact across four world-model workloads. Attention kernel speedup To isolate the scheduling optimization, the original and optimized NVFP4 kernels were compared using identical \(Q/K/V\) inputs, packed tensors, and log-sum-exp settings. Workload / mask Original (ms) Optimized (ms) Speedup LongLive 7,040 / noncausal 0.75052 0.63548 1.18x LongLive 7,040 / causal 0.44992 0.37927 1.19x Synthetic 4,096 / noncausal 0.28962 0.23190 1.25x Synthetic 4,096 / causal 0.21199 0.16087 1.32x Synthetic 8,192 / noncausal 1.00177 0.85648 1.17x Synthetic 8,192 / causal 0.76466 0.46659 1.64x Synthetic 16,384 / noncausal 3.80862 3.25377 1.17x Synthetic 16,384 / causal 2.20630 1.78152 1.24x Table 1. Core NVFP4 latency before and after optimization on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell All cases use batch size 1, 24 heads, head dimension 128, and equal query/key lengths. The 7,040-token input was captured from LongLive; the other inputs are synthetic. Core timing excludes Q/K/V quantization and output-stride restoration Measurements used three fresh processes per implementation, alternating run order, active prewarming, and repeated CUDA-event timing blocks. End-to-end model inference performance Reactor integrated this NVFP4 attention kernel into its production serving infrastructure and used it to serve real customer traffic across several models. Table 2 shows the impact on end-to-end model inference latency on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell. Latency was measured for the complete model path per video chunk, full generation, or action prediction. The table specifies which attention operations use NVFP4; other attention operations and model weights remain BF16. The terms idle and moving refer to camera scenarios with the same NVFP4 coverage. For the video-chunk and action-prediction benchmarks, the BF16 baseline uses native cuDNN attention. Timings include quantization, layout conversion, and decoded CPU-frame or action output, but exclude model loading, warmup, networking, queueing, and client pacing. End-to-end inference latency on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell with BF16 and NVFP4 attention, measured for the output listed in each row Long-run rows measure complete warmed generations through decoded CPU frames, excluding model loading and transport. LongLive and Helios report medians of three independent process runs per arm using eager execution; OmniDreams reports one process per arm/scenario. Latency reductions are calculated from unrounded measurements. This approach helps accelerate world model inference. The core optimization has been merged into the FlashInfer main branch .
