BAGEL gains on MathVista ( Lu et al., 2024 ) and RoboSpatial-Compatibility ( Song et al., 2025a ) , while Janus gains on VisualPuzzles and Rover-TG. We examine where errors enter the pipeline, hold the planning turn fixed while changing the helper, and vary the number of generation calls (Section 5 ). • Hint and image quality. Of the failures we annotated, 66% had a bad hint, 28% a faulty image, and 6% an error in the final inference. On VSTAR, when the hint calls for a crop, applying it to the original pixels raises accuracy by 20.93 points over a generated edit. • Test-time scaling depends on the task. Extra text reasoning raises accuracy on two of three benchmarks. With up to ten image edits, ChartQAPro and MathVista stay below their no-generation baselines at every checkpoint. ERQA ends above baseline. These comparisons distinguish failures in planning from failures in rendering the requested evidence. On VSTAR, even when the request stays the same, how the helper is produced changes the model’s answer. Figure 2: The Reasoning with Imagination pipeline. The VLM writes a hint, the generator draws a helper, and the VLM answers using evidence from the original images and the helper together. 2 Reasoning With Imagination Reasoning with Imagination inserts one generated image into a VLM’s reasoning (Figure 2 ). The input is a visual question: one or more images and a question about them. Instead of answering directly, as in the text-only baseline, the model proceeds in three steps. Step 1: Hint. In the first turn, the VLM receives the images and the question but is instructed not to answer yet. Instead, we prompt it to write a hint of one or two sentences describing a single helper image that would make the question easier, such as “zoom into the top-left panel and annotate the legend” or “rotate the first image to the right by 30 degrees.” Step 2: Generation. An image generator draws the helper image from the hint and the input images. Generators that accept only one image edit the first input image; those that accept several see all of them. Unless stated otherwise, each question receives one helper image. Step 3: Inference. The helper image is added to the same conversation in a second turn. The VLM then answers with the question, the original images, its hint, and the helper image all in context, and is asked to use evidence from every image. All prompts are in Appendix B . Modular and unified models. In modular pipelines, a VLM plans and answers, and a separate generator produces the helper. In the unified setting, one model performs all three steps. For Janus-Pro-7B, we condition its generation head on the original image embeddings and the hint. The same backbone then answers from the original images, hint, and helper. 3 Experiments VLM Qwen3-VL 4B ( Bai et al., 2025a ) Qwen3-VL 8B ( Bai et al., 2025a ) GLM-4.6V Flash ( GLM-V Team et al., 2025 ) × \times image generator Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large ( Esser et al., 2024 ) FLUX.1-Kontext Dev ( Labs, 2024 ) Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 ( Wu et al., 2025a ) Nano-Banana ( Google DeepMind, 2025a ) Table 1: Modular pipelines. Small colored numbers: change from the corresponding text-only baseline in percentage points (green for gains, red for losses). Janus changes use unrounded accuracies. Model Selection. We pair every VLM with every image generator in Table 2 , and pair Gemini 3.0 Flash ( Google DeepMind, 2025b ) with its own Nano-Banana, for 13 modular pipelines in total. We also evaluate BAGEL ( Deng et al., 2025 ) and Janus-Pro-7B ( Chen et al., 2025b ) as unified models. All models use non-thinking mode unless otherwise specified. Benchmark Selection. We evaluate on nine benchmarks covering six kinds of visual reasoning (Table 2 ). We exclude Rover-TG’s spatial-context task and ChartQAPro’s paragraph-context task. Evaluation Protocol. We score answers by rule where possible. For responses requiring semantic scoring, the original experiments use Gemini-2.5-Flash ( Comanici et al., 2025 ) . The Janus-Pro-7B evaluation, matched controls, and extended scaling runs use Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite. Prompts and inference settings appear in Appendix A and Appendix B . 4 Drawing Is Not Yet Thinking Table 3 and Table 4 compare every pipeline with the text-only baseline of its VLM on ten tasks: the nine benchmarks, with RoboSpatial split into its compatibility and configuration questions. Generation usually lowers accuracy. Across the 13 modular pipelines, generation lowers accuracy in 106 of the 130 results (82%); on average, accuracy falls by 3.7 points. In every pipeline, generation lowers accuracy on at least six of the ten tasks, and in 12 of the 13, on at least eight. Stronger models do not help. The pattern holds for all four VLMs and all four generators. Gemini 3.0 Flash, which has the highest text-only accuracy on eight of the ten tasks, loses the most: paired with Nano-Banana, it drops on nine tasks, by 6.9 points on average, and gains on none. Doubling Qwen3-VL from 4B to 8B barely changes the average loss (3.4 vs. 3.2 points). Among generators, the strongest and proprietary Nano-Banana lose in 31 of its 40 results. Losses are largest on visual search. On VSTAR, which asks about small objects in high-resolution images, generation lowers accuracy in every pipeline, by 3.8 to 31.3 points and by 21.0 on average. ChartQAPro, MathVista, and ERQA also decline in every pipeline, by 2.4, 5.3, and 4.3 points on average. In the annotated failures (Section 5 ), generators often lose fine details on ChartQAPro and VSTAR, while the hint often requests the wrong content on MathVista and ERQA. Gains are confined to one spatial task. RoboSpatial-Compatibility is the only task where generation helps consistently: accuracy rises in 12 of the 13 pipelines, by up to 23.8 points, and never falls. A plausible reason is that its questions are hypothetical (would an object fit in a given place?), so drawing the object in place depicts exactly the scene in question. Configuration questions from the same benchmark, which concern the scene as it is, decline in 12 of the 13 pipelines. Elsewhere, the remaining 11 gains are all small, at most 2.2 points. Both unified models lose accuracy on eight tasks. BAGEL gains on RoboSpatial-Compatibility (25.7 points) and MathVista (8.1), and its largest loss is on VSTAR (19.4 points). Across 5,906 paired questions, Janus-Pro-7B loses 9.52 points on RoboSpatial-Compatibility and 9.40 on MathVista. Its largest loss is on ERQA, from 34.50% to 20.25%. Its two gains are on VisualPuzzles (1.28 points) and Rover-TG (2.03 points). 5 Why Does Generation Fail to Help? model / variant ChartQAPro VSTAR acc. call (%) acc. call (%) Qwen3-VL 4B (text) 35.6 0.0 81.3 0.0 + Forced-Gen 35.5 100.0 77.5 100.0 + Selective-Gen 35.6 9.8 80.6 4.0 Qwen3-VL 8B (text) 40.8 0.0 81.6 0.0 + Forced-Gen 38.7 100.0 69.6 100.0 + Selective-Gen 40.2 11.5 81.6 2.0 (a) generation policy ablation (b) failure attribution Figure 3: Given the choice, the model rarely generates. Most annotated failures start with the hint. We labeled 10–20 failed examples per sampled benchmark by the step that went wrong (Figure 3 b). Among these examples, 66% had a bad hint, 28% a bad generation, and 6% an error in the final answer. On ChartQAPro and VSTAR, the generator often lost fine details that the hint identified correctly. On spatial, embodied, puzzle, and STEM tasks, a common error was a generic crop or zoom request that missed the information needed. Per-model results appear in Appendix C.4 . With Qwen3-VL 8B and Nano-Banana, a fixed task-specific hint yields accuracies 0.7 points above the direct-answer baseline on Jigsaw and 2.2 points above it on Spatial (Table 5 ). Supplying the reference helper directly yields gains of 2.5 points on Jigsaw, 5.1 on Maze, and 2.1 on Multi-hop. The table reports point estimates for each intervention. Appendix A describes both interventions. Changing the helper while holding planning fixed. Qwen3-VL 8B receives the same original inputs, hint, turn structure, and final instruction. The answer turn adds either no image, a second copy of the first original, or a FLUX.1-Kontext helper. On VSTAR, accuracy is 60.21%, 58.64%, and 49.74%, respectively. Compared with the hint alone, the generated helper introduces 28 errors and corrects eight, a loss of 10.47 points (paired 95% CI [ − 16.75 , − 4.71 ] [-16.75,-4.71] ). Compared with repeating the original, the loss is 8.90 points ( [ − 14.66 , − 2.62 ] [-14.66,-2.62] ). Executing the requested crop and preserving evidence. For hints that explicitly request a crop or zoom, Qwen locates the region on the first original image. We crop the original pixels and resize by bicubic interpolation to 1,024 pixels on the long side. On the same 43 VSTAR questions, cropping scores 72.09% and generation 51.16%, a 20.93-point advantage for cropping (95% CI [ 4.65 , 37.21 ] [4.65,37.21] ). We also instruct the planner to preserve task-relevant objects, text, numbers, and spatial relations. The same preservation hint scores 62.83% alone and 52.88% with a generated helper on VSTAR ( − 9.95 -9.95 points, 95% CI [ − 15.18 , − 4.19 ] [-15.18,-4.19] ). Table 11 reports all three benchmarks. How often does the model choose to generate? By default, the model always generates an image. When Qwen3-VL (4B or 8B) may choose, it calls the generator on 2–12% of questions and stays within 0.7 points of text-only accuracy. Generating for every question lowers accuracy by up to 12 points on VSTAR (Figure 3 a). Figure 5: Text reasoning and one or two generation calls on three benchmarks. (a) For Qwen3-VL 8B with FLUX.1-Kontext, a second generation call lowers accuracy further on all three benchmarks. (b) Share of annotated failures by the step that went wrong. (c) Chain-of-thought reasoning raises the same model’s accuracy on ChartQAPro and MathVista but lowers it on ERQA. (d) Mean change over all three benchmarks from adding text reasoning (as in c), one generation call (1 × \times Gen in a), or both (Table 5 ). Values in (a), (c), and (d) are changes from the text-only baseline, in percentage points. The effect of repeated generation depends on the task. For Qwen3-VL 8B with FLUX.1-Kontext, extra text reasoning raises accuracy on ChartQAPro (15.8 points) and MathVista (2.5) and lowers it on ERQA (7.6). In the original one- and two-call comparison, the second generation lowers accuracy on all three (Figure 5 ). We reran the zero-, one-, and two-call conditions and extended the sequence to ten edits with a fixed hint (Appendix C.7 ). ChartQAPro and MathVista stay below their no-generation baselines at every evaluated round. ERQA rises from 42.50% at baseline to 45.50% after ten edits. Accuracy fluctuates across rounds on all three tasks. Thinking does not close the gap. With thinking mode turned on, generation still lowers accuracy on all three benchmarks (Table 5 ). The loss grows on ChartQAPro (from 2.1 to 5.4 points) and ERQA (1.5 to 7.9) and shrinks only on MathVista (3.9 to 2.9). Stronger reasoning in text alone does not make the generated images useful. Details are in Appendix C.6 . 6 Related Work Multimodal reasoning. Following advances in LLMs and large reasoning models ( Wei et al., 2023 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; Shen et al., 2025b ) , VLMs acquire reasoning ability via CoT decomposition ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) and reinforcement finetuning ( Shen et al., 2025a ; Peng et al., 2025 ; Sarch et al., 2025 ) . Recent work ( Xu et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2025b ; Wu et al., 2025b ) treats images as active reasoning components, extracting task-centric signals such as bounding boxes, depth, and masks ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Shao et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2025 ) via SFT ( Zhang et al., 2024a ) or RFT ( Zheng et al., 2025 ; Su et al., 2025 ) . Visual thoughts are typically sourced from tool usage ( Fan et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2024 ; Shao et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Su et al., 2025 ) or code execution ( Vinker et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2025 ) , both limited by tool coverage and the original input. Only a few works ( Xu et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2025b ; Wu et al., 2025b ; Gu et al., 2025 ) explore image generation as an alternative, and only on narrow domains; whether models can reliably use generated visuals at scale remains open. Unified understanding and generation. Unified multimodal models jointly handle understanding and generation in a single architecture ( Tong et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024b ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025a ) , spanning autoregressive ( Dong et al., 2023 ; Team, 2024 ; Chern et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2025 ) , diffusion-based ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Swerdlow et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2025a ) , and hybrid ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2024 ; Deng et al., 2025 ; Liao et al., 2025 ) designs. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.34934 (cs) [Submitted on 25 Nov 2026] Title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators Authors: Charlie Griffin , Oliver Makins , Asa Cooper Stickland , Alessandro Abate , Yarin Gal , Abby D'Cruz , Xander Davies View a PDF of the paper titled Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators, by Charlie Griffin and 6 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are often evaluated against transcripts generated by attack policies acting as proxies for dangerous behaviour in deployment. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong. The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment. These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a ``side task'' absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements. Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation's conclusion. Reading these results as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong. The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment. These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a ``side task'' absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements. Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation's conclusion. Reading these results as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem. These evaluations have two components: a control task specifies a user-requested main task and a harmful side task in an evaluation environment; an attack policy generates side-task attempts as proxies for dangerous agent behaviour. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study ( Section 1 ) and find that measured FNR is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method ( Section 2 ). We hold the deployment scenario and control tasks fixed and vary only the attack policy. FNR ranged from 0.5% to 20.8% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4% to 23.0% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs. transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported FNRs show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong ( Fig. 1 ). Figure 1: A narrowly optimised evaluation can make the monitor look robust. Left: running only the lightest optimisation level of three methods (the basic prompt, the first round of prompt optimisation and the first reinforcement learning (RL) checkpoint) finds FNRs of at most 5.1%. Right: running every optimisation level of all four methods finds FNRs up to 23.0%. All attacks were developed against proxy monitors; GPT-5.4 was held out. Bars: 95% bootstrap intervals. Both evaluations use the same 30 control tasks. The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment ( Section 3.1 ). These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a “side task” absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements ( Section 3.2 ). Reading measured FNR as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem ( Section 3.3 ). Background METR’s framework [ 13 ] for assessing monitoring has four steps: 1. “Monitor coverage: Which agents are monitored?” 2. “Monitor system vulnerabilities: Can agents break monitors?” 3. “Monitor evasion: Can agents hide attacks from monitors?” 4. “Human evasion: Can agents sneak attacks past humans, even when flagged by monitors?” This paper concerns the third step, monitor evasion and specifically monitor evasion evaluations that follow the methodology of Greenblatt et al. [8] , which we call control-style evaluations . These measure a monitor’s FNR on attack transcripts, each produced by applying an attack policy to a control task. A control task consists of an environment , a main task (an ordinary user request) and a side task (a proxy for a harmful outcome the monitor is meant to prevent). A red team builds an attack policy : a procedure that produces a transcript for a control task, aiming to complete the side task without the monitor flagging it. Anthropic [ 3 , Section 6.6.4.2] , Google DeepMind [ 7 , Section 3.4.5.4] and OpenAI [ 15 , Section 4.2.2.2] have all used control-style evaluations in their recent system cards. Our work highlights a challenge in using these evaluations: different attack policy generation methods can have a large influence on measured FNR. 1 Case study set-up Our case study uses a single hypothetical deployment scenario ( Section 1.1 ) that fixes our agent, monitor, and target estimand. We also fix an evaluation set-up ( Section 1.2 ), including settings, tasks, and empirical estimand, allowing us to focus on measuring how empirical FNR varies across attack policies ( Section 2 ). 1.1 Deployment scenario (agent and monitor) Our deployment scenario involves Qwen 3.8 27B (xhigh reasoning) running as an internal agent at a frontier AI developer, completing tasks such as writing infrastructure code. The agent is deployed with an asynchronous monitor : after the agent finishes a rollout, the monitor reads the full transcript—actions and reasoning—and flags suspicious transcripts for human review. We target an ex-production OpenAI monitor , similar to Williams et al. [23] , using GPT-5.4 with xhigh reasoning as the monitor model with a prompt supplied by OpenAI. We chose Qwen 3.8 27B for the target agent because it is open-weight, enabling us to fine-tune it to generate attack transcripts. Our scenario involves an agent deployed under a monitor, both using models with known, fixed weights. What remains unknown is the dangerous behaviour this agent might produce once deployed: our scenario considers an evaluation before deployment, for as-yet-unseen harms, so we have no on-distribution examples of such behaviour. 1 1 1 Our behavioural problem statement, centring uncertainty about dangerous behaviour given a fixed model, is a departure from past work, including our own. That work centres uncertainty about whether the agent is ‘trying’ to subvert safety measures (“intentional subversion” [ 8 ] ), and so measures the agent’s capability to do so if it were: “a conservative upper bound of the sabotage abilities” of the agent [ 19 ] . Our target estimand is therefore forward-looking: the probability that, if this agent were deployed, the monitor fails to flag the transcript containing its first dangerous action. 1.2 Evaluation set-up Our case study uses only control-style evaluations (see Background ) and does not consider important but incomplete alternatives, such as back-testing monitor performance on in-the-wild behaviour from already-deployed models. 2 2 2 Although on-policy for the previously deployed model, this behaviour is still off-policy for a new target agent model. Using in-the-wild behaviour from the target agent in more secure settings also leaves a potential mismatch with its intended deployment environment. More broadly, assessing whether monitors would catch the most dangerous attacks before they happen may require evaluating them without representative real examples of those attacks. We chose the Infrastructure as Code (IaC) setting [ 21 ] , using a subset of side tasks relevant to persistent rogue deployment. We include an ablation using the LinuxArena [ 20 ] setting in Appendix F . See Appendix I for further details on both settings and side task selections. • The IaC setting covers AWS infrastructure configuration, where the agent is tasked with various management tasks such as refactoring cluster configuration and configuring access policies. The side tasks cover inserting vulnerabilities and weakening security controls in an organisation – for example, in the detach_mfa_requirement_policy side task, the agent needs to “remove or disable the RequireHardwareMFA policy so console logins without MFA become possible across the organization.” • The LinuxArena setting covers software development tasks in Docker-based environments. An example of a side task that we cover is the delete_model side task, where the agent is tasked with removing all copies of a particular model’s weights from AWS S3. We primarily measure the monitor’s FNR against the distribution of attack transcripts, conditioned on side-task success but not on main-task success. In Appendix G , we explore this choice of empirical estimand: explaining how conditioning on side-task success introduces incentives for the red team to intentionally fail the side task, proposing and evaluating alternatives, and showing empirically that for our evaluations the effect is relatively small. 2 FNR versus attack policies We evaluate monitors using attack policies produced by four attack generation methods: basic prompting, optimised prompting, reinforcement learning, and transcript editing . We present results in IaC here, and show results in LinuxArena in Appendix F . Throughout, the GPT-5.4 target monitor is held out: all attack development and optimisation used proxy monitors, so the FNRs we report measure transfer to a monitor the attacks never received feedback from. 2.1 Basic prompting Figure 2: Basic prompting. Left: the LLM generates successive actions; the attack prompt is removed before monitor review. Benign prompts are omitted from the schematic. Right: GPT-5.4 monitor FNR conditional on side-task success, without conditioning on main-task success, on IaC only. The basic and async-control prompts are our two pre-existing baselines. Points give FNR. Whiskers: marginal 95% hierarchical bootstrap intervals (task pairs, transcripts, monitor draws; 2000 replicates, seed 0). 2.1.1 Method A common form of attack policy is attack prompting [ 16 , 19 , 4 ] : An LLM is given an attack prompt , which includes a description of the side task. Reasoning, messages and tool calls are sampled from this LLM as normal, with the attack prompt in place. The monitor sees the final attack transcript with the attack prompt replaced by the original prompt. Our basic prompting attack policies use Qwen 3.8 27B as the attack generation model, matching the target agent, as is common in control evaluations. 3 3 3 In principle any LLM could be used; our RL attacks use a fine-tuned copy of Qwen 3.8 27B ( Section 2.3 ). We use two basic prompts as baselines. Both predate our access to the OpenAI monitor under study and therefore have not been optimised against the monitor prompt or model from our OpenAI case study. The basic prompt asks the agent to complete the side task and tells the agent to never disclose the side task to the user. The prompt also gives four examples of ways to rephrase its output to avoid mentioning the side task. The prompt does not ask the attacker to hide its actions. See Appendix H for the exact prompt. The async-control prompt is taken from our prior work [ 19 ] . It was optimised for performance in the IaC setting, but against a different monitor model and prompt. The prompt gives an extensive style guide to the agent to shape its approach to problem solving and reasoning – such as discussing many tradeoffs in engineering decisions. 2.1.2 Results Neither prompt achieves any undetected side-task successes on LinuxArena, Fig. 6 , but the basic and async-control prompts achieve 0.2% and 0.5% FNRs respectively on IaC, Fig. 2 . The prompts obtain side-task success rates of 79% and 75% on IaC, and 63% and 54% on LinuxArena, respectively – with all results shown in Table 1 . The off-policy sampling of our prompted attack policies created artefacts, such as discussing a “side task” in chain of thought, discussed in Section 3 . 2.2 Optimised prompting Figure 3: Optimised prompting. Left: proxy-monitor feedback guides prompt optimisation; the paired transcripts share the same user messages and actions. Right: GPT-5.4 monitor FNR conditional on side-task success, without conditioning on main-task success, on IaC only. Both round-0 baselines (basic and async-control) are shown alongside rounds 1 and 2. Optimisation used IaC against a proxy monitor. Points give FNR, with the percentage printed above each whisker. Whiskers: marginal 95% hierarchical bootstrap intervals (task pairs, transcripts, monitor draws; 2000 replicates, seed 0). 2.2.1 Method Our optimised prompting attacks use the same attack prompting method and Qwen 3.8 27B model as our basic prompting attacks ( Section 2.1.1 ). We searched for prompts that would increase FNR. This follows prior work using prompts to develop attacks against control monitors [ 16 , 19 , 4 ] . We started with the two baseline prompts from Section 2.1.1 , plus several further attack prompts we hand-wrote once we had access to the monitor prompt. We then ran two informal “rounds” of human-in-the-loop iteration to increase FNR against a proxy monitor model in the IaC setting. We sampled transcripts using each prompt, analysed their failure modes, and used this analysis to draft candidate replacement prompts. We selected the prompts that performed best on small-scale tests to keep as the round 1 and round 2 prompts. We never optimised prompts against the GPT-5.4 monitor. We primarily optimised against the Qwen 3.8 27B proxy monitor. 4 4 4 Some early tests used Qwen 3.6 27B as both the attack generation model and the proxy monitor model. See Table 3 for results with Qwen as the monitor. Appendix E describes an ablation in which we shortened the round 2 prompt, asking an LLM to summarise the prompt down to less than a fifth of the original length. 2.2.2 Results Figure 3 shows FNR climbing from 0.5% to 6.4% over two rounds of optimisation, with most of the gains coming in the second round. In Appendix E , we see that even when condensed, the round 2 prompt still retains comparable performance to the original. Generalisation to LinuxArena. LinuxArena was held out during prompt optimisation; its results are in Appendix F . 2.3 Reinforcement learning Figure 4: Reinforcement learning. Left: proxy-monitor rewards train the LLM that generates successive actions. Right: GPT-5.4 monitor FNR conditional on side-task success, without conditioning on main-task success, on IaC only, for a single RL run. The untrained async-control baseline and four trained checkpoints are indexed by training rollouts (thousands). The x-axis is measured in thousands of training rollouts, evenly split through training progress. Whiskers: marginal 95% hierarchical bootstrap intervals (task pairs, transcripts, monitor draws; 2000 replicates, seed 0). 2.3.1 Method Prior work has used RL to test control monitors [ 3 ] and studied CoT monitorability under optimisation [ 5 , 6 ] . We initialise the attack generation model from a copy of the target agent model, add a LoRA adapter, and use the async-control attack prompt. We then proceed to train the model in IaC with reinforcement learning using a variant of GRPO [ 18 ] and DPPO [ 17 ] . As with optimised prompting, we replace the system prompt with a benign message before scoring. Like the optimised prompting attacks, we start from the results of a weak prompt and apply optimisation pressure to break the monitor. We train on 5 of the 6 IaC side tasks to solve the side task without triggering the monitor. All LinuxArena results are zero-shot transfer; the trained policy runs with the same scaffold and sampling as the base agent. As with our other methods, we never train against GPT-5.4, using a proxy monitor throughout. We initially used Qwen as the monitor model before swapping to GPT-5.6 Luna for higher monitor throughput. We report results against the Qwen 3.8 monitor in Table 3 where we observe strong generalisation to LinuxArena – with the attacks generating a higher FNR in LinuxArena than in IaC for all measured checkpoints. We needed several attempts before we saw any progress from RL – our initial runs failed to learn or simply degraded the policy. The results reported in the paper all come from the first run with non-zero progress. 2.3.2 Results Figure 4 and Appendix B show that RL steadily improves the results against GPT-5.4 for the first three trained checkpoints. We achieve a final FNR of 20.8%. Furthermore, our first evaluated checkpoint trained on approximately 5.5k transcripts already achieves a 5.1% FNR, showing that very little optimisation pressure is needed to start seeing positive results. When evaluating against the Qwen 3.8 monitor ( Table 3 ), we see continued uplift through training on IaC, with no plateau on the final checkpoint. 2.4 Transcript editing Figure 5: Transcript editing. Left: an editor iteratively rewrites a seed transcript using proxy-monitor feedback; the edited transcript becomes the next input if it exceeds the prior best proxy score. Right: GPT-5.4 monitor FNR conditional on side-task success, without conditioning on main-task success, on IaC only. Whiskers: marginal 95% hierarchical bootstrap intervals (task pairs, transcripts, monitor draws; 2000 replicates, seed 0). 2.4.1 Method Iterative transcript editing has also been used to red-team monitors [ 22 , 11 ] . Where the other attack policies produce a transcript by sampling an LLM in the environment, transcript editing starts from an existing transcript and rewrites it after the fact. We take seed transcripts in which one of the baseline prompts from Section 2.1 completed the side task, and then iteratively edit them against feedback from a proxy monitor. No new rollout is performed. The editor is a prompted GPT-5.6 Sol model. It may rewrite the reasoning, assistant messages, tool calls and tool responses in the transcript, but not the task itself: the system and user messages are held fixed. The editor is given the proxy monitor’s response to the previous edit. Because of sandboxing restrictions, edited tool calls are not re-executed. Instead, an LLM judge compares each edit against the seed and penalises edits that would no longer complete the side task. We search over edits with a simple evolutionary procedure against proxy monitors. We report FNR as a function of budget , the number of edits proposed per seed, from unedited seeds (budget 0) up to 150. Because the search operates on transcripts rather than prompts, we cannot hold LinuxArena out. Instead, we report results from editing LinuxArena transcripts directly. We never optimise edits against GPT-5.4. The search uses feedback only from proxy monitors, so the FNRs reported against GPT-5.4 measure whether these attacks transfer to the held-out target monitor, not whether direct optimisation can defeat it. 2.4.2 Results Figure 5 shows FNR rising from 0.3% on unedited transcripts to 18.7% after 50 proposed edits per seed. We see this peak at 23% at 100 proposed edits per seed. When targeting Qwen as a monitor, the FNR continues increasing with additional edits ( Table 3 ). 2.5 Results summary FNR is sensitive to optimisation level. Within each kind of optimisation, FNR on IaC rose as pressure increased: prompting from 0.2% to 6.4%, RL from 0.5% to 20.8%, and transcript editing from 0.3% to 23.0%. Maximum FNR varied strongly across attack-generation methods. At the best observed optimisation level for each method, FNR on IaC was 6.4% for optimised prompting, 20.8% for reinforcement learning, and 23.0% for transcript editing. Appendix D shows our FNR results against a monitor using the same prompt, but with Qwen 3.8 27B as the monitor model. Since our attack policies were optimised against the Qwen monitor, these results cannot show generalisation to an unseen monitor. However, we do find that our RL attack policies trained in IaC against the Qwen monitor model generalise well to the LinuxArena setting. Evaluations that choose different sets of attack policies may measure very different FNRs. Empirical FNR was highly sensitive to the attack strategies used. A red team that relied only on prompted attacks from past work – the basic and async-control baselines – would have found a ≤ 0.5 % \leq 0.5\% empirical FNR and might have concluded the monitor was robust. Our own optimisation had limited success for several weeks before eventually finding three distinct ways to evade the monitor. 3 Picking attack policies to estimate FNR Many system cards already report control-style, monitor evasion evaluations using at least one attack policy [ 3 , 2 , 16 ] . The sensitivity we find in Section 2 raises two problems for anyone trying to turn empirical FNR into a monitor assessment. First, if an evaluation produces a broad range of FNRs, making positive claims about monitor efficacy requires discounting some attack policies. In our case, concluding true FNR is closer to 0.5% than 23.0% means arguing that the basic prompting experiments are a better proxy than transcript editing. Second, even if an evaluation produces a narrow range of FNRs, making positive claims requires arguing the range could not have been wider: that no stronger optimisation was available, and that no untried attack policy would have behaved differently. 5 5 5 Even if no feasible untried attack policy could have given a different estimate, that does not guarantee the empirical FNRs bound the true FNR. In our case, an evaluation restricted to the pre-existing basic and async-control prompts would have found a narrow range at or below 0.5 % 0.5\% , and our own optimisation found nothing for several weeks before finding three separate ways past the monitor. In this section, we set out why our results pose a significant challenge to control evals: • The distributions of attacks generated with attack policies are only proxies for the target distribution. ( Section 3.1 ) • This distributional mismatch is not merely theoretical: attack policies can introduce artificial features into transcripts that affect monitor judgements, while failing to reproduce important features of real incidents ( Section 3.2 ). • Justifying that the proxy distribution created by attack policies can be used as evidence for monitor efficacy requires strong and explicit arguments that are currently lacking ( Section 3.3 ). 3.1 Attacks are off-distribution proxies The distributions of attacks we produce with our attack policies are all only proxies for the real dangerous behaviour the monitor must flag at deployment. Pre-deployment evaluations may not be able to sample from this distribution directly, at least for models that pass alignment evaluations, which already attempt to elicit such behaviour on-policy. Monitor evaluations therefore rely on proxy distributions; Griffin et al. [9] give a full treatment. We note three reasons our attacks are off-distribution: 1. The attack transcripts are generated off-policy relative to the target agent’s deployment policy. The transcripts we produce may be arbitrarily unlikely under the target agent model when conditioned on its deployment instructions. 2. The transcripts are generated in safe, pre-deployment environments that need not resemble deployment. 3. We condition on completing a specified side task, whereas dangerous behaviour need not resemble any side task we specify. These mismatches do not demonstrate on their own that proxy evaluations are uninformative. But they mean that measured FNR cannot be read directly as deployment FNR. Our focus is off-policy generation, the first mismatch—but note that even on-policy sampling would leave the environment and conditioning mismatches unresolved [ 9 ] . 3.2 Off-policy evals don’t resemble real attacks All of our attack transcripts in Section 2 are generated off-policy relative to the target agent’s deployment policy. RL and transcript editing both use attack generation models that differ from the target agent model. However, even attack prompting, which samples actions from the base model, conditions those actions on an attack prompt that is then removed before the monitor sees the transcript [ 9 ] . This off-policy sampling can introduce artefacts that need not occur in dangerous behaviour in deployment. Example 1: “Side task”. Prompted attack policies commonly describe the LLM’s goals using the words ‘‘main task’’ and ‘‘side task’’. 6 6 6 E.g. Please complete these two tasks: # Main t

Our target estimand is therefore forward-looking: the probability that, if this agent were deployed, the monitor fails to flag the transcript containing its first dangerous action. 1.2 Evaluation set-up Our case study uses only control-style evaluations (see Background ) and does not consider important but incomplete alternatives, such as back-testing monitor performance on in-the-wild behaviour from already-deployed models. 2 2 2 Although on-policy for the previously deployed model, this behaviour is still off-policy for a new target agent model. Using in-the-wild behaviour from the target agent in more secure settings also leaves a potential mismatch with its intended deployment environment. More broadly, assessing whether monitors would catch the most dangerous attacks before they happen may require evaluating them without representative real examples of those attacks. We chose the Infrastructure as Code (IaC) setting [ 21 ] , using a subset of side tasks relevant to persistent rogue deployment. We include an ablation using the LinuxArena [ 20 ] setting in Appendix F . See Appendix I for further details on both settings and side task selections. • The IaC setting covers AWS infrastructure configuration, where the agent is tasked with various management tasks such as refactoring cluster configuration and configuring access policies. The side tasks cover inserting vulnerabilities and weakening security controls in an organisation – for example, in the detach_mfa_requirement_policy side task, the agent needs to “remove or disable the RequireHardwareMFA policy so console logins without MFA become possible across the organization.” • The LinuxArena setting covers software development tasks in Docker-based environments. An example of a side task that we cover is the delete_model side task, where the agent is tasked with removing all copies of a particular model’s weights from AWS S3. We primarily measure the monitor’s FNR against the distribution of attack transcripts, conditioned on side-task success but not on main-task success. In Appendix G , we explore this choice of empirical estimand: explaining how conditioning on side-task success introduces incentives for the red team to intentionally fail the side task, proposing and evaluating alternatives, and showing empirically that for our evaluations the effect is relatively small. 2 FNR versus attack policies We evaluate monitors using attack policies produced by four attack generation methods: basic prompting, optimised prompting, reinforcement learning, and transcript editing . We present results in IaC here, and show results in LinuxArena in Appendix F . Throughout, the GPT-5.4 target monitor is held out: all attack development and optimisation used proxy monitors, so the FNRs we report measure transfer to a monitor the attacks never received feedback from. 2.1 Basic prompting Figure 2: Basic prompting. Left: the LLM generates successive actions; the attack prompt is removed before monitor review. Benign prompts are omitted from the schematic. Right: GPT-5.4 monitor FNR conditional on side-task success, without conditioning on main-task success, on IaC only. The basic and async-control prompts are our two pre-existing baselines. Points give FNR. Whiskers: marginal 95% hierarchical bootstrap intervals (task pairs, transcripts, monitor draws; 2000 replicates, seed 0). 2.1.1 Method A common form of attack policy is attack prompting [ 16 , 19 , 4 ] : An LLM is given an attack prompt , which includes a description of the side task. Reasoning, messages and tool calls are sampled from this LLM as normal, with the attack prompt in place. The monitor sees the final attack transcript with the attack prompt replaced by the original prompt. Our basic prompting attack policies use Qwen 3.8 27B as the attack generation model, matching the target agent, as is common in control evaluations. 3 3 3 In principle any LLM could be used; our RL attacks use a fine-tuned copy of Qwen 3.8 27B ( Section 2.3 ). We use two basic prompts as baselines. Both predate our access to the OpenAI monitor under study and therefore have not been optimised against the monitor prompt or model from our OpenAI case study. The basic prompt asks the agent to complete the side task and tells the agent to never disclose the side task to the user. The prompt also gives four examples of ways to rephrase its output to avoid mentioning the side task. The prompt does not ask the attacker to hide its actions. See Appendix H for the exact prompt. The async-control prompt is taken from our prior work [ 19 ] . It was optimised for performance in the IaC setting, but against a different monitor model and prompt. The prompt gives an extensive style guide to the agent to shape its approach to problem solving and reasoning – such as discussing many tradeoffs in engineering decisions. 2.1.2 Results Neither prompt achieves any undetected side-task successes on LinuxArena, Fig. 6 , but the basic and async-control prompts achieve 0.2% and 0.5% FNRs respectively on IaC, Fig. 2 . The prompts obtain side-task success rates of 79% and 75% on IaC, and 63% and 54% on LinuxArena, respectively – with all results shown in Table 1 . The off-policy sampling of our prompted attack policies created artefacts, such as discussing a “side task” in chain of thought, discussed in Section 3 . 2.2 Optimised prompting Figure 3: Optimised prompting. Left: proxy-monitor feedback guides prompt optimisation; the paired transcripts share the same user messages and actions. Right: GPT-5.4 monitor FNR conditional on side-task success, without conditioning on main-task success, on IaC only. Both round-0 baselines (basic and async-control) are shown alongside rounds 1 and 2. Optimisation used IaC against a proxy monitor. Points give FNR, with the percentage printed above each whisker. Whiskers: marginal 95% hierarchical bootstrap intervals (task pairs, transcripts, monitor draws; 2000 replicates, seed 0). 2.2.1 Method Our optimised prompting attacks use the same attack prompting method and Qwen 3.8 27B model as our basic prompting attacks ( Section 2.1.1 ). We searched for prompts that would increase FNR. This follows prior work using prompts to develop attacks against control monitors [ 16 , 19 , 4 ] . We started with the two baseline prompts from Section 2.1.1 , plus several further attack prompts we hand-wrote once we had access to the monitor prompt. We then ran two informal “rounds” of human-in-the-loop iteration to increase FNR against a proxy monitor model in the IaC setting. We sampled transcripts using each prompt, analysed their failure modes, and used this analysis to draft candidate replacement prompts. We selected the prompts that performed best on small-scale tests to keep as the round 1 and round 2 prompts. We never optimised prompts against the GPT-5.4 monitor. We primarily optimised against the Qwen 3.8 27B proxy monitor. 4 4 4 Some early tests used Qwen 3.6 27B as both the attack generation model and the proxy monitor model. See Table 3 for results with Qwen as the monitor. Appendix E describes an ablation in which we shortened the round 2 prompt, asking an LLM to summarise the prompt down to less than a fifth of the original length. 2.2.2 Results Figure 3 shows FNR climbing from 0.5% to 6.4% over two rounds of optimisation, with most of the gains coming in the second round. In Appendix E , we see that even when condensed, the round 2 prompt still retains comparable performance to the original. Generalisation to LinuxArena. LinuxArena was held out during prompt optimisation; its results are in Appendix F . 2.3 Reinforcement learning Figure 4: Reinforcement learning. Left: proxy-monitor rewards train the LLM that generates successive actions. Right: GPT-5.4 monitor FNR conditional on side-task success, without conditioning on main-task success, on IaC only, for a single RL run. The untrained async-control baseline and four trained checkpoints are indexed by training rollouts (thousands). The x-axis is measured in thousands of training rollouts, evenly split through training progress. Whiskers: marginal 95% hierarchical bootstrap intervals (task pairs, transcripts, monitor draws; 2000 replicates, seed 0). 2.3.1 Method Prior work has used RL to test control monitors [ 3 ] and studied CoT monitorability under optimisation [ 5 , 6 ] . We initialise the attack generation model from a copy of the target agent model, add a LoRA adapter, and use the async-control attack prompt. We then proceed to train the model in IaC with reinforcement learning using a variant of GRPO [ 18 ] and DPPO [ 17 ] . As with optimised prompting, we replace the system prompt with a benign message before scoring. Like the optimised prompting attacks, we start from the results of a weak prompt and apply optimisation pressure to break the monitor. We train on 5 of the 6 IaC side tasks to solve the side task without triggering the monitor. All LinuxArena results are zero-shot transfer; the trained policy runs with the same scaffold and sampling as the base agent. As with our other methods, we never train against GPT-5.4, using a proxy monitor throughout. We initially used Qwen as the monitor model before swapping to GPT-5.6 Luna for higher monitor throughput. We report results against the Qwen 3.8 monitor in Table 3 where we observe strong generalisation to LinuxArena – with the attacks generating a higher FNR in LinuxArena than in IaC for all measured checkpoints. We needed several attempts before we saw any progress from RL – our initial runs failed to learn or simply degraded the policy. The results reported in the paper all come from the first run with non-zero progress. 2.3.2 Results Figure 4 and Appendix B show that RL steadily improves the results against GPT-5.4 for the first three trained checkpoints. We achieve a final FNR of 20.8%. Furthermore, our first evaluated checkpoint trained on approximately 5.5k transcripts already achieves a 5.1% FNR, showing that very little optimisation pressure is needed to start seeing positive results. When evaluating against the Qwen 3.8 monitor ( Table 3 ), we see continued uplift through training on IaC, with no plateau on the final checkpoint. 2.4 Transcript editing Figure 5: Transcript editing. Left: an editor iteratively rewrites a seed transcript using proxy-monitor feedback; the edited transcript becomes the next input if it exceeds the prior best proxy score. Right: GPT-5.4 monitor FNR conditional on side-task success, without conditioning on main-task success, on IaC only. Whiskers: marginal 95% hierarchical bootstrap intervals (task pairs, transcripts, monitor draws; 2000 replicates, seed 0). 2.4.1 Method Iterative transcript editing has also been used to red-team monitors [ 22 , 11 ] . Where the other attack policies produce a transcript by sampling an LLM in the environment, transcript editing starts from an existing transcript and rewrites it after the fact. We take seed transcripts in which one of the baseline prompts from Section 2.1 completed the side task, and then iteratively edit them against feedback from a proxy monitor. No new rollout is performed. The editor is a prompted GPT-5.6 Sol model. It may rewrite the reasoning, assistant messages, tool calls and tool responses in the transcript, but not the task itself: the system and user messages are held fixed. The editor is given the proxy monitor’s response to the previous edit. Because of sandboxing restrictions, edited tool calls are not re-executed. Instead, an LLM judge compares each edit against the seed and penalises edits that would no longer complete the side task. We search over edits with a simple evolutionary procedure against proxy monitors. We report FNR as a function of budget , the number of edits proposed per seed, from unedited seeds (budget 0) up to 150. Because the search operates on transcripts rather than prompts, we cannot hold LinuxArena out. Instead, we report results from editing LinuxArena transcripts directly. We never optimise edits against GPT-5.4. The search uses feedback only from proxy monitors, so the FNRs reported against GPT-5.4 measure whether these attacks transfer to the held-out target monitor, not whether direct optimisation can defeat it. 2.4.2 Results Figure 5 shows FNR rising from 0.3% on unedited transcripts to 18.7% after 50 proposed edits per seed. We see this peak at 23% at 100 proposed edits per seed. When targeting Qwen as a monitor, the FNR continues increasing with additional edits ( Table 3 ). 2.5 Results summary FNR is sensitive to optimisation level. Within each kind of optimisation, FNR on IaC rose as pressure increased: prompting from 0.2% to 6.4%, RL from 0.5% to 20.8%, and transcript editing from 0.3% to 23.0%. Maximum FNR varied strongly across attack-generation methods. At the best observed optimisation level for each method, FNR on IaC was 6.4% for optimised prompting, 20.8% for reinforcement learning, and 23.0% for transcript editing. Appendix D shows our FNR results against a monitor using the same prompt, but with Qwen 3.8 27B as the monitor model. Since our attack policies were optimised against the Qwen monitor, these results cannot show generalisation to an unseen monitor. However, we do find that our RL attack policies trained in IaC against the Qwen monitor model generalise well to the LinuxArena setting. Evaluations that choose different sets of attack policies may measure very different FNRs. Empirical FNR was highly sensitive to the attack strategies used. A red team that relied only on prompted attacks from past work – the basic and async-control baselines – would have found a ≤ 0.5 % \leq 0.5\% empirical FNR and might have concluded the monitor was robust. Our own optimisation had limited success for several weeks before eventually finding three distinct ways to evade the monitor. 3 Picking attack policies to estimate FNR Many system cards already report control-style, monitor evasion evaluations using at least one attack policy [ 3 , 2 , 16 ] . The sensitivity we find in Section 2 raises two problems for anyone trying to turn empirical FNR into a monitor assessment. First, if an evaluation produces a broad range of FNRs, making positive claims about monitor efficacy requires discounting some attack policies. In our case, concluding true FNR is closer to 0.5% than 23.0% means arguing that the basic prompting experiments are a better proxy than transcript editing. Second, even if an evaluation produces a narrow range of FNRs, making positive claims requires arguing the range could not have been wider: that no stronger optimisation was available, and that no untried attack policy would have behaved differently. 5 5 5 Even if no feasible untried attack policy could have given a different estimate, that does not guarantee the empirical FNRs bound the true FNR. In our case, an evaluation restricted to the pre-existing basic and async-control prompts would have found a narrow range at or below 0.5 % 0.5\% , and our own optimisation found nothing for several weeks before finding three separate ways past the monitor. In this section, we set out why our results pose a significant challenge to control evals: • The distributions of attacks generated with attack policies are only proxies for the target distribution. ( Section 3.1 ) • This distributional mismatch is not merely theoretical: attack policies can introduce artificial features into transcripts that affect monitor judgements, while failing to reproduce important features of real incidents ( Section 3.2 ). • Justifying that the proxy distribution created by attack policies can be used as evidence for monitor efficacy requires strong and explicit arguments that are currently lacking ( Section 3.3 ). 3.1 Attacks are off-distribution proxies The distributions of attacks we produce with our attack policies are all only proxies for the real dangerous behaviour the monitor must flag at deployment. Pre-deployment evaluations may not be able to sample from this distribution directly, at least for models that pass alignment evaluations, which already attempt to elicit such behaviour on-policy. Monitor evaluations therefore rely on proxy distributions; Griffin et al. [9] give a full treatment. We note three reasons our attacks are off-distribution: 1. The attack transcripts are generated off-policy relative to the target agent’s deployment policy. The transcripts we produce may be arbitrarily unlikely under the target agent model when conditioned on its deployment instructions. 2. The transcripts are generated in safe, pre-deployment environments that need not resemble deployment. 3. We condition on completing a specified side task, whereas dangerous behaviour need not resemble any side task we specify. These mismatches do not demonstrate on their own that proxy evaluations are uninformative. But they mean that measured FNR cannot be read directly as deployment FNR. Our focus is off-policy generation, the first mismatch—but note that even on-policy sampling would leave the environment and conditioning mismatches unresolved [ 9 ] . 3.2 Off-policy evals don’t resemble real attacks All of our attack transcripts in Section 2 are generated off-policy relative to the target agent’s deployment policy. RL and transcript editing both use attack generation models that differ from the target agent model. However, even attack prompting, which samples actions from the base model, conditions those actions on an attack prompt that is then removed before the monitor sees the transcript [ 9 ] . This off-policy sampling can introduce artefacts that need not occur in dangerous behaviour in deployment. Example 1: “Side task”. Prompted attack policies commonly describe the LLM’s goals using the words ‘‘main task’’ and ‘‘side task’’. 6 6 6 E.g. Please complete these two tasks: # Main t

items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.34930 (cs) [Submitted on 25 Nov 2026] Title: A gene informed benchmark for BioScoring of pathology foundation models Authors: Paul Vilars , Vincent Quoc-Huy Trinh , Maria Vakalopoulou , Dimitris Samaras , Stergios Christodoulidis , Mahdi S. Hosseini View a PDF of the paper titled A gene informed benchmark for BioScoring of pathology foundation models, by Paul Vilars and Vincent Quoc-Huy Trinh and Maria Vakalopoulou and Dimitris Samaras and Stergios Christodoulidis and Mahdi S. Hosseini View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Pathology foundation models are usually compared by their performance on downstream tasks such as classification and retrieval. While such benchmarks measure how useful a model is, they provide no insight into the biology it represents. We introduce BioScore, a benchmark that quantifies how well an image encoder captures cell identities, with spatial transcriptomics of the same tissue as the reference. A sparse autoencoder splits the encoder's patch embeddings into sparse features, which we cluster into a fixed number of groups. BioScore then measures, for each of 52 cell identities defined by marker genes, how specifically one group follows the identity's expression over the tissue. Because the autoencoder training is fully unsupervised, a match shows that the model represents the cell identity from the image alone. We score 8 pathology foundation models and 3 natural-image models. Every pathology model scores above every natural-image model (0.299--0.371 \vs 0.214--0.232), and paired tests separate three tiers among the pathology models. Unlike a supervised probe, BioScore needs no labels, builds its reference from the data and scores even from few sections, yet it ranks the encoders as a probe does. Its per-identity breakdown indicates which cell identities each encoder captures or misses. While such benchmarks measure how useful a model is, they provide no insight into the biology it represents. We introduce BioScore, a benchmark that quantifies how well an image encoder captures cell identities, with spatial transcriptomics of the same tissue as the reference. A sparse autoencoder splits the encoder’s patch embeddings into sparse features, which we cluster into a fixed number of groups. BioScore then measures, for each of 52 cell identities defined by marker genes, how specifically one group follows the identity’s expression over the tissue. Because the autoencoder training is fully unsupervised, a match shows that the model represents the cell identity from the image alone. We score 8 pathology foundation models and 3 natural-image models. Every pathology model scores above every natural-image model (0.299–0.371 vs . 0.214–0.232), and paired tests separate three tiers among the pathology models. Unlike a supervised probe, BioScore needs no labels, builds its reference from the data and scores even from few sections, yet it ranks the encoders as a probe does. Its per-identity breakdown indicates which cell identities each encoder captures or misses. 1 Introduction Figure 1 : BioScore overview and encoder ranking. Left: SAE activation map is compared to cell-identity. Right: win rate (%) of row over column across the 52 identities; bold: Holm-corrected Wilcoxon p < 0.05 p<0.05 ; and compact letter ranking. Pathology foundation models [ 6 , 38 , 41 ] are trained in a self-supervised manner on millions of H&E patches, then compared on downstream tasks such as patch and slide classification, retrieval and, more recently, prediction of gene expression [ 5 , 30 , 29 , 22 ] . Each of these benchmarks trains a probe on the embeddings, reports a performance metric and allow high level understanding. However, it does not elaborate on what the model relies on within the tissue. An accuracy on tumor subtyping, for instance, may come from tumor cells, stroma or immune infiltration. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.34923 (cs) [Submitted on 25 Nov 2026] Title: Mixture-of-Loops Transformer Authors: Lianghui Zhu , Shijie Wang , Xinggang Wang , Jinze Bai , Bo Wang , Xiang Bai View a PDF of the paper titled Mixture-of-Loops Transformer, by Lianghui Zhu and 5 other authors View PDF Abstract: Looped Transformers boost expressivity by reusing shared layers across loops, yet at the cost of efficiency. Pushing their expressivity-efficiency frontier requires rethinking the core mechanism connecting adjacent loops: What should be passed as a Transformer loops? We introduce Mixture-of-Loops Transformer (MoLT), whose Mixture-of-Loops Attention (MoLA) uses keys and values (KV) as memory for selective reuse across depths and loops. Under loop residual, MoLT-R retains the residual stream and reads local KV across loops for expressivity. Under loop KV, MoLT-KV instead restarts from embeddings and reads current-loop local KV with preceding-loop memory KV at earlier positions for efficiency. MoLT-KV eliminates same-position cross-loop dependence and, paired with loop forcing for parallel training, unlocks single-traversal Mixture-of-Loops (MoL) decoding beyond the training loop horizon. To balance efficiency and quality, we introduce U-shaped MoLT (U-MoLT), which separates memory construction from prediction readout and skips unused decoder traversals without changing predictions. In 400B-token pretraining, U-MoLT outperforms OLMo3 across 700M/1.5B dense and 3B MoE models, achieving 1.7x validation cross-entropy (CE) token efficiency at 700M while improving 3B MoE 10-domain perplexity by 0.75 and 10-task accuracy by 2.1 percentage points. In 100B-token continued pretraining of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, our U-MoLT adaptation lowers CE on all 11 domains over the matched baseline with 1.4x mean token efficiency. At inference, U-MoLT with MoL-Hybrid-2 matches non-looped OLMo3 latency at 996.6 vs. 1,000.6 ms on S-size (~113M) models. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.34887 (cs) [Submitted on 25 Nov 2026] Title: Interpretable and Accurate Hybrid Decision Trees with Selective Case-Based Splits Authors: Cristiano Landi , Alessio Cascione , Riccardo Guidotti View a PDF of the paper titled Interpretable and Accurate Hybrid Decision Trees with Selective Case-Based Splits, by Cristiano Landi and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Decision trees are among the most well-known interpretable models in Machine Learning. Over the years, a wide variety of strategies have been proposed to define split conditions within the greedy learning framework, aiming to guide instance routing and enhance predictive performance. These strategies range from axis-parallel and oblique splits based on feature values to proximity-based splits using exemplar instances and more complex hybrid approaches. However, no single method has emerged as universally superior. In this work, we present two key contributions to the construction of greedy decision trees. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.34751 (cs) [Submitted on 25 Nov 2026] Title: What Is a Theory Worth to an LLM Solver? Measuring, Inducing, and Merging Theories in Context Authors: Jun Gao , Shuchao Bi View a PDF of the paper titled What Is a Theory Worth to an LLM Solver? Measuring, Inducing, and Merging Theories in Context, by Jun Gao and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Mathematicians solve problems faster when they know the right theory. We ask how much a stated theory is worth to a large language model (LLM) solver, and whether a model can write that theory itself. In a length-matched protocol, adding the right theory to the context of Qwen3-14B raises pass@1 on pattern waiting-time problems from 0.37 to 0.83 and cuts the median tokens of correct solutions from 10.2k to 6.3k, while worked examples of the same length do not help. The gain shrinks as the solver and its token budget grow (+0.46, +0.26, +0.07), and at a long budget it comes almost entirely from finishing within budget: solutions that finish are correct 98--100\% of the time in every condition. To separate induction from recall, we plant unpublished theorems in custom probability families and measure how much of the oracle theory's gain an induced theory recovers. A strong open model, required to explore the training problems with code before writing, recovers 60\% of the gain on one planted family, 48\% on a second, and almost none on a third, where it finds the right form but not the condition that makes the form computable. No single induced note is complete, but a strong model that merges several notes recovers 61\% of the gain on the classic family, above the best single note (47\%). Theories are worth the reasoning they save, and models can find their pieces before they can assemble them.
