items.content: What Is a Theory Worth to an LLM Solver? Measuring, Inducing, and Merging Theories in Context Jun Gao Shuchao Bi Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Inc. Abstract Mathematicians solve problems faster when they know the right theory. We ask how much a stated theory is worth to a large language model (LLM) solver, and whether a model can write that theory itself. In a length-matched protocol, adding the right theory to the context of Qwen3-14B raises pass@1 on pattern waiting-time problems from 0.37 to 0.83 and cuts the median tokens of correct solutions from 10.2k to 6.3k, while worked examples of the same length do not help. The gain shrinks as the solver and its token budget grow (+0.46, +0.26, +0.07), and at a long budget it comes almost entirely from finishing within budget: solutions that finish are correct 98–100% of the time in every condition. To separate induction from recall, we plant unpublished theorems in custom probability families and measure how much of the oracle theory’s gain an induced theory recovers. A strong open model, required to explore the training problems with code before writing, recovers 60% of the gain on one planted family, 48% on a second, and almost none on a third, where it finds the right form but not the condition that makes the form computable. No single induced note is complete, but a strong model that merges several notes recovers 61% of the gain on the classic family, above the best single note (47%). Theories are worth the reasoning they save, and models can find their pieces before they can assemble them. 1 Introduction A student who knows Conway’s leading numbers computes the expected waiting time for a coin pattern in a few lines; a student who does not sets up and solves a linear system over the pattern’s prefixes. Both can be right, but only one is efficient. Large language models (LLMs) increasingly solve such problems with long chains of thought [ 14 ] , and their resource use grows with the reasoning they must produce [ 11 ] . This raises two questions. First, how much is a stated theory worth to an LLM solver: how much accuracy does it add and how much reasoning does it save? Second, can a model induce such a theory from problems alone, so that it uses the compute of discovery once rather than on every problem? Answering either question cleanly is harder than it looks. Adding text to the context changes its length; examples and theory can carry the same information; and a model that “induces” a classic theorem may simply be recalling it. We address these confounds with three design choices. (i) All conditions use contexts of the same length, and we compare the oracle theory with irrelevant text, a generic hint, and worked examples of the same length. (ii) We report the recovery ratio R R , the share of the oracle theory’s accuracy gain that an induced theory recovers. (iii) To separate induction from recall, we plant unpublished theorems in custom probability families, verify that no model can state them before seeing the problems, and only then let models induce theories from training problems. Contributions. • A controlled protocol for measuring the value of a theory in context, with length-matched controls, paired bootstrap intervals and a recovery ratio (Section 2 ). • Evidence that a stated theory makes a solver both more accurate and cheaper, that worked examples do not substitute for it, and that at long budgets its value is almost entirely the reasoning it saves (Sections 3 and 6 ). • A planted-theorem design that separates induction from recall: custom probability families with unpublished theorems that no model can state before seeing the problems, with evidence that a strong open model can induce such theorems when forced to explore with code, and a characterization of how it fails: the right form without the condition, or a special case without the general law (Section 4 ). • Evidence that no single induced theory is complete but that a strong model can merge partial theories from several inducers, without test information, into one that passes our success bar (Section 5 ). 2 Setup 2.1 Problem families Every family has an automatically graded numeric answer, a key theory that makes the problems easy, a generator for fresh parameters, and a solver accuracy without the theory that leaves room for improvement. Table 1 summarizes them. • Family (a): pattern waiting times (classic). Expected waiting times for coin patterns, probabilities that one pattern appears before another, and waiting times for either of two patterns. The key theory is Conway’s overlap numbers and the martingale method [ 5 , 3 ] . Every answer is computed twice, from the overlap numbers and from the pattern automaton, and the two must agree. We use 40 training and 160 test problems at the difficulty where the solver without theory scores 0.38 in calibration. • Family (b): symmetric colouring counts (classic). Counting colourings up to symmetry, with Burnside’s lemma and Pólya enumeration [ 8 ] as the theory; 156 problems, about 20% of them traps. • F1: carry-over rearrangements on a necklace (planted). A ring of L L sites with K K colours. Each window of three sites ( x , y , z ) (x,y,z) moves forward to ( y , z , x ⊕ 1 ) (y,z,x\oplus 1) at rate f ⁡ ( x , y , z ) f(x,y,z) and backward at rate g g , so the chain is not reversible. The planted theorem states that if a weighted flux is constant on every orbit of the window map, the stationary law is a product law with explicit weights. Held-out problems have between 1.4 × 10 7 1.4\times 10^{7} and 3.9 × 10 8 3.9\times 10^{8} states. • F2: carry-over swaps of neighbouring pairs (planted). A pair ( x , y ) (x,y) becomes ( y , x ⊕ 1 ) (y,x\oplus 1) at a rate that also depends on the two outer neighbours. The planted theorem states that if f ⁡ ( u , x , y , v ) ​ M ​ ( u , x ) ​ M ​ ( x , y ) ​ M ​ ( y , v ) f(u,x,y,v)\,M(u,x)M(x,y)M(y,v) is constant on every orbit of the pair map, the stationary law is a nearest-neighbour (transfer-matrix) law π ⁡ ( η ) ∝ ∏ j M ⁡ ( η j , η j + 1 ) \pi(\eta)\propto\prod_{j}M(\eta_{j},\eta_{j+1}) , not a product law. • F3: a random collision process (planted). Pairs of particles of K K kinds collide and either vanish or turn into another pair. The planted theorem states that if weights b b satisfy one linear equation per pair of kinds, the expected total penalty until the box is empty is ∑ c b c ​ n c \sum_{c}b_{c}n_{c} , by optional stopping on a linear potential. For the planted families, the exact solution equals the planted theorem on every verification instance (F2 48/48, F3 48/48), about 20% of held-out problems are traps on which the theorem does not apply, and misapplying the theorem on a trap gives one predictable wrong number, so misapplication is measurable. A planted family is used only if the oracle theory raises held-out accuracy by at least 0.20 in calibration (F2 +0.83, F3 +0.58). As a classic control under the identical planted-family protocol, we also run family (a) (“P5b”). Table 1: Problem families. “Oracle gain” is held-out pass@1 with the oracle theory minus without it, for the confirmatory solver and cap (Table 2 ). Family Kind Theory Oracle gain (a) waiting times classic Conway overlap numbers / martingale +0.46 (12k) (b) colouring counts classic Burnside / Pólya solver already knows it F1 necklace rearrangements planted orbit-flux condition ⇒ \Rightarrow product law +0.76 (12k) F2 neighbouring-pair swaps planted orbit condition ⇒ \Rightarrow transfer-matrix law +0.82 (32k) F3 collision process planted linear potential ⇒ \Rightarrow expected penalty +0.63 (32k) P5b = (a) under planted protocol classic Conway overlap numbers +0.35 (32k) 2.2 Conditions The solver is fixed within each comparison and sees one of the following contexts, all padded with neutral text to the same token count: NoTheory (padding only); Oracle (the human-written theory; in family (a) it includes one worked example that is not a test problem); Irrelevant (an unrelated theory of the same length; family (a)); GenericHint (a generic hint to look for a product form or invariant; planted families); Examples (worked training solutions that use the method; family (a)); Induced-weak and Induced-strong (theories induced by Qwen3-32B and by Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 [ 15 ] , respectively; in family (a), the strong inducers also include the original Qwen3-235B-A22B); and Merged (a theory produced by a model that merges several induced theories). Appendix A maps these names to the condition labels of our preregistrations. Induction. An inducer sees only the training problems and its own solution attempts, may run code on small instances, and writes a theory no longer than the oracle text that states when it applies and contains no answer to a specific problem. It never sees the planted theorem or any held-out problem. We run three independent inductions per inducer. In our first protocol, models wrote theories without running any code, and their theories were guesses; even the strong model attempted to write a theory before any exploration in all three runs. Our second protocol, used for all planted-family results, shows the model how to read the data and accepts a theory only after at least three code runs. In family (a), induction instead generates several candidate theories and selects among them on a validation split of the training problems (Appendix D ). Solvers and sampling. Qwen3-14B in thinking mode (temperature 0.6, top- p p 0.95, top- k k 20) is the main solver, at token caps of 12k and 32k; Qwen3.6-27B at 32k and 64k is a second, stronger solver. We draw k = 8 k=8 samples per problem in family (a) and k = 3 k=3 in the planted families. 2.3 Metrics We report pass@1, the median number of tokens of correct solutions, and the share of samples truncated at the cap. The recovery ratio of an induced theory is R = acc ⁡ ( induced ) − acc ⁡ ( NoTheory ) acc ⁡ ( Oracle ) − acc ⁡ ( NoTheory ) , R\;=\;\frac{\mathrm{acc}(\text{induced})-\mathrm{acc}(\textsc{NoTheory})}{\mathrm{acc}(\textsc{Oracle})-\mathrm{acc}(\textsc{NoTheory})}, (1) computed on non-trap held-out problems with 95% paired bootstrap intervals; with three inductions, R R uses the mean accuracy over the three theories. Induction succeeds (H2) if R ≥ 0.5 R\geq 0.5 and the induced theory beats GenericHint (or Irrelevant ) with an interval excluding zero. On traps we report the misapplication rate. A blind LLM judge classifies each induced theory against the planted theorem as (i) the same, (ii) equivalent, (iii) a partial or special case, (iv) wrong but useful, or (v) wrong, by two-of-three majority. Two judges agree poorly (Appendix E ), so judge classes are descriptive and solver accuracy is the primary evidence. Recall controls. Before any inducer sees the problems, we ask it whether it knows a closed form for the family (the contamination probe). In family (a) we also rename symbols and stories. For the planted families, no probe answer states the planted condition (Section 4 ). 3 A theory in context makes the solver more accurate and cheaper Figure 1: Family (a): pass@1 (left) and median tokens of correct solutions (right) without and with the oracle theory, for three solver and cap settings. The accuracy gain shrinks as the solver and budget grow. The theory halves tokens at 12k and 32k and matches NoTheory at 64k (where it is about 30% cheaper than Irrelevant and a searched induced theory). On family (a) with Qwen3-14B at a 12k cap, the oracle theory raises pass@1 from 0.37 to 0.83 (paired difference + 0.46 +0.46 [ + 0.41 +0.41 , + 0.52 +0.52 ]) and pass@8 from 0.68 to 0.99. Correct solutions use a median of 6.3k tokens instead of 10.2k, and the share of samples truncated at the cap falls from 59% to 14% (Figure 1 ). Length alone does nothing: an irrelevant theory of the same length changes pass@1 by − 0.02 -0.02 (interval including zero). Worked examples do not substitute for the theory either: training solutions that use exactly the method change pass@1 by − 0.02 -0.02 , and the theory beats them by + 0.48 +0.48 . The gain is not surface matching: with renamed symbols and stories it is + 0.51 +0.51 , against + 0.47 +0.47 on the same original problems. The gain shrinks as the solver gets stronger. The 12k cap truncates most solutions without the theory, so part of the gain is finishing within budget. With a 32k cap the same solver without the theory reaches 0.65 and truncation falls to 1%; the theory still adds + 0.26 +0.26 [ + 0.22 +0.22 , + 0.31 +0.31 ] and halves the tokens of correct solutions (12.6k to 6.4k). Qwen3.6-27B at a 64k cap is close to the ceiling without the theory (0.88); the theory adds + 0.07 +0.07 [ + 0.04 +0.04 , + 0.10 +0.10 ], and its correct solutions are about as long as those without it (22.0k vs. 21.1k) but about 30% shorter than with the irrelevant theory or a searched induced theory (29–33k). Negative control: a theory the solver already knows. On family (b), Qwen3-14B scores 0.86–0.95 without the theory, and even with Qwen3-4B the Burnside/Pólya theory adds only + 0.022 +0.022 (not significant) at 12k and 32k; trap problems did not induce the solver to misapply it. A theory is worth what the solver does not already know. 4 Can a model induce an unpublished theory? Table 2: Induced theories across families (non-trap held-out accuracy, k = 3 k=3 ). The three numbers in the induced columns are the three independent inductions. R R is reported with 95% paired bootstrap intervals; H2 requires R Induced-strong ≥ 0.5 R_{\textsc{Induced-strong}}\geq 0.5 and Induced-strong > GenericHint \textsc{Induced-strong}>\textsc{GenericHint} . Judge classes are the blind classification of the three Induced-strong theories by the primary judge (gpt-oss-120b) and, after the slash, the secondary judge (Muse Spark 1.3); the two agree poorly (Appendix E ). Generated from the result files by a script (Appendix F ). Family Solver, cap NoTheory GenericHint Oracle Induced-weak Induced-strong R Induced-weak R_{\textsc{Induced-weak}} / R Induced-strong R_{\textsc{Induced-strong}} H2; judge F1 Qwen3-14B, 12k 0.02 0.08 0.78 .17/.69/.10 .40/.43/.59 0.39 [.34,.46] / 0.60 [.51,.68] met; ii, split, iii / – F1 Qwen3-14B, 32k 0.16 0.28 0.94 .40/.87/.26 .62/.70/.66 0.45 [.37,.53] / 0.65 [.55,.74] (robustness) F1 Qwen3.6-27B, 32k 0.01 0.08 0.48 .07/.41/.06 .15/.04/.31 0.35 [.27,.44] / 0.33 [.24,.43] (robustness) F1 Qwen3.6-27B, 64k 0.58 0.65 0.99 – .88/.69/.65 – / 0.40 [.24,.54] (mechanism) F2 Qwen3-14B, 32k 0.00 0.01 0.82 .00/.00/.00 .00/.00/.01 0.00 [.00,.00] / 0.00 [.00,.01] fails; v, iii, iii / iii, iii, v F3 Qwen3-14B, 32k 0.37 0.72 1.00 .15/.65/.18 .01/1.00/.99 − - 0.07 [ − - .24,.07] / 0.48 [.38,.54] not met; v, ii, ii / v, ii, i P5b Qwen3-14B, 32k 0.56 0.60 0.91 .44/.55/.58 .74/.96/.82 − - 0.11 [ − - .41,.10] / 0.81 [.67,.96] met; iii, iii, iii / iii, ii, iii Figure 2: Recovery ratio R R by family and inducer (confirmatory settings of Table 2 ), with 95% intervals. The strong inducer passes the bar on one planted family (F1) and on the classic control (P5b), reaches it on average on F3 with one harmful theory, and fails on F2. Table 2 and Figure 2 give the results across families. The strong inducer succeeds on F1, comes close on F3, fails on F2, and succeeds on the classic control, where recall cannot be ruled out. The weak inducer recovers 39% on F1 and essentially nothing elsewhere. F1: induction succeeds. The strong inducer’s theories recover R = 0.60 R=0.60 [0.51, 0.68] of the oracle gain and beat the generic hint by + 0.40 +0.40 [0.32, 0.48]. Two of its three runs rediscover the planted condition: executed literally, their rules agree with the planted theorem on all 30 training problems, all 48 held-out non-trap problems, and all 12 traps, which they correctly reject. The best single theory comes from the weak inducer (the planted condition in reciprocal form, R = 0.89 R=0.89 ), but the weak inducer finds the rule in one run of three and the strong inducer in two. The result holds at a 32k cap ( R = 0.65 R=0.65 ). With Qwen3.6-27B at 32k it falls to 0.33, because 99% of that solver’s samples without the theory and 53% with it are truncated; of the solutions that finish, 284 of 285 are correct. A post-hoc analysis at 12k shows that the largest loss in every condition is failing to write an answer within the budget; one strong theory’s recipe is off by one in a single step, and exactly 18 answers equal the resulting wrong value; and problems with backward moves are hard for every condition, including the oracle (29 of 54 correct). This is induction, not recall. Before seeing any problem, neither inducer states the planted condition: all 16 probe answers reason through detailed balance, and none gives the condition. The models’ prior is that the beads are independent; the condition is induced from the data. F2: the right form without the condition. On F2 the strong inducer recovers R = 0.003 R=0.003 [0.000, 0.008]. Two of its three theories state the correct nearest-neighbour form, but neither states the orbit condition that determines the weight matrix M M , so the solver cannot compute M M and the theory is useless (Box 4 ). items.raw_text: What Is a Theory Worth to an LLM Solver? Measuring, Inducing, and Merging Theories in Context Jun Gao Shuchao Bi Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Inc. Abstract Mathematicians solve problems faster when they know the right theory. We ask how much a stated theory is worth to a large language model (LLM) solver, and whether a model can write that theory itself. In a length-matched protocol, adding the right theory to the context of Qwen3-14B raises pass@1 on pattern waiting-time problems from 0.37 to 0.83 and cuts the median tokens of correct solutions from 10.2k to 6.3k, while worked examples of the same length do not help. The gain shrinks as the solver and its token budget grow (+0.46, +0.26, +0.07), and at a long budget it comes almost entirely from finishing within budget: solutions that finish are correct 98–100% of the time in every condition. To separate induction from recall, we plant unpublished theorems in custom probability families and measure how much of the oracle theory’s gain an induced theory recovers. A strong open model, required to explore the training problems with code before writing, recovers 60% of the gain on one planted family, 48% on a second, and almost none on a third, where it finds the right form but not the condition that makes the form computable. No single induced note is complete, but a strong model that merges several notes recovers 61% of the gain on the classic family, above the best single note (47%). Theories are worth the reasoning they save, and models can find their pieces before they can assemble them. 1 Introduction A student who knows Conway’s leading numbers computes the expected waiting time for a coin pattern in a few lines; a student who does not sets up and solves a linear system over the pattern’s prefixes. Both can be right, but only one is efficient. Large language models (LLMs) increasingly solve such problems with long chains of thought [ 14 ] , and their resource use grows with the reasoning they must produce [ 11 ] . This raises two questions. First, how much is a stated theory worth to an LLM solver: how much accuracy does it add and how much reasoning does it save? Second, can a model induce such a theory from problems alone, so that it uses the compute of discovery once rather than on every problem? Answering either question cleanly is harder than it looks. Adding text to the context changes its length; examples and theory can carry the same information; and a model that “induces” a classic theorem may simply be recalling it. We address these confounds with three design choices. (i) All conditions use contexts of the same length, and we compare the oracle theory with irrelevant text, a generic hint, and worked examples of the same length. (ii) We report the recovery ratio R R , the share of the oracle theory’s accuracy gain that an induced theory recovers. (iii) To separate induction from recall, we plant unpublished theorems in custom probability families, verify that no model can state them before seeing the problems, and only then let models induce theories from training problems. Contributions. • A controlled protocol for measuring the value of a theory in context, with length-matched controls, paired bootstrap intervals and a recovery ratio (Section 2 ). • Evidence that a stated theory makes a solver both more accurate and cheaper, that worked examples do not substitute for it, and that at long budgets its value is almost entirely the reasoning it saves (Sections 3 and 6 ). • A planted-theorem design that separates induction from recall: custom probability families with unpublished theorems that no model can state before seeing the problems, with evidence that a strong open model can induce such theorems when forced to explore with code, and a characterization of how it fails: the right form without the condition, or a special case without the general law (Section 4 ). • Evidence that no single induced theory is complete but that a strong model can merge partial theories from several inducers, without test information, into one that passes our success bar (Section 5 ). 2 Setup 2.1 Problem families Every family has an automatically graded numeric answer, a key theory that makes the problems easy, a generator for fresh parameters, and a solver accuracy without the theory that leaves room for improvement. Table 1 summarizes them. • Family (a): pattern waiting times (classic). Expected waiting times for coin patterns, probabilities that one pattern appears before another, and waiting times for either of two patterns. The key theory is Conway’s overlap numbers and the martingale method [ 5 , 3 ] . Every answer is computed twice, from the overlap numbers and from the pattern automaton, and the two must agree. We use 40 training and 160 test problems at the difficulty where the solver without theory scores 0.38 in calibration. • Family (b): symmetric colouring counts (classic). Counting colourings up to symmetry, with Burnside’s lemma and Pólya enumeration [ 8 ] as the theory; 156 problems, about 20% of them traps. • F1: carry-over rearrangements on a necklace (planted). A ring of L L sites with K K colours. Each window of three sites ( x , y , z ) (x,y,z) moves forward to ( y , z , x ⊕ 1 ) (y,z,x\oplus 1) at rate f ⁡ ( x , y , z ) f(x,y,z) and backward at rate g g , so the chain is not reversible. The planted theorem states that if a weighted flux is constant on every orbit of the window map, the stationary law is a product law with explicit weights. Held-out problems have between 1.4 × 10 7 1.4\times 10^{7} and 3.9 × 10 8 3.9\times 10^{8} states. • F2: carry-over swaps of neighbouring pairs (planted). A pair ( x , y ) (x,y) becomes ( y , x ⊕ 1 ) (y,x\oplus 1) at a rate that also depends on the two outer neighbours. The planted theorem states that if f ⁡ ( u , x , y , v ) ​ M ​ ( u , x ) ​ M ​ ( x , y ) ​ M ​ ( y , v ) f(u,x,y,v)\,M(u,x)M(x,y)M(y,v) is constant on every orbit of the pair map, the stationary law is a nearest-neighbour (transfer-matrix) law π ⁡ ( η ) ∝ ∏ j M ⁡ ( η j , η j + 1 ) \pi(\eta)\propto\prod_{j}M(\eta_{j},\eta_{j+1}) , not a product law. • F3: a random collision process (planted). Pairs of particles of K K kinds collide and either vanish or turn into another pair. The planted theorem states that if weights b b satisfy one linear equation per pair of kinds, the expected total penalty until the box is empty is ∑ c b c ​ n c \sum_{c}b_{c}n_{c} , by optional stopping on a linear potential. For the planted families, the exact solution equals the planted theorem on every verification instance (F2 48/48, F3 48/48), about 20% of held-out problems are traps on which the theorem does not apply, and misapplying the theorem on a trap gives one predictable wrong number, so misapplication is measurable. A planted family is used only if the oracle theory raises held-out accuracy by at least 0.20 in calibration (F2 +0.83, F3 +0.58). As a classic control under the identical planted-family protocol, we also run family (a) (“P5b”). An inducer sees only the training problems and its own solution attempts, may run code on small instances, and writes a theory no longer than the oracle text that states when it applies and contains no answer to a specific problem. In our first protocol, models wrote theories without running any code, and their theories were guesses; even the strong model attempted to write a theory before any exploration in all three runs. Our second protocol, used for all planted-family results, shows the model how to read the data and accepts a theory only after at least three code runs. In family (a), induction instead generates several candidate theories and selects among them on a validation split of the training problems (Appendix D ). Solvers and sampling. Qwen3-14B in thinking mode (temperature 0.6, top- p p 0.95, top- k k 20) is the main solver, at token caps of 12k and 32k; Qwen3.6-27B at 32k and 64k is a second, stronger solver. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2611.34708 (cs) [Submitted on 25 Nov 2026] Title: From Shared Patterns to Individual Evidence: Two-Stage Reasoning for Emerging Entities in Temporal Knowledge Graphs Authors: Jinchuan Zhang , Lei Gao , Hongyu Jiang , Chong Mu , Chenang Cai , Ke Yan View a PDF of the paper titled From Shared Patterns to Individual Evidence: Two-Stage Reasoning for Emerging Entities in Temporal Knowledge Graphs, by Jinchuan Zhang and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) continually introduce emerging entities whose interaction histories evolve from zero-shot debuts into sparse, bursty few-shot trajectories. However, current paradigms are fragmented: pattern-transfer methods lack catalog-wide event memory, whereas online memory models suffer from endpoint-role asymmetry that degrades unseen-answer ranking. Furthermore, sparse early interactions exhibit both long-range dispersion and local redundancy under skewed distribution. To address these challenges, we propose INSPIRE (Integrating Shared Patterns and Individual Evidence for Reasoning), a two-stage forecasting framework over a known catalog. In Stage I, INSPIRE learns an availability-aware shared-pattern predictor that fuses event-updated memory across the full candidate catalog while applying coordinated query- and catalog-side masking. Subsequently, Stage II freezes this predictor and optimizes a lightweight individual-evidence adapter (EA) combining textual semantic priors with correlation-weighted long-range event statistics under support- and role-balanced co-answer supervision with prior-odds debiasing and soft residual alignment. In addition, we decompose evaluation by endpoint roles and track longitudinal emerging-answer cohorts via query-micro and answer-entity macro metrics. Across four benchmarks based on the ICEWS and GDELT event datasets, INSPIRE improves Emerging MRR by 16.73%-88.83% over the strongest baselines. Relative to paired Stage I predictors, EA further increases Emerging MRR by 8.28%-32.63%, Answer-new MRR by 7.81%-41.24%, and cohort macro MRR by 9.64%-39.94%, gains attributed to semantic priors and candidate-level score competition suppressing mismatched established competitors without zero-support prior shortcuts. The official code is publicly available at this https URL . Abstract. Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) continually introduce emerging entities whose interaction histories evolve from zero-shot debuts into sparse, bursty few-shot trajectories. However, current paradigms are fragmented: pattern transfer methods lack catalog-wide event memory, whereas online memory models suffer from endpoint role asymmetry that degrades unseen answer ranking. Furthermore, sparse early interactions exhibit both long-range dispersion and local redundancy under skewed distribution. To address these challenges, we propose INSPIRE ( Integrating Shared Patterns and Individual Evidence for Reasoning ), a two-stage forecasting framework over a known catalog. In Stage I, INSPIRE learns an availability-aware shared-pattern predictor that fuses event-updated memory across the full candidate catalog while applying coordinated query-side and catalog-side masking. Subsequently, Stage II freezes this predictor and optimizes a lightweight evidence adapter ( EA ) combining textual semantic priors with correlation-weighted long-range event statistics under support-stratified and role-balanced co-answer supervision with prior-odds debiasing and soft residual alignment. In addition, we decompose evaluation by endpoint roles and track longitudinal emerging-answer cohorts via query micro and answer entity macro metrics. Across four benchmarks based on the ICEWS and GDELT event datasets, INSPIRE improves Emerging MRR by 16.73 % 16.73\% – 88.83 % 88.83\% over the strongest baselines. Relative to paired Stage I predictors, EA further increases Emerging MRR by 8.28 % 8.28\% – 32.63 % 32.63\% , Answer-new MRR by 7.81 % 7.81\% – 41.24 % 41.24\% , and cohort macro MRR by 9.64 % 9.64\% – 39.94 % 39.94\% , gains attributed to semantic priors and candidate score competition suppressing mismatched established competitors without zero-support prior shortcuts. The official code is publicly available at https://github.com/KcAcoZhang/INSPIRE . PVLDB Reference Format: Jinchuan Zhang, Lei Gao, Hongyu Jiang, Chong Mu, Chenang Cai, and Ke Yan. PVLDB, 20(1): XXX-XXX, 2027. doi:XX.XX/XXX.XX † † This work is licensed under the Creative Commons BY-NC-ND 4.0 International License. Visit https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/ to view a copy of this license. For any use beyond those covered by this license, obtain permission by emailing info@vldb.org . Copyright is held by the owner/author(s). Publication rights licensed to the VLDB Endowment. Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment, Vol. 20, No. 1 ISSN 2150-8097. doi:XX.XX/XXX.XX 1. Introduction Real-world relational event streams, ranging from geopolitical repositories such as ICEWS and GDELT to evolving distributed graph systems, are modeled as temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) of timestamped quadruples ( h , r , o , t ) (h,r,o,t) ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Tian et al., 2021 ; Tian et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2022 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . Temporal extrapolation forecasts future links ( h , r , ? , t ) (h,r,?,t) from strictly past facts prior to t t by ranking candidate entities across a catalog ( Jin et al., 2020 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . While recent models capture snapshot evolution, multigraph dependencies, logical rules, and histories relevant to the query ( Jin et al., 2020 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) , continuous streams constantly introduce new actors whose histories are initially absent and accumulate sparsely ( Wang et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2023b ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . Consequently, forecasting in dynamic streams hinges on the few-shot temporal reasoning problem: predicting reliably over entities that transition from zero-shot debuts to sparse, unevenly observed trajectories. Empirical profiling across four standard benchmarks exposes a sharp structural tension, as illustrated in Figure 1 (c) (with complete statistics in the supplemental material). At the identity level, entities first observed during the test interval constitute 13.33 % 13.33\% – 25.20 % 25.20\% of test-active actors; however, at the traffic level, queries touching a zero-support endpoint represent only 0.166 % 0.166\% – 4.54 % 4.54\% of evaluated queries. Furthermore, emergence extends well beyond an entity’s first appearance: on ICEWS05–15, 83.32 % 83.32\% of test queries targeting test-emergent answer entities occur after debut under limited positive support, whereas on ICEWS18 70.35 % 70.35\% remain at zero support. Hence, emerging-entity reasoning spans a continuous spectrum from zero-shot priors to sparse few-shot evidence. To illustrate this dilemma concretely, Figure 1 (a)–(b) tracks the emerging entity Takata in ICEWS14, which is preregistered in the candidate catalog with textual metadata prior to its first recorded interaction ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . At its debut ( t = 310 t=310 ), Takata has zero graph history ( n o = 0 n_{o}=0 ). Whereas querying an unseen head can transfer interaction patterns from semantically related actors, ranking Takata as the ground-truth answer to ( Newspaper ( Japan ), Make statement , ?, 310 310 ) requires it to outrank thousands of richly observed catalog competitors. Subsequently, before the follow-up query ( Japan , Make statement , ?, 332 332 ), Takata accumulates only six sparse facts spanning t = 310 t=310 – 330 330 : two early isolated interactions ( t = 310,317 t=310,317 ), an independent statement from Jay Rockefeller ( t = 328 t=328 ), and repeated contacts from the U.S. government including two identical Demand events ( t = 323,330 t=323,330 ). Because short sliding windows discard those earlier sparse facts while independent aggregation overcounts the repeated demands, both heuristics skew Takata ’s latent state. Figure 1. Motivation from emergence events across ICEWS and GDELT benchmarks: (a) C1 zero-support debut ( t = 310 t=310 ) competing against richly observed actors; (b) C2 sparse early facts ( t = 310,317 t=310,317 ), correlated U.S. Gov repeats ( t = 323,330 t=323,330 ), and an independent partner ( t = 328 t=328 ); (c) C3 identity–traffic skew and debut vs. post-debut cohort splits. Three stacked panels illustrating challenges C1, C2, and C3 using the ICEWS14 Takata entity trajectory and four-benchmark statistics. However, existing temporal inductive methods address only isolated ends of this continuum. Pattern transfer models such as TransFIR ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) map unseen entities to semantic interaction clusters at debut, yet omit event-updated candidate memory across the catalog. In contrast, online memory models such as AdaTKG ( Lee et al., 2026 ) update per-entity exponential moving average (EMA) states, yet exhibit pronounced endpoint role asymmetry: across all four benchmarks ( Table 3 ), AdaTKG improves unseen query prediction (Query-new) over TransFIR while consistently degrading unseen answer ranking (Answer-new), dropping by 57.6 % 57.6\% on GDELT ( 0.0801 → 0.0340 0.0801\to 0.0340 ). Therefore, bridging shared patterns with individual evidence requires resolving three coupled challenges: C1: Heterogeneous history availability and role asymmetry. Within any timestamp batch, query heads and catalog candidates span zero-support newcomers and mature actors. Restricting memory readout to active query heads leaves competing candidates misaligned, whereas naive memory fusion causes excessive reliance on history when observations are absent. C2: Long-range sparsity versus bursty evidence redundancy. Early interactions are simultaneously sparse across long temporal spans and correlated within short bursts. Updating a high-capacity pattern encoder with sparse gradients risks overfitting; conversely, independent aggregation lets repetitive bursts overwhelm informative facts. C3: Long-tail supervision dilution and micro-averaged evaluation. Since low-support queries occupy a small fraction of natural batches, standard cross-entropy is dominated by high-support entities and neglects asymmetric endpoint roles (Query-new, Answer-new, Both-new). In addition, conventional micro averaging over queries masks systematic errors on infrequent emerging identities. To address the aforementioned challenges, we propose INSPIRE ( Integrating Shared Patterns and Individual Evidence for Reasoning ), a two-stage framework decoupling low-variance shared-pattern learning from lightweight posterior refinement for individual entities. In Stage I, INSPIRE learns an availability-aware shared-pattern predictor that fuses event-updated memory across the entire candidate catalog, inclusive of non-query candidates, while applying coupled query-side and catalog-side availability masking during training ( C1 ). Subsequently, in Stage II, we freeze the Stage I predictor to prevent sparse overfitting and train a lightweight Evidence Adaptation ( EA ) module. Specifically, EA combines a textual semantic prior with bounded long-range evidence over the full revealed prefix, discounts bursty redundancy via a descriptor Gram matrix covariance model, and adds a strictly positively scaled translational Gaussian compatibility residual to full-catalog scores ( C2 ). Stage II is trained offline under support-stratified and role-balanced co-answer supervision equipped with training-only prior-odds debiasing across support buckets and soft residual alignment to prevent prior shortcuts induced by balanced losses, whereas evaluation drops the training bias, keeps parameters frozen, and updates persistent states strictly after each timestamp is scored ( C3 ). Across ICEWS14, ICEWS18, ICEWS05–15, and GDELT, INSPIRE attains Emerging MRRs of 0.2264 0.2264 , 0.1877 0.1877 , 0.2587 0.2587 , and 0.1623 0.1623 , improving over the strongest baseline by 34.48 % 34.48\% , 32.15 % 32.15\% , 16.73 % 16.73\% , and 88.83 % 88.83\% . Relative to paired Stage I predictors ( INSPIRE w/o EA ), EA further increases Emerging MRR by 8.28 % 8.28\% – 32.63 % 32.63\% , Query-new MRR by 9.29 % 9.29\% – 21.94 % 21.94\% , and cohort macro MRR by 9.64 % 9.64\% – 39.94 % 39.94\% , while also improving overall test MRR on every dataset. Notably, EA achieves substantial calibrated gains ( + 7.81 % +7.81\% – + 41.24 % +41.24\% ) on Answer-new queries where the true answer has zero prior events. Nevertheless, our functional decomposition resolves this apparent paradox, showing that these gains are attributed jointly to the learned semantic prior and candidate score competition, whereby correlated posterior updates demote mismatched established competitors without inflating a blanket zero-support bias. Our contributions are threefold: (1) Availability-aware shared-pattern learning. We formulate emerging-entity reasoning across the continuum from zero-shot to few-shot reasoning and introduce catalog-wide gated memory fusion with coordinated query-side and catalog-side masking to resolve role asymmetry. (2) Correlated Bayesian evidence adaptation. We build a lightweight residual adapter over a frozen predictor combining textual priors, bounded long-range queues, and Gram matrix correlation weighting with balanced supervision. (3) Longitudinal evaluation and mechanism dissection. We evaluate endpoint roles and emerging-answer cohorts via micro and entity macro metrics on four event benchmarks, isolating how candidate competition drives zero-support gains. 2. Problem Formulation 2.1. Temporal Extrapolation for Emerging Entities A TKG is an event stream ℱ ⊆ ℰ × ℛ × ℰ × 𝒯 \mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{R}\times\mathcal{E}\times\mathcal{T} , where ℰ \mathcal{E} , ℛ \mathcal{R} , and 𝒯 \mathcal{T} denote the entity catalog, relation set, and ordered timestamp set. Each quadruple ( h , r , o , t ) ∈ ℱ (h,r,o,t)\in\mathcal{F} records an interaction from head h h to tail o o under relation r r at timestamp t t . Let ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} collect facts at timestamp t t and ℋ < t = ⋃ τ < t ℱ τ \mathcal{H}_{<t}=\bigcup_{\tau<t}\mathcal{F}_{\tau} denote the strictly past revealed prefix. Consistent problem boundary. Following the standard emerging-entity benchmark of TransFIR ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) and AdaTKG ( Lee et al., 2026 ) , we retain original timestamps split chronologically into training ( 50 % 50\% ), validation ( 20 % 20\% ), and test ( 30 % 30\% ) intervals, with candidate catalog ℰ \mathcal{E} and fixed textual vectors { x e } e ∈ ℰ \{x_{e}\}_{e\in\mathcal{E}} available prior to an entity’s first interaction ( emergence ). At each timestamp t t , every fact ( h , r , o , t ) ∈ ℱ t (h,r,o,t)\in\mathcal{F}_{t} forms a forward tail query ( h , r , ? , t ) (h,r,?,t) (answer o o ) and an inverse head query ( o , r − 1 , ? , t ) (o,r^{-1},?,t) (answer h h ). Let ℬ t d \mathcal{B}_{t}^{d} denote the directional query batch for d ∈ { fwd , inv } d\in\{\mathrm{fwd},\mathrm{inv}\} and 𝒰 t d = { h : ( h , r , t ) ∈ ℬ t d } \mathcal{U}_{t}^{d}=\{h:(h,r,t)\in\mathcal{B}_{t}^{d}\} its active query heads. Accordingly, both directions are scored over the full catalog ℰ \mathcal{E} using only ( h , r , t ) ∈ ℬ t d (h,r,t)\in\mathcal{B}_{t}^{d} , 𝒰 t d \mathcal{U}_{t}^{d} , and ℋ < t \mathcal{H}_{<t} strictly before ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} is revealed; labels are used exclusively for training losses or ranking after scoring. During evaluation, learned parameters remain frozen while revealed events ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} subsequently advance persistent states for future timestamps, and raw full-catalog bidirectional ranks are computed under the released history construction pipeline ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) across all comparators. 2.2. Evaluation Protocol To trace entities from zero-shot debut through sparse few-shot evolution, we define the observed support of entity e ∈ ℰ e\in\mathcal{E} before timestamp t t as (1) n e ( t ) = ∑ ( h , r , o , τ ) ∈ ℋ < t [ e ∈ { h , o } ] , n_{e}(t)=\sum_{(h,r,o,\tau)\in\mathcal{H}_{<t}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[e\in\{h,o\}\right], counting distinct original incident facts strictly before t t (self-loops count once, whereas inverse queries add no observations). Hence, n e ​ ( t ) n_{e}(t) reflects lifetime revealed support independently of finite model history windows. Asymmetric endpoint roles. Queries touching at least one zero-support endpoint decompose into three disjoint roles: (1) Query-new ( n h ​ ( t ) = 0 , n o ​ ( t ) > 0 n_{h}(t)=0,\ n_{o}(t)>0 ): an unobserved query head predicts an established answer; (2) Answer-new ( n h ​ ( t ) > 0 , n o ​ ( t ) = 0 n_{h}(t)>0,\ n_{o}(t)=0 ): an established head ranks an unobserved answer over ℰ \mathcal{E} ; and (3) Both-new ( n h ​ ( t ) = 0 , n o ​ ( t ) = 0 n_{h}(t)=0,\ n_{o}(t)=0 ): both endpoints have zero prior support. Their union defines the Emerging query set. Abstract. Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) continually introduce emerging entities whose interaction histories evolve from zero-shot debuts into sparse, bursty few-shot trajectories. However, current paradigms are fragmented: pattern transfer methods lack catalog-wide event memory, whereas online memory models suffer from endpoint role asymmetry that degrades unseen answer ranking. Furthermore, sparse early interactions exhibit both long-range dispersion and local redundancy under skewed distribution. To address these challenges, we propose INSPIRE ( Integrating Shared Patterns and Individual Evidence for Reasoning ), a two-stage forecasting framework over a known catalog. In Stage I, INSPIRE learns an availability-aware shared-pattern predictor that fuses event-updated memory across the full candidate catalog while applying coordinated query-side and catalog-side masking. Subsequently, Stage II freezes this predictor and optimizes a lightweight evidence adapter ( EA ) combining textual semantic priors with correlation-weighted long-range event statistics under support-stratified and role-balanced co-answer supervision with prior-odds debiasing and soft residual alignment. In addition, we decompose evaluation by endpoint roles and track longitudinal emerging-answer cohorts via query micro and answer entity macro metrics. Across four benchmarks based on the ICEWS and GDELT event datasets, INSPIRE improves Emerging MRR by 16.73 % 16.73\% – 88.83 % 88.83\% over the strongest baselines. Relative to paired Stage I predictors, EA further increases Emerging MRR by 8.28 % 8.28\% – 32.63 % 32.63\% , Answer-new MRR by 7.81 % 7.81\% – 41.24 % 41.24\% , and cohort macro MRR by 9.64 % 9.64\% – 39.94 % 39.94\% , gains attributed to semantic priors and candidate score competition suppressing mismatched established competitors without zero-support prior shortcuts. Introduction Real-world relational event streams, ranging from geopolitical repositories such as ICEWS and GDELT to evolving distributed graph systems, are modeled as temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) of timestamped quadruples ( h , r , o , t ) (h,r,o,t) ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Tian et al., 2021 ; Tian et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2022 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . Temporal extrapolation forecasts future links ( h , r , ? , t ) (h,r,?,t) from strictly past facts prior to t t by ranking candidate entities across a catalog ( Jin et al., 2020 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . While recent models capture snapshot evolution, multigraph dependencies, logical rules, and histories relevant to the query ( Jin et al., 2020 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) , continuous streams constantly introduce new actors whose histories are initially absent and accumulate sparsely ( Wang et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2023b ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . Consequently, forecasting in dynamic streams hinges on the few-shot temporal reasoning problem: predicting reliably over entities that transition from zero-shot debuts to sparse, unevenly observed trajectories. Empirical profiling across four standard benchmarks exposes a sharp structural tension, as illustrated in Figure 1 (c) (with complete statistics in the supplemental material). At the identity level, entities first observed during the test interval constitute 13.33 % 13.33\% – 25.20 % 25.20\% of test-active actors; however, at the traffic level, queries touching a zero-support endpoint represent only 0.166 % 0.166\% – 4.54 % 4.54\% of evaluated queries. Furthermore, emergence extends well beyond an entity’s first appearance: on ICEWS05–15, 83.32 % 83.32\% of test queries targeting test-emergent answer entities occur after debut under limited positive support, whereas on ICEWS18 70.35 % 70.35\% remain at zero support. Hence, emerging-entity reasoning spans a continuous spectrum from zero-shot priors to sparse few-shot evidence. To illustrate this dilemma concretely, Figure 1 (a)–(b) tracks the emerging entity Takata in ICEWS14, which is preregistered in the candidate catalog with textual metadata prior to its first recorded interaction ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . At its debut ( t = 310 t=310 ), Takata has zero graph history ( n o = 0 n_{o}=0 ). Whereas querying an unseen head can transfer interaction patterns from semantically related actors, ranking Takata as the ground-truth answer to ( Newspaper ( Japan ), Make statement , ?, 310 310 ) requires it to outrank thousands of richly observed catalog competitors. Subsequently, before the follow-up query ( Japan , Make statement , ?, 332 332 ), Takata accumulates only six sparse facts spanning t = 310 t=310 – 330 330 : two early isolated interactions ( t = 310,317 t=310,317 ), an independent statement from Jay Rockefeller ( t = 328 t=328 ), and repeated contacts from the U.S. government including two identical Demand events ( t = 323,330 t=323,330 ). Because short sliding windows discard those earlier sparse facts while independent aggregation overcounts the repeated demands, both heuristics skew Takata ’s latent state. Figure 1. Motivation from emergence events across ICEWS and GDELT benchmarks: (a) C1 zero-support debut ( t = 310 t=310 ) competing against richly observed actors; (b) C2 sparse early facts ( t = 310,317 t=310,317 ), correlated U.S. Gov repeats ( t = 323,330 t=323,330 ), and an independent partner ( t = 328 t=328 ); (c) C3 identity–traffic skew and debut vs. post-debut cohort splits. Three stacked panels illustrating challenges C1, C2, and C3 using the ICEWS14 Takata entity trajectory and four-benchmark statistics. However, existing temporal inductive methods address only isolated ends of this continuum. Pattern transfer models such as TransFIR ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) map unseen entities to semantic interaction clusters at debut, yet omit event-updated candidate memory across the catalog. In contrast, online memory models such as AdaTKG ( Lee et al., 2026 ) update per-entity exponential moving average (EMA) states, yet exhibit pronounced endpoint role asymmetry: across all four benchmarks ( Table 3 ), AdaTKG improves unseen query prediction (Query-new) over TransFIR while consistently degrading unseen answer ranking (Answer-new), dropping by 57.6 % 57.6\% on GDELT ( 0.0801 → 0.0340 0.0801\to 0.0340 ). Therefore, bridging shared patterns with individual evidence requires resolving three coupled challenges: C1: Heterogeneous history availability and role asymmetry. Within any timestamp batch, query heads and catalog candidates span zero-support newcomers and mature actors. Restricting memory readout to active query heads leaves competing candidates misaligned, whereas naive memory fusion causes excessive reliance on history when observations are absent. C2: Long-range sparsity versus bursty evidence redundancy. Early interactions are simultaneously sparse across long temporal spans and correlated within short bursts. Updating a high-capacity pattern encoder with sparse gradients risks overfitting; conversely, independent aggregation lets repetitive bursts overwhelm informative facts. C3: Long-tail supervision dilution and micro-averaged evaluation. Since low-support queries occupy a small fraction of natural batches, standard cross-entropy is dominated by high-support entities and neglects asymmetric endpoint roles (Query-new, Answer-new, Both-new). In addition, conventional micro averaging over queries masks systematic errors on infrequent emerging identities. To address the aforementioned challenges, we propose INSPIRE ( Integrating Shared Patterns and Individual Evidence for Reasoning ), a two-stage framework decoupling low-variance shared-pattern learning from lightweight posterior refinement for individual entities. In Stage I, INSPIRE learns an availability-aware shared-pattern predictor that fuses event-updated memory across the entire candidate catalog, inclusive of non-query candidates, while applying coupled query-side and catalog-side availability masking during training ( C1 ). Subsequently, in Stage II, we freeze the Stage I predictor to prevent sparse overfitting and train a lightweight Evidence Adaptation ( EA ) module. Specifically, EA combines a textual semantic prior with bounded long-range evidence over the full revealed prefix, discounts bursty redundancy via a descriptor Gram matrix covariance model, and adds a strictly positively scaled translational Gaussian compatibility residual to full-catalog scores ( C2 ). Stage II is trained offline under support-stratified and role-balanced co-answer supervision equipped with training-only prior-odds debiasing across support buckets and soft residual alignment to prevent prior shortcuts induced by balanced losses, whereas evaluation drops the training bias, keeps parameters frozen, and updates persistent states strictly after each timestamp is scored ( C3 ). Across ICEWS14, ICEWS18, ICEWS05–15, and GDELT, INSPIRE attains Emerging MRRs of 0.2264 0.2264 , 0.1877 0.1877 , 0.2587 0.2587 , and 0.1623 0.1623 , improving over the strongest baseline by 34.48 % 34.48\% , 32.15 % 32.15\% , 16.73 % 16.73\% , and 88.83 % 88.83\% . Relative to paired Stage I predictors ( INSPIRE w/o EA ), EA further increases Emerging MRR by 8.28 % 8.28\% – 32.63 % 32.63\% , Query-new MRR by 9.29 % 9.29\% – 21.94 % 21.94\% , and cohort macro MRR by 9.64 % 9.64\% – 39.94 % 39.94\% , while also improving overall test MRR on every dataset. Notably, EA achieves substantial calibrated gains ( + 7.81 % +7.81\% – + 41.24 % +41.24\% ) on Answer-new queries where the true answer has zero prior events. Nevertheless, our functional decomposition resolves this apparent paradox, showing that these gains are attributed jointly to the learned semantic prior and candidate score competition, whereby correlated posterior updates demote mismatched established competitors without inflating a blanket zero-support bias. Our contributions are threefold: (1) Availability-aware shared-pattern learning. We formulate emerging-entity reasoning across the continuum from zero-shot to few-shot reasoning and introduce catalog-wide gated memory fusion with coordinated query-side and catalog-side masking to resolve role asymmetry. (2) Correlated Bayesian evidence adaptation. We build a lightweight residual adapter over a frozen predictor combining textual priors, bounded long-range queues, and Gram matrix correlation weighting with balanced supervision. (3) Longitudinal evaluation and mechanism dissection. We evaluate endpoint roles and emerging-answer cohorts via micro and entity macro metrics on four event benchmarks, isolating how candidate competition drives zero-support gains. 2. From February 18, 2002, to February 9, 2006, the U.S. Treasury published a factor for adjusting the daily nominal 20-year constant maturity in order to estimate a 30-year nominal rate. The historical adjustment factor can be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . Source: U.S. Treasury. 10. Yields on Treasury inflation protected securities (TIPS) adjusted to constant maturities. Source: U.S. Treasury. Note: Current and historical H.15 data, along with weekly, monthly, and annual averages, are available on the Board's Data Download Program (DDP) at www.federalreserve.gov/datadownload/Choose.aspx?rel=H15 ). Weekly, monthly and annual rates are averages of business days unless otherwise noted. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: November 25, 2026 Back to Top

The 1-, 2-, and 3-month rates are equivalent to the 30-, 60-, and 90-day dates reported on the Board's Commercial Paper Web page ( www.federalreserve.gov/releases/cp/ ). 6. Financial paper that is insured by the FDIC's Temporary Liquidity Guarantee Program is not excluded from relevant indexes, nor is any financial or nonfinancial commercial paper that may be directly or indirectly affected by one or more of the Federal Reserve's liquidity facilities. Thus the rates published after September 19, 2008, likely reflect the direct or indirect effects of the new temporary programs and, accordingly, likely are not comparable for some purposes to rates published prior to that period. 7. Rate posted by a majority of top 25 (by assets in domestic offices) insured U.S.-chartered commercial banks. Prime is one of several base rates used by banks to price short-term business loans. 8. The rate charged for discounts made and advances extended under the Federal Reserve's primary credit discount window program, which became effective January 9, 2003. This rate replaces that for adjustment credit, which was discontinued after January 8, 2003. For further information, see www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/press/bcreg/2002/200210312/default.htm . The rate reported is that for the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Historical series for the rate on adjustment credit as well as the rate on primary credit are available at www.federalreserve.gov/releases/h15/data.htm . 9. Yields on actively traded non-inflation-indexed issues adjusted to constant maturities. The 30-year Treasury constant maturity series was discontinued on February 18, 2002, and reintroduced on February 9, 2006. From February 18, 2002, to February 9, 2006, the U.S. Treasury published a factor for adjusting the daily nominal 20-year constant maturity in order to estimate a 30-year nominal rate. The historical adjustment factor can be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . Source: U.S. Treasury. 10. Yields on Treasury inflation protected securities (TIPS) adjusted to constant maturities. Source: U.S. Treasury. Additional information on both nominal and inflation-indexed yields may be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . 11. Based on the unweighted average bid yields for all TIPS with remaining terms to maturity of more than 10 years. Note: Current and historical H.15 data, along with weekly, monthly, and annual averages, are available on the Board's Data Download Program (DDP) at www.federalreserve.gov/datadownload/Choose.aspx?rel=H15 ). Weekly, monthly and annual rates are averages of business days unless otherwise noted. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: November 25, 2026 Back to Top
